full_judgment:
Mainur Reza Chowdhury J: By this Rule Nisi the respondents were called upon to show cause as to why the impugned order as contained in case No. 9-24/94-764/1(4) dated 29-1l-84 (Annexure) issued by respondent No. 1 should not be declared to have been made without lawful authority and is of no legal effect.

2. The case of the petitioner, in short, is as follows:

The petitioner and his grand-parents were originally residents of Mouza Rohai Ramnagar, PS Sadarpur District Faridpur. His grandfather Babar Ali Sheikh along with others had lands and homesteads in Mouza Rabairamnagar, PS Bhanga (now Sadarpur), District Faridpur. Due to erosion of the river Padma the lands and homestead of the petitioner and other co-villagers were diluviated and went under water in 1947. So they shifted their residence and settled in Mouza Charbhadrason, Kallyanpur, etc. within the district of Faridpur in 1948. When the lands appeared the petitioner and other co-villagers took settlement from the Government and the usufruct thereof. Due to subsequent erosion the petitioner and co-villagers Shifted their homestead to Jhaukanda, Char Kurulla,Char Deaobhet, Char Hatni, Partuil, etc. within the Dohar Police Station in the district of Dhaka in 1956 and took lands from the old tenants by purchase and took permanent settlement from the Government and have been residing there with their families and became inhabitants of Dohar Police Station in the district of Dhaka. Due to erosion of the river Padma they shifted their residence in the interior side of the Dohar Police Station in 1991 and the petitioner purchased 6.14 acres of land from the recorded tenants Nuni Gopal Gopini and others on 24-1-1977 appertaining to SA Khatian Nos. 144, 206, 380 of Plot No. 332, 832 and 396 Mouza Kartickpur within PS Dohar, district Dhaka. The petitioner filed a Civil suit being Title Suit No. 19 of 1984 in the Court of Assistant Judge Dohar, Dhaka against Nuni Gopal Gopini and others for specific performance of Contract and the said suit was decreed in favour of the petitioner on 3-2-1987 and in execution of the decree in Title Execution Case No. 2 of 1987 the petitioner got the deed registered through Civil Court being Deed No. 2419 dated 16-11-1991. The aforesaid lands of the petitioner was again diluviated and went under the water of river Padma in 1992. The lands of the petitioner and other co- villagers of Mouza Charbhadrason, PS Char Bhadrason District Faridpur were diluviated and went under water due to erosion of the river Padma and subsequently appeared and reformed in situ and the petitioner and other co-villagers took settlement from the Government and paid rents, Thereafter again the lands was diluviated and went under water in 1991. This way the petitioner was affected by diluvion of his lands 11 times and lastly, in 1991-1992 when the aforesaid mentioned land was diluviated in the district of Faridpur and in Dohar PS District Dhaka.

3. The petitioner has given a short background of the law relating to diluvion land alluvion of lands By the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (EB Act No. XXVIII of 1951) the rent-receivers intervening between the Government and the actual occupants of the said land were abolished and such occupants became tenants directly under the Government, subject to a ceiling as to the maximum area of land which a tenant could hold. No substantial charge with regard to this law as to accretion or reformation in situ was brought about by this enactment excepting the law of accretion (which was so long regulated by the provisions of Bengal Regulation XXI of 1825) was made in section 87 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The provisions relating to abatement of rent due to diluvion of some land of the tenancy and subsistence of the tenant's title in respect of such land, similar to those contained in section 86(A) of the Bengal Tenancy Act and section 86 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Section 86 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 provides for abatement of rent on account of diluvion and re-entry into lands which re-appear, Time to time the law relating to the tenant's fight on his diluviated land were passed. On 13-7-1994 the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act (Amendment) Act, 1994 (Act No. 15 of 1994) was promulgated substituting in place of the old section 86 with regard to abatement of rent on account of diluvion and determination of right in land reappearing on account of alluvion. By the said Act the right, title and interest of the original tenant or his successor-in-interest would subsist in the lands of a holding or portion thereof during the period of loss by diluvion if such lands re-appeared in situ within thirty years of their loss instead of 20 years. The respondent No. 1 by the impugned order as contained in letter No ML/S-9-24/94-764/1(40) dated 29-11-1994 issued to all the Deputy Commissioners of the districts containing guidelines for implementation of the State Acquisition and Tenancy (Amendment) Act, 1994 and directing them to take necessary steps for processing the diluvion and reformation of land. By the said impugned order it was directed that all land already diluviated and alluviated shall vest in the Government as the said Act dated 13th July, 1994 was prospective and not retrospective. The petitioner is aggrieved by the circular because it is not in accordance with the State Acquisition and Tenancy (amendment) Act of 1994 and by the said circular his subsisting right on the lands diluviated in 1991 and 1992 in the district of Faridpur and in Dohar Police Station, District Dhaka has been taken away, and is therefore, constrained to file this writ petition challenging the validity of the impugned order (Annexure 'D').

4. The question before us is, whether the petitioners right on his lands diluviated in 1991 and 1992 subsists under the State Acquisition and Tenancy (amendment) Act, 1994. It may be convenient to quote the relevant portion of the laws passed at different times with regard to the abatement of rent, right, title and interest of the owner on diluvion and alluvion of his land. By the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 the rent was abated and the right, title and interest of the owner to diluvion subsisted for 20 years under section 86 of the said Act which reads as follows:

Abatement of rent on account of diluvion and extinguishment of right, title and interest of the tenant thereto-86(1) if the lands of a holding or a portion of such lands are lost by diluvion, the rent of the holding shall, on application made by the tenant in the prescribed form to the Revenue-Officer, be abated by such amount as may be considered by the Revenue-Officer to be fair and equitable in accordance with the rule made in his behalf by the Provincial Government.

2) Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, the right, title and interest of the tenant or his successor-in-interest shall subsist in such lands or portion thereof during the period of loss by diluvion, not exceeding twenty years, whether partly before and partly after or wholly after the commencement of this Order and the tenant or his successors-in-interest shall have the right to immediate re-possession on the re-appearance of such lands or portion thereof within twenty years of their loss by diluvion, and be liable to pay such fair and equitable rent in respect thereof as may be settled by the Revenue-Officer:

Section 86 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 was amended by President's Order No.135 of 1972. The rent abated. The right, title and interest of tenant extinguished whether loss was due to diluvion before or after commencement of said order. The relevant portion of the Bangladesh State Acquisition and Tenancy Act (4th Amendment) Order 1972 President's Order No. 135 of 1972. President Order No. 135 of 1972 by Article 2 provided as follows:

2. In the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (EB XXVIII of 1951), hereinafter referred to as the said Act for section 86 the following shall be substituted, namely:

86(1) If the lands of a holding or a portion of such lands are lost by diluvion, the rent of the holing shall be abated by such amount as may be considered by the Revenue Officer to be fair and equitable in accordance with the rule made in this behalf by the Government.

(2) Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, the right, title and interest of the tenant or his successors-in-interest shall be extinguished in such lands or a portion thereof, whether the loss of such lands or portion by diluvion took or takes place before or after the commencement of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act (Fourth Amendment) Order, 1972.

(3) All lands, so lost by diluvion under sub-section (2), which re-appeared before the date of amendment of the said order, but in respect of which the right of the tenant, whose land was so lost or his successors-in-interest, to re-possession was not finally recognised or declared by a competent authority or Court under any law for the time being in force and also all lands, so lost by diluvion under the said sub-section, which may re-appear on or after the said date, shall vest absolutely in the Government free from all encumbrances shall be at its disposal.

(1) Notwithstanding anything contained elsewhere in this Act, in making settlement of any land vested in the Government under sub-section (3), preference shall be given to a person who has been affected by diluvion provided the total quantity of land, if any, already held by him and the other members of his family is less than twenty-five standard big has".

5. By Ordinance LXI of 1975 section 86 (4) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 was further amended. By this amendment it provides that in making the settlement of any land vested in the Government under sub-section(3), preference would be given to the person or his successors-in-interest who, immediately before loss by diluvion, was owner of such land, subject to the condition that if the land re-appears within 20 years.

Section 2 of the said Ordinance reads as follows:

"In the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (EB Act XXVIII of 1951) in section 86, for sub-section (4) the following shall be substituted, namely, "(1) Notwithstanding anything contained elsewhere in this Act, in making settlement of any land vested in Government under sub section (3), preference shall be given to the person or his successor-in-interest who, immediately before loss by diluvion, was owner of such land, subject to the condition that such land or portion thereof reappears within twenty years from the date of such loss:"

6. Lastly, by the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act (Amendment) Act 1994 (Act XV of 1994) section 86 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 was again amended whereby the rent abated The right, title and interest of the owner subsists for 30 years. It provided for the right of Collector to possess the land immediately upon reappearance and publication of notice, survey, map and allotment to tenant, the amendment of section 86 by Act XV of 1994 reads as follows:

"86 Abatement of rent on account of diluvion and determination of right in land re-appeared on account of alluvion (I) If the lands of a holding or a portion of such lands are lost by diluvion, the rent or the land development tax of holding shall, on application or intimation made by the tenant in the prescribed form to the Revenue Officer, be abated by such amount as may be considered by the Revenue Officer to be fair and equitable in accordance with the Rule made in this behalf by the Government and the act of such loss by diluvion shall be recorded in accordance with such rules, which shall be treated as proof of title to the lands when the same re-appear in situ.

(2) Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, the right, title and interest of the original tenant or his successor-in-interest shall subsist in the lands of a holding or portion thereof during the period of loss by diluvion if such lands re-appear in situ within thirty years of their loss."

(3) Notwithstanding the right, title and interest under sub-section (2), the right to immediate possession of the lands re-appeared shall first be exercised by the Collector, either on his own motion or on intimation made in writing by the tenant or his successors-in-interest whose land was so lost or by any other person.

(4) Notwithstanding anything, contained elsewhere in this Act, the Collection or the Revenue Officer shall, on taking possession of such land, give public notice of the fact of his taking possession in accordance with the rules made in this behalf by the Government and cause a survey to be made of the lands so re-appeared and prepare maps thereof:

(5) The Collector shall, within 45 days of the completion of survey and preparation of map under sub-section (4), allot to the tenant whose lands was so lost by diluvion or, as the case may be, to his successors-in-interest, shall not exceed sixty standard bighas and the excess land of the tenant or his successors-in-interest, if any, after the allotment shall vest in and be at the disposal of the Government."

7. The petitioner's case is that by the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1994 (Act XV of 1995) the right, title and interest in his land lost by diluvion in 1991 and 1992 has been restored and on its re-appearance he is entitled to get its allotment subject to ceiling imposed by the Act as tenant of the land. If the impugned order is not interfered with his right of ownership which has been restored by the Act, 1994 will be taken away. It is submitted that the respondent has misconstrued both the provisions of President's Order No. 135 of 1972 and the Act of 1994 which amended section 86 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act of 1950. The respondent has illegally notified that the State Acquisition and Tenancy Amendment Act, 1994 is effective from 13th July, 1994 that the right, title and interest of all lands which had diluviated or alluviated prior to that date i.e. 13th July, 1994 will vest in the Government and that the said Act of 1994 will be applicable only to dilluvion and alluvion of land after 13th July, 1994 i.e. the Act is retrospective and not re-prospective. It may be convenient to quote the impugned order Annexure 'D' to see whether it has been passed in accordance with law.

The State Acquisition & Tenancy (Amendment) Act, 1994

“সংসদ কর্তক গৃহীত আইনটি ১৩ই জুলাই তারিখে মহামান্য রাষ্ট্রপতির সম্মতি লাভ করেছে এবং বাংলাদেশ গেজেট প্রকজাশিত হয়েছে। উক্ত তারিখ থেকে আইনটি কার্যকর বলে গন্য করতে হবে। তাই ১৩ই জুলাই/৯৪ এর পূর্বদিন পর্যন্ত সে সমস্ত জসি সিকস্তি/পয়স্তি হয়েছে ঐ জমির ক্ষেত্রে এই আইন কার্যকর নয় বলে গন্য করতে হবে। অর্থাৎ ১৩-৭-৯৪ তারিখের পূর্ব যথনই সিকস্তি বা পয়স্তি হোক না কেন সে ধরনের জমির ক্ষেত্রে এ আইন শানাক্ত্য হবে না বরং পূর্বতন আইন মোতাবেক ঐ জমি সরকারের খাস খতিয়ান ভূক্ত হবে। তদনুসারে সকল জেলা প্রশাসককে কার্য্যকর ব্যবস্থা গ্রহনের নির্দেশ দেয়া হল।”

The order says that the Act XV of 1994 will be effective from 13th July, 1994. Therefore all lands which had diluviated and alluviated prior to 13th July, 1994 will not be affected by the Act of 1994. All diluvion or alluvion which took place prior to the Act of 1994 would according to the old law be included in Khas Khatian.

<u>8. The learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing for the respondents has defended the impugned order as being in accordance with law. He argued that the Act of 1994 was not retrospective as was specifically provided in President's Order 135 of 1972. Because if was not made re-Prospective the lands which had diluviated and alluviated prior to 13th July, 1994 would be recorded in Khas Khatian. He particularly relied on the amendment made to section 86 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 the President's Order No. 135 of 1972 by which the right, title and interest of the land vested in the Government. He argued since the right, title and interest of the tenant extinguished by diluvion under President's Order No. 135 of 1972 the right, title and interest vested with the Government. As such, the right of the Government could not be substituted under sub-section (2) of section 86 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 as amended by Act (XV of 1994,) because it was not given retrospective effect. The right, title and interest in land which vested in the Government on diluvion by amendment of the Act under President's Order No. 135 of 1972 was not taken away, The learned Deputy Attorney-General has submitted that the land vested absolutely in the Government at point of diluvion under the President's Order 1972. In this connection we may refer to the amendment made by the President's Order No. 135 of 1972 in respect of section 86 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 with regard to abatement of rent by diluvion and extinguishment of right, title and interest of the tenant thereto. Sub-section (2) of Ordinance 2 of the Order relates to the extinguishment of the right, title and interest of the tenant by diluvion. This sub-section does not say that on diluvion the tenant's right, title and interest shall vest in the government, Clause 3 of Article 2 of the said Order says about vesting in the Government and this clause (3) says all lands lost by diluvion under sub-section (2) which re-appeared before the date of commencement of the said order but in respect of which the right of the tenant whose land was lost on his successors-in-interest to re- possession was not recognised or declared by a competent authority or court under any law for the time being in force and also all lands, so lost by diluvion under the said sub-section, which may re-appear on or after the said date shall vest absolutely in the Government free from all encumbrances and shall be at its disposal (our emphasis) It is clear from this clause 3 that although by clause 2 of the article the right, title and interest of the tenant is extinguished on diluvion the right, title and interest will vest in the Government in respect of such diluviated land on its re-appearance. Therefore, we are not in agreement with the statement made by the learned Deputy Attorney-General that the diluviated land vest absolutely in the Government at the point of diluvion. The Government can claim title and interest in the land diluviated after re-appearance. It cannot claim vesting under the said order while the land remains diliuviated By sub-section (2) of section 86 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act as amended by Act XV of 1994 the right, title and interest of the original tenant or his successors-in-interest shall subsist in the lands of a holding on operation thereof during the period of loss by diluvion if such lands re-appear in situ within thirty years of their loss It would only follow that the land which were in diluvion prior to 13th July, 1994 the right of the original tenant or his successors in those lands would continue if the land re-appear in situ within 30 years. The Government can only claim such of these lands in diluvion which had re-appeared prior to 13th July, 1994 under the President's Order No. 135 of 1972 but cannot claim such right in respect of lands which is still is diluvion. Therefore, the impugned order in respect of land which re-appeared (alluviated) prior to 13th July, 1994 will vest in the Government and that the Act XV of 1994 was not applicable to such lands. We find that the impugned order 'Annexure D' to the extent giving a direction that all lands diluviated prior to 13th July, 1994 will vest in the Government and that the Act XV of 1994 was not applicable to such lands in diluvion to be illegal and without lawful authority.</u>

9. The Rule is therefore, made absolute only in respect of the order directing to treat all lands diluviated prior to 13th July, 1994 to have vested in the Government.

There shall be no order as to cots.

End.

lawyer:
Md Emdadul Haque Azad, Advocate------For the Petitioner. 
M Ashraf Ali for Farhad Ahmed, Advocate------For the Opposite Parties.
parties:
Mahbubur Rahman ------ Petitioner
vs
Syed Mostofa Jaman and  others ------ Opposite Party
full_judgment:
Bijan Kumar Das, J: By this Rule the opposite party No. 1 was called upon to show cause as to why the impugned order dated 11-3-1999 passed by the Election Tribunal, Gaibandha Sadar in Election Case No. 3 of 1998 should not be set aside or such other or further order or orders passed as to this court may seem fit and proper.

2. The opposite party No. 1 instituted Election Case No. 3 of 1998 in the court of the Election Tribunal, Gaibandha against the petitioner praying for declaration that election of the petitioner as Member of Ward No. 9 of Kholahati Union Parishad was illegal, null and void and for further declaration that the opposite party No.1 was elected member of the said Union Parishad alleging, inter alia, that the election of Kholahati Union Parishad was held on 10-12-1997 and the petitioner rigged the election and occupied polling booths and started counting of votes finally, in the result sheet he was shown to have secured 100 votes though he got 103 votes and his rival candidate, the present petitioner was shown to have got 100 votes though he got 97 votes and he complained before the Presiding Officer and asked the Presiding Officer for recounting of the votes which was refused and the election was materially affected. The petitioner appeared in the election case and filed written statement denying all the allegations and contending, inter alia, that the election was held peacefully and the counting of ballot papers was held fairly and correctly in presence of the agents of all the candidates and the petitioner was legally declared elected member and his name was duly published in the gazette and he took oath and was functioning as a member of the Union Parishad concerned.

3.  witness were examined on behalf of the opposite party No. 1 who was the petitioner in the election case and the date was fixed for the examination of the present petitioner, who was opposite party in the election petition. On the said date the petitioner prayed for adjournment but the tribunal rejected the prayer and fixed 11-3-1999 for argument. On 11-3-1999 the petitioner again filed an application for adducing oral evidence which was alIowed and the petitioner filed an application for re-counting of ballot papers and the Learned Judge of Election Tribunal by the impugned order dated 11-3-1999 illegally allowed the prayer for re-counting of ballot papers before the examination of the witness of the petitioner was over.

4. Being aggrieved thereby the present petitioner moved this court and obtained the present Rule.

5. Mr. Md. Emdadul Haque Azad, the learned Advocate appears on behalf of the petitioner and Mr. M. Ashraf Ali for Mr. Farhad Ahmed, the learned Advocates appeared on behalf of the opposite party.

6. Mr. M. Ashraf Ali, the learned Advocate for the opposite party, raised a preliminary point submitting that the election tribunal being not a civil court this revisional application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure was not maintainable. The learned Advocate has invited my attention to various provisions of Union Parishad Ordinance, 1983 and submits that the election tribunal was set up by the election commission and though the election tribunal was invested with the power of a civil Court trying a suit under the Code of Civil Procedure and shall be deemed to be a Civil Court but the same was for a limited purpose and the entire Code of the Civil Procedure has no application in the disposal of an election petition. The learned Advocate has invited my attention to Rule 47 also which provides that subject to the provision of this rule, every election petition would be tried as practically as may be, in accordance with the procedure laid down for the trial of suits under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. The learned Advocate has relied on a decision in the case of Mohmud Hussain vs Md Sayeb Ali and others reported in 1989 BLD 173.

7. Mr. Md. Emdadul Haque Azad, the learned Advocate for the petitioner submits that the election tribunal has been invested with all the powers of the Code of Civil Procedure for deciding an election and as such a decision passed by the election tribunal is amenable to the revisional jurisdiction of the High Court Division.

<u>8. I have considered the submissions of the learned Advocates for both the parties and perused the relevant provision of law and the decision referred to by the parties. Union Parishad Ordinance, 1983 provides that the Election Tribunal shall be set up by the Election Commission for speedy disposal of election disputes. Provision has been made in the Union Parishad Ordinance, 1983 for the relief that may be claimed in an election dispute and the election petition may be filed before the election tribunal challenging an election on the ground as provided in Union Parishad Ordinance, 1983 and the Rules framed thereunder. On a consideration of various provisions of the Union Parishad Ordinance, 1983 and the rules framed thereunder, it appears that the election tribunal was created by the executive authority of the election commission for special and limited purposes and the election tribunal cannot travel beyond the scope provided in Union Parishad Ordinance, 1983 and the rules framed thereunder and cannot invoke all the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure for deciding an election petition. Article 29(4) of the Union Parishad Ordinance, 1983 though provides for an appeal to the learned District Judge against a decision of the election tribunal, but for the purpose of transfer of an election petition from one tribunal to another tribunal the learned District Judge has not been invested with any power but it is the Election Commission who may transfer an election petition from one election tribunal to another election tribunal which indicates that all the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure have not been made available to the election tribunal and the power of superintendence remains with the election commission. In that view of the matter it appears that a decision passed by the election tribunal is not amenable to the revisional jurisdiction of the High Court Division. It may therefore, be concluded that the election tribunal is not a court and therefore the impugned decision passed by the election tribunal is not amenable to the revisional jurisdiction of the High Court Division. This view is supported by the decision reported in 1989 BLD  173. A learned Senior Judge of this court while deciding the said decision considered large number of authorities of this court touching Union Parishad Ordinance, 1973, 1976 and the present one of the year 1983 and has concluded, "Lastly, since the Election Tribunals are not civil Courts they also are not amenable to the revisional jurisdiction of the High Court Division. This view was also taken by my learned brother Daliluddin Ahmed, J. in the case reported in 38 DLR 262."</u>

9. In view of the aforesaid finding and the proposition oflaw laid down in 1989 BLD 173, I am of the opinion that the Election Tribunal is not a Civil Court established under the Civil Court Acts and the Election Tribunal is not amenable to the revisional jurisdiction of the High Court Division. The preliminary objection of the opposite party has therefore substance. I am not inclined to enter into the merit of the matter in view of my finding that the impugned decision is not amenable to the revisional jurisdiction of the High Court Division.

In the result, this Rule is discharged without any order as to costs. The order of stay of all further proceedings of Election Case No. 3 of 1998 now pending in the Election Tribunal. Gaibandha Sadar is vacated.

End.

lawyer:
Raisuddin Ahmed, Advocate------For the Petitioner. 
Md Ibrahim Mollah, Advocate------For the Respondent.
parties:
Ambala Cold Storage (Pvt)   ------ Petitioner
Vs
Prime Insurance Co. Ltd  ------ Respondent
full_judgment:
This application under sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act, 1994 has been made by the petitioner Ambala Cold Storage (Pvt) Ltd. Initially, notice was issued upon the respondent company to show cause as to why this application for winding up of the respondent company should not be admitted for hearing.

2. The case of the petitioner is that, the petitioner is a private limited company carrying on business of cold storage having its office at House No. 39, Road No.2. Dhanmondi, Dhaka. The petitioner set up their cold storage where potatoes are stored upon purchasing from market against loan obtained by it from Sonali Bank and the Sonali Bank disbursed the working capital to the petitioner to purchase potatoes to store them in the petitioner's cold storage, by their sanction letter No. Daibasha/Shilparin/ Ambala/Cold/257 dated 22-3-1998. In the sanction letter there was stipulation, inter alia, that the petitioner will take insurance policies against Fire, Deterioration of Stocks (DoS) and Machinery Breakdown (MBD), etc from an insurance company. Pursuant to the stipulation of the sanction letter the petitioner obtained 3 policies from the respondent company of various kinds for potatoes stored in the cold storage located at Manikganj covering fire, machinery breakdown and deterioration of stock and the petitioner obtained 3 policies being Fire Policy No. Prime/RJK/FP-004/03/98 dated 16-3-1998 for Taka 1,50 crore, Machinery Breakdown Insurance Policy No. Prime/RJK/MBD/P-001/03/98 dated 16-3-98 for Taka 1.46 crore. Deterioration of Cold Storage Insurance Policy No. PRIME/RJ K/DoS/P-001/03/98 for Taka 2 crore respectively. It is the case of the petitioner that an unprecedented flood in the country in 1998 occurred and consequently, Dhaka Electric Supply Authority stopped electricity supply to petitioner's cold storage on 9-9-1998. The respondent was informed by the petitioner to that effect on 11-9-1998. General diary was made with the local Police Station. Due to stoppage of electricity the Cold Storage was run by the Generator and Direct Drive. The main generator ceased to function on 15-9-1998 and information was made to the respondent by letter dated 16-9-1998. The Cold Storage remained without power for over 24 hours. The regular power supply was restored on 16-9-1999. Thereafter, when the delivery of potatoes started it was found that due to stoppage of electricity and cessation of Generator 35% of the potatoes kept in the cold storage were damaged and an initial claim was filed with the respondent on 11-10-1998 for Taka 80,12,256 only for DoS and Taka 5,00,000 for cost of repair of the machinery under MBD. Having received the initial claim the respondent by their letter dated 20-10-1998 appointed two Surveyor Companies, namely, Engineers Survey Associates Ltd and Rupali Surveyors as joint surveyors to survey the loss. The respondents also asked the petitioner to submit formal claim in prescribed form along with documents. The surveyors made a joint survey on 25-10-1998 in presence of petitioner's Director Mr M Waliul Haque and assessed the loss of weight 5% total loss 8% and partial loss 4% of which 20% is total loss. The report was jointly signed by both the surveyors and the Director of the petitioner's company. On the basis of the report formal claim was lodged by the petitioner with the respondent on 8-11-1998 which was countersigned by the Advocate of the petitioner. The respondent by their letter dated 15-12-1998 informed the petitioner that the claim of the petitioner is under scrutiny and the petitioner will be informed about the result in due course. It has been stated that the respondent by their letter dated 18-12-1998 addressed to Sonali Bank, Foreign Exchange Corporate Branch, Dhaka confirmed that the claim. amount will be directly paid to the petitioner through their branch. Thereafter, the petitioner made several demands upon the respondent company and made series of correspondence and requested the respondent company to settle their claim and the respondent promised to pay but ultimately the claim was not settled. Upon receiving no response from the respondent company the petitioner through their Advocate served a legal notice upon the respondent on 9-8-1999 requesting the respondent to pay the petitioner's admitted claim, but the respondent company did not make any response whatsoever. Then on September 20, 1999 the petitioner's lawyer served a notice under section 242 of the Companies Act 1994 upon the respondent to settle the petitioner's claim within 21 days, but the respondent did not respond to such notice. Subsequently, on September 20, 1999 the respondent through special messenger sent a reply to the petitioner's legal notice dated 9-8-1999 by which they denied the claim of the petitioner, but no reply was given to the notice served under section 242 of the Companies Act. It has been stated that the respondent company sent a frivolous letter to the petitioner on 24-10-1999 denying the petitioner's claim. The petitioner thereafter, made relentless efforts to get the outstanding amount against the claim as assessed by the Surveyors but the respondent company did not pay the claim amount and that the respondent company is unable to pay its liabilities and to pay its admitted debt and since the respondent company is unable to pay its debt the company is liable to be wound up under the aforesaid provision of law.

3. The respondent has filed an affidavit-in-opposition to resist the prayer of the petitioner for winding up the company and denying the material allegations, the respondent has stated that the petition has been filed as a pressure tactics to recover the so-called dues which is highly disputed by the respondent Company. It has been stated that the respondent company is a well reputed Insurance company which is transacting general insurance business and the petitioner obtained the aforesaid 3 policies covering the risk as mentioned in the policies. The DOS policies was subsequently revised on 31-8-1998 for Taka 1.60 crore. The respondent has denied that the joint survey report was signed by the surveyors as well as the director of the respondent. It is the case of the respondent company that the respondent never admitted the claim of the petitioner as the claim does not fall under the respective policies and the terms and condition laid down therein. The respondent has pleaded that the petitioner was informed regarding the flood situation in 1998 and after receiving information the respondent appointed Messrs Engineers Survey Associates and Rupali Surveys for inspection in order to ascertain the loss and damages of the petitioner's property and the surveyors after inspection submitted their report stating that the compressor No. 1 was in operation and that the motors of the compressor Nos. 2 and 3 were affected by flood water and, as such, those compressors could be put into operation, but the compressor No. 1 was saved by giving brick wall around it and they also observed that the. insurer took precautionary measures to prevent entering the flood water by making flood protection wall with sand bags. It is contended by the respondent that the capital of the company is 25 crore and wherein the paid up capital is Taka 15 crore which is far more than the claim of the petitioner. Therefore, it cannot be said that the respondent is unable to pay the debt of the petitioner even if it is established the said amount is due to the petitioner.

4. It is contended by the learned Advocate for the petitioner that the joint survey report was made and the same was communicated to the respondent company the damage was assessed by that report and, according to the report, the respondent company is liable to pay on account of loss caused to the petitioner which is covered by the 3 insurance policies. He has further contended that the respondent company having not denied the claim of the petitioner is bound to pay the same and since the notice under section 242 of the Companies Act had been served upon the respondent company, the respondent under the provision of law is liable to pay the debt and having failed to pay the debt the company is liable to be wound up. He has argued that the subsequent denial by their letter dated 20-9-1999 is an after-thought as the respondent company avoided to pay the dues to the petitioner. The plea taken by the respondent company that the policy does not cover the alleged loss is not tenable.

5. Mr Md Ibrahim Mollah, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the respondent, has contended that the survey report annexed to the application is not a joint survey report pursuant to the terms of the policy and the joint surveyors namely, Engineers Survey Associates Ltd and Rupali Surveyor, were appointed and after physical verification they submitted the report wherein it has been stated that as per physical finding of the documents which were produced it appears that no breakdown of machinery occurred and the temperature was normal during the period and the surveyors opined that the loss suffered by the insured falls outside scope of the policies and hence no such liabilities were attached to the policies. He has further argued that the respondent company has never admitted the claim of the petitioner, rather the respondent disputed the claim relying on the survey report as well as the terms of the policies. Since the claim is not admitted it is not a debt as contemplated under sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act and on such disputed claim the company cannot be wound up under the provision of law.

<u>6. It appears that petitioner obtained 3 policies covering the aforesaid risk laying down the terms and that, according to the petitioner, the claim was made on the basis of the report submitted by the Surveyors Annexure E but the claim was not accepted as genuine made by the petitioner and the respondent company disputed the claim saying that it is not based on any proper survey report and that the claim is not covered by the policies. Unless the disputed claim is assessed by it competent Court having received the evidence for determining the loss and damage the respondent company is not liable to pay the amount. From the papers and materials submitted before the Court it does not seem to me that the claim made by the petitioner has been accepted as a liability of the respondents company and that they agreed to pay the claim amount. The claim is not undisputedly ascertained, and unless it is admitted it cannot be said it is a debt and the respondent company is liable to pay the debt. Winding up of a company by Court for debt is not called for where there is a bonafide dispute relating to the existence of the debt.</u>

In that view, the application under sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act cannot be maintained. The prayer for winding up of the company is refused and the petition is dismissed without any order as to costs.

The petitioner may, however, make their claim before the competent civil Court in terms of the policy.

End.

lawyer:
MA Wahhab Miah, Advocate instructed by Shamsul Haque Siddique, Advocate-on-Record --- For the Appellant.
Mvi. Md. Wahidullah, Advocate-on-Record ---- For the Respondents.
parties:
Nesar Ahmed also known as Babul ----- Appellant
vs. 
Government of Bangladesh, represented by the Deputy Commissioner, Noakhali and another ----- Respondents
case_source: (From the Judgment and Order dated 10-5-94 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 720 of 1994).
full_judgment:
Mustafa Kamal J: This appeal by leave by the convicted-appellant is from the judgment and order of a Division Bench of the High Court Division dated 10-5-94 in Writ Petition No.720 of 1994 rejecting the writ petition in limine on the ground that it was not maintainable, there being an alternative remedy of appeal under section 30 of the Special Powers Act, 1974 which the appellant did not avail of.

2. The appellant's case in the writ petition was that on 19-9-91 one Tabarakullah, Chairman-in-Charge of No.8, Sonapur Union Parishad under PS Begumganj lodged a first information report with Begumganj PS against the appellant and another's Anwarullah alleging, inter alia, that the gram police of the said Union on being directed to strengthen patrolling in the night to prevent theft, dacoity, hijacking, etc., then taking place in various villages of the Union, found 6/7 persons moving suspiciously on the road of Bogalia Amishapara at village Paschim Doulatpur towards the west of Kalikapur (Khelafat Bazar) on 18-9-91 at about 8-00 PM. The patrol party rounded them up, but some of the suspiciously moving persons escaped with arms after a scuffle. The appellant and the said Anwarullah were apprehended by the gram police. A rope and an electrically-charged torchlight were recovered from the person of the appellant and a knife measuring 11 inches was recovered from the possession of Anwarullah. Begumganj PS Case No.20 dated 19-9-91 was started on the FIR against the appellant and Anwarullah. The police after investigation submitted charge-sheet against both of them on 3-12-91. The appellant obtained bail from the Thana Magistrate, Begumganj. The case was then sent to the Court of Senior Special Tribunal and Sessions Judge, Noakhali for trial where it was numbered as Special Tribunal Case No.21 of 1992. Charge was framed against the appellant and Anwarullah under section 19(f) of the Arms Act, 1878 read with section 26 of the Special Powers Act, 1974. The case was transferred to the Court of Special Tribunal No. 3 and Assistant Sessions Judge, Noakhali for trial. It is the appellant's case that when the case was sent to the Court of Senior Special Tribunal and Sessions Judge, Noakhali for trial the learned Advocate for the appellant did not inform him of the said transmission. Consequently he had no knowledge about the subsequent proceedings and he could not appear before the Special Tribunal and face the trial and the case proceeded in his absence. The order sheet of the Special Tribunal shows that no notice was issued either by the Senior Special Tribunal or by Special Tribunal No.3 for appearance of the appellant or upon the sureties for production of the appellant.

3. At the trial the prosecution examined 6 witnesses and in the absence of any defence no defence witness was examined. The Special Tribunal No.3, Noakhali by its judgment and order dated 14-2-93 convicted the appellant and Anwarullah under section 19(f) of the Arms Act read with section 26 of the Special Powers Act and sentenced each of them to suffer rigorous imprisonment for 10 years and also to pay a fine of Taka 500.00 in default to suffer rigorous imprisonment for 1 month more.

4. The appellant was at his village home where he was suddenly arrested by the police on 1-11-93 and was forwarded to Noakhali District Jail. The appellant came to know of the trial, conviction and sentence after his arrest. He obtained certified copies of the relevant papers on 12-1-94 and filed an application under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure in the High Court Division against the aforesaid judgment and order of conviction and sentence. The application was moved on 13-2-94 but as the learned Judges of the High Court Division observed that the said application was not maintainable the learned Advocate for the appellant took it back. Thereafter the appellant filed the instant writ petition against the impugned judgment and order of conviction and sentence.

5. About the background of the impugned judgment Mr. MA Wahhab Miah, learned Advocate for the appellant submits that on the day that he moved the instant writ petition in the High Court Division, he also moved an analogous writ petition earlier, namely, Writ Petition No.721 of 1994 in which the writ petitioner was a different person, the occurrence was different and the trial was also held by a different Special Tribunal, but the point of law involved in the said writ petition was the same as in the instant writ petition. The learned Judges of the High Court Division in rejecting Writ Petition No.721 of 1994 in limine delivered an elaborate judgment holding that there was an alternative remedy of appeal under section 30 of the Special Powers Act and the Writ petitioner of the said writ petition not having availed of it cannot obtain any relief under Article 102 of the Constitution on the facts of the said case. The High Court Division also held that there was no want of lawful authority in passing the impugned judgment by the Special Tribunal concerned. Therefore, the other writ petitioner in the other writ petition was not entitled, upon the facts of the said case, to the remedy under Article 102 of the Constitution.

6. While disposing of the instant Writ Petition No.720 of 1994 by a separate judgment on the same day the learned Judges of the High Court Division observed as follows :

"In this application the facts of the case although are different but the points mooted at the Bar are similar to that of earlier petition i.e. Writ Petition No. 721 of 1994.

Therefore, the decision just given in the earlier application will govern the fate of the present application."

7. Leave was granted to the appellant to consider his submission that recovery of possession from his person of a rope and an electrically-charged torchlight does not render him liable for an offence under section 19(f) of the Arms Act or any other section of the Arms Act and, as such, the Special Tribunal acted without jurisdiction in taking cognisance of the case against him and in ultimately convicting and sentencing him. Leave was also granted to consider his submission that the order of conviction and sentence of the appellant being without jurisdiction the High Court Division erred in law in holding that the application under Article 102 of the Constitution is not maintainable.

8. We shall take up the second point first on which leave has been granted. This point should have been formulated differently, namely, whether an application under Article 102 of the Constitution is available to an accused person when he had no reasonable opportunity to avail of the statutory remedy of appeal under section 30 of the Special Powers Act.

9. It is free from any doubt that when an equally efficacious alternative statutory remedy is provided for in section 30 of the Special Powers Act enabling the accused to prefer an appeal to the High Court Division the question of invoking the jurisdiction of the High Court Division under Article 102 of the Constitution normally does not arise. When, for example, an accused person is tried, convicted and sentenced in his presence by a Special Tribunal, his remedy lies under section 30 of the Special Powers Act. So also in a case under sub-section (6) or (6A) of section 27 of the Special Powers Act, 1974 which are as follows :

"(6) Where a Special Tribunal has reason to believe that an accused person has absconded or is concealing himself so that he cannot be arrested and produced before it for trial and there is no immediate prospect of arresting him, it shall, by order published in at least two Bengali daily newspapers having wide circulation, direct such person to appear before it within such period as may be specified in the order, and if such person fails to comply with such direction, he shall be tried in his absence. (6A) Where in a case after the production or appearance of an accused person before the Tribunal or his release on bail, the accused person absconds or fails to appear before it, the procedure as laid down in sub-section (6) shall not apply and the Tribunal shall, after recording its decision so to do, try such person in his absence."

<u>10. But the presence of an alternative remedy does not debar the exercise of jurisdiction by the High Court Division under Article 102 of the Constitution when the facts and circumstances of a particular case are such that the accused person had no reasonable opportunity to avail of the statutory remedy under section 30 of the Special Powers Act. Whether or not the accused person had such a reasonable opportunity is a question of fact to be decided in each case upon case-records and no hard and fast formula can be laid down to settle the criteria in advance.</u>

11. The High Court Division failed to notice that in this case the appellant stated in his writ petition that after he obtained bail from the learned Magistrate, his learned Advocate failed to communicate to him the fact of transmission of case records to the Senior Special Tribunal for trial. He did not know about the trial and could not face the trial only because he was unaware of the subsequent developments. No Court shall take such statements on their face value as these are commonplace statements often designedly made to attract the Court's jurisdiction. The Court should therefore look into the case records for corroboration of such statements of the accused person to satisfy itself that the statements have a ring of truth in them.

<u>12. Mr. MA Wahhab Miah had taken us through the order sheet (enclosed as Annexure-K to the writ petition) of the Senior Special Tribunal and Special Tribunal No.3, Noakhali. The High Court Division has failed to notice and consequently it has fallen upon us to find that upon receipt of the case records on 7-7-92 from the Thana Magistrate, Begumganj, the Senior Special Tribunal at once on the same day labelled the appellant as an absconde (presumably under sub-section (6A) of section 27 of the Special Powers Act) without fixing a date for his appearance and without directing the sureties to produce the appellant. Without passing such an order the Senior Special Tribunal could not have treated the appellant as an absconding accused under sub-section (6A) of section 27, because an absent person should not be too readily assumed to be an absconder without fixing a date for his appearance and without directing his sureties to produce him. On 10-8-92 it passed an order directing his trial under section 339B (2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which again ought to have been mentioned as a trial under sub-section (6A) of section 27 of the Special Powers Act. We therefore find that there is a strong basis for the appellant's contention that the trial took place without his knowledge. The conduct of the appellant is not so reprehensible or indefensible as to disentitle him from any forum other than the one provided for in section 30 of the Special Powers Act. The High Court Division failed to apply its mind to the facts and circumstances of the instant case. We find that the appellant has made out a case that although he was found to be absconding after obtaining bail, his explanation that he was unaware of the subsequent developments after he obtained bail is not without foundation.</u>

<u>13. In all such types of cases therefore it will be for the High Court Division to satisfy itself in the facts and circumstances of each case whether the person seeking remedy under Article 102 of the Constitution has adequately explained his conduct in not pursuing the statutory remedy under section 30 of the Special Powers Act which the High Court Division failed to do in the instant case. The High Court Division was swayed by the facts and circumstances of the other writ petition and was totally unmindful of the facts of the present case and did not at all consider that the appellant has made out a case that he had no opportunity of availing of the alternative remedy in section 30 of the Special Powers Act. If and when such a case is made out it will be improper, inequitable and indeed a denial of justice if the door is shut upon the face of the accused person. The High Court Division was wrong in holding that the instant writ petition was not maintainable. The appellant had no reasonable opportunity to avail of the alternative remedy. In such circumstances, his writ petition was fully maintainable.</u>

14. Upon satisfying itself that the accused person had no reasonable opportunity to avail of the statutory remedy, the High Court Division however, in exercise of jurisdiction under Article 102 of the Constitution, will not sit on appeal over the judgment of the Special Tribunal and will not convert itself into a Court of Appeal under section 30 of the Special Powers Act. It will confine itself to the jurisdictional issues that are usually associated with judgments of inferior Tribunals and quasi-judicial bodies.

15. That takes us to the first point on which leave was granted. Mr. M A Wahhab Miah submits that a rope and an electrically-charged torchlight do not come within the definition of "arms" or "ammunition" within the meaning of section 4 of the Arms Act, 1878. He has taken us through the evidence of PWs 1-4 who have uniformly deposed that only a rope and an electrically-charged torchlight were recovered from the possession of the appellant. As such, he submits, the taking of cognizance of an offence under section 19(f) of the Arms Act by the Special Tribunal was without jurisdiction and the trial, conviction and sentence of the appellant were also consequently without jurisdiction.

<u>16. It appears that the High Court Division rejected the writ petition in limine without adverting to the appellant's contention on the lack of jurisdiction of the Special Tribunal. We have gone through the schedule of the Special Powers Act and we find that in the state of evidence on record the materials recovered from the appellant do not attract the mischief of the Arms Act, 1878 and the alleged offence could not have been taken cognisance of by the Special Tribunal. As such the whole trial and the order of conviction and sentence passed by the Special Tribunal were without jurisdiction. The High Court Division acted wrongly in dismissing the writ petition in limine.</u>

17. The appeal is allowed without any order as to costs.

18. The judgment and order dated 14-2-1993 passed by Special Tribunal No.3, Noakhali in ST Case No.21 of 1992 convicting the appellant under section 19(f) of the Arms Act read with section 26 of the Special Powers Act and sentencing him to suffer rigorous imprisonment for 10 (ten) years and also to pay a fine of Taka 500.00 in default to suffer rigorous imprisonment for one month more are set aside.

The appellant be set at liberty forthwith if not required in connection with any other case.

End.

lawyer:
AFM Hassan Arif, Advocate ----- For the Petitioner. 
No one ----- For the Respondents.
parties:
Sharif and Brothers ------ Petitioners
vs
Commissioner of Customs and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Md Awlad Ali J: This Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the impugned order dated 2-12-97 in File No. CEVT/Case/(CRF) Review-Chatta-07/97 relating to the cancelling of CRF by the Review Committee, Chittagong vide order dated 28-7-97 should not be declared to have 'been made without lawful authority and of no legal effect.

2. The petitioner is the proprietor of Shariff and Brothers, a registered importer and is engaged in the business, inter alia, of import of Sodium Saccharin. The petitioner opened a letter of Credit No. AIB/MVI/97 149 dated 7-5-97 with the Al Arafah Islami Bank Ltd Moulvi Bazar for import of sodium saccharin as specified under HS Code No. 2925.11.00. It is stated that pursuant to 25A of the Customs Act. 1969 the National Board of Revenue issued notification being SRO No. 316/AIN/ 94/1568/Customs dated 3-11-94 and provided for import of goods on the basis of certificate as to the quality, quantity value and H.S. code and description issued by an approved pre-shipment inspection agent (PSI agent). Before shipment of the imported goods of the petitioner the pre-shipment inspection was made on 22-5-97 by the Inspectorate Griffith Ltd. an approved pre-shipment inspection agency, which issued Clean Report of Finding (CRF) certificate No. FOIBAN 701559 HKG dated 17-6-97 (Annexure-B). The said imported goods arrived at Chittagong Port on13-797 under Commercial invoice dated 17-5-97. The petitioner through his clearing agent submitted bill of entry registration No. C 65861 Dated 24-7-97 for clearing the goods from the vessel on payment of Custom duty and other charges on the basis of CRF value. The respondent No. 2, the Assistant Commissioner of Customs, Customs Office, Chittagong by his order dated 28-7-97 in file No. 78/AP/Group-2/97-98 illegally sent the CRF to the Review Committee and the Review Committee cancelled the CRF illegally and arbitrarily (Annexure-D(1). Against the order of the Review Committee the petitioner preferred an appeal under section 193C (2) of the Customs Act (as amended in 1997) by Finance Act, 1997 before the Appellate Tribunal. After hearing the parties the Appellate Tribunal upheld the cancellation order of CRF by the Review Committee. The Tribunal, however, did not agree with the view of the Review Committee in the matter of valuation of the consignment at tariff value and set aside the valuation fixed by the Review Committee and fixed a valuation of its own at the rate of US $ 5500.00 per Metric Ton. The petitioner claims that the Tribunal had passed the order without considering the relevant material and arrived at a decision with our any basis. The decision and order of the Tribunal which has been annexed as Annexure E has been challenged in this Writ petition.

3. Various grounds have been taken in order to assail the decision of the impugned order of the Tribunal (Annexure E) and it has been contended that the cancellation of the CRF by the Review Committee is without any materials being considered by it and the impugned order of the Tribunal being based on CRF certifications No. 960-101-05101 showing value of saccharin at US $ 6.30 was not in existence and the same is fake. The foundation of the above argument is that, after the disposal of the appeal the petitioner sub Milted a review petition against the decision of the Appellate Tribunal in which it has been stated that the petitioner enquired about the above CRF certification and it revealed that the said CRF is fake and no goods were assessed against CRF bearing No. 96010105101 dated 25-3-07 issued by Bureau Veritas and that the goods alleged to have been covered by the said fake certifications has been cleared against CRF certifications bearing No 960101-05570 which shows the price of Saccharin at US $ 3.23 per kg under LC No. AlB/MVU97/13 dated 16-1-97 under invoice No. 972B X 00 dated 3-3-97, the bill of lading No. HTV/015 dated 15-397 and bill of entry being No. C-87 808 dated 17-6, 97 of which the buyer was Sabuj Enterprise of 10, Mokim Katra Dhaka a Photostat copy of which was enclosed with the review petition. The review petition was, however, summarily rejected by the Appellate Tribunal by order dated 24-1-97.

4. It is emphatically contended by Mr Hassan Arif that the Tribunal had not exercised its jurisdiction vested in it by Jaw in not having considered the CRF certificate No. 960-101-05570 in the name of Sabuj Enterprise in connection with lever of credit dated 16-1-97 in which price was shown 1 $ 3.23 per kg which is much lower than the CRF certificate relied upon by the Appellate Tribunal and the Review Committee. It is further contended that the Tribunal had no legal and valid document before it to arrive at a conclusion on objective information and the very consideration of an invalid document is an error of law and the Tribunal has not exercised its jurisdiction in accordance with law and failed to exercise its jurisdiction not having called for ilk genuine and relevant CRF from the custody of Bank and thus arrived at a wrong conclusion for determining the value of the goods.

5. The CRF certificate is issued by the Pre shipment Inspection Agency as per provision as laid down under section 25A of the Customs Act, 1969 which reads as follows:

"Assessment on the basis of certificate issued by Pre-shipment inspection agencies:

Notwithstanding anything contained in any other section of this Act the Government may by notification in the official gazette, declare that the quality, quantity, price and customs classification of goods verified and certified in the prescribed manner by an approved Pre shipment inspection agency will be accepted as the basis for assessment."

6. According to the aforesaid provision, the CRF certificates was issued by the pre-shipment inspection agency for the goods imported under the aforesaid letter of credit. In June 1995, section 193C was enacted which provided for an appeal to the Board by the Commissioner against the certificate issued by any pre-shipment inspection agency for fixing the price of the subject goods for the purposes of final assessment. Section 193C was substituted by new section 193C in September, 1996 under which provision was made to appeal to the Appellate Tribunal constituted under section 196 of the Act. Section 193C was again substituted by Finance Act 1997 (Act XV of 1997) which is as follows:

193C. Review Committee—(1) There shall be constituted a Review Committee for the purpose of reviewing valuation of imports under pre-shipment inspection scheme consisting of such number of members as the Government may determine.

(2) Any person aggrieved by any decision of the Review Committee may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Tribunal constituted under section 196.

(3) The Appellate Tribunal may, after making such enquiry as it considers necessary and after giving the Commissioner or his authorized representative, the local representative of the concerned pre-shipment inspection agency, and the importer an opportunity of being heard, if they so desire, pass such order as it thinks fit, including fixing the price of the subject goods for the purpose of final assessment."

7. The paper and documents with respect to the imported goods including CRF was referred to the Review Committee by the Customs Authority for the purpose of reviewing valuation under pre-shipment inspection scheme, and the Review Committee considering the relevant papers and documents made an order on 28-7-97 and thereby rejected the valuation on the basis of CRF. In the order passed by the review Committee, the finding to the following effect was clearly noted:

“TV এবং রেকর্ড মূল্য অপক্ষো CRF এতে প্রত্যোয়নকৃত মূল্য কম হওয়ায় একক পন্য ইতিপূর্বে একাধিক CRF বাতিল করা হয়েছে। বর্তমান ক্ষেত্রের CRF বাতিলের সিদ্ধান্ত গৃহীত হয়।”

8. The decision for cancellation of CRF value was made unanimously by the members of the review committee which was validly constituted. Against the said decision cancelling the CRF value the petitioner preferred an appeal before the Appellate Tribunal. The Appellate Tribunal notified all the parties concerned including the local representative of the concerned pre-shipment agency and at the time of hearing of the appeal the Appellate Tribunal asked all the parties including the petitioner to produce the relevant papers and documents, which had been done accordingly. After careful scrutiny of the papers and documents in the relevant file and produced by the parties including CRF No. 96010105101 dated 25-3-97 issued by the reshipment inspection agency Bureau Veritas. in connection with similar goods, ie sodium saccharin imported from China by Sabuj Enterprise, Dhaka under letter of credit dated 16-1-97. In that CRF the valuation was fixed at US $ 6030 per metric ton. It is contended by the petitioner that the said CRF is a fake one and that should not have been relied upon by the appellate authority. The question whether the particular CRF is a fake or genuine one cannot be determined by this Court under Writ jurisdiction. Mr Hasan Arif contended that the relevant CRF which has nexus with the letter of credit of the said Sabuj Enterprise bearing registration No. AIB/MVI/ 97/105 dated 20-3-1997 in which lower price was shown was not considered by the Appellate Tribunal by calling the same from the relevant Bank and thereby the tribunal acted beyond its jurisdiction as the valuation has been fixed without any objective information.

9. It appears from the language of sub-section (3) of section 193C that the power of the tribunal is discretionary, the Appellate Tribunal has the power to make such inquiry as it considers necessary, and after giving the concerned parties an opportunity of being heard if they so desire it may pass such order as it thinks fit including fixing the price of the subject goods for final assessment. Now the question which requires determination is whether the Appellate Tribunal has exercised the statutory discretion arbitrarily, or it has exercised the description fairly and reasonably. It appears from the judgment of the Appellate Tribunal, that the Tribunal considered all the relevant papers and all the parties were given opportunity of being heard and after hearing the parties and considering the necessary papers including the CRF dated 25-3-97 issued by the same Inspection Agency of the same kind of goods found that the cancellation order made by the Review Committee was justified. But the Appellate Tribunal having regard to other consideration such as fluctuation of price in the international market of the same goods within the period between 16-1-97 and 7-5-97 reduced the value of the goods as assessed by the Review Committee and ultimately, the price was fixed at US $ 5500 per metric ton upholding the order of cancellation of CRF value by the Review Committee.

We have already noticed that although the review application was filed against the decision of the Appellate Tribunal in which a particular document was mentioned for the determination of the valuation of the imported goods but no step was taken by the petitioner to call for the said document from the Bank. The Tribunal considered the relevant papers meticulously and arrived at a decision in fixing the value of the goods. Having perused the judgment and order of the Tribunal it does not seem to us that the Tribunal has not exercised the statutory discretion in accordance with law or that the Tribunal had exercised the discretionary power arbitrarily and unreasonably.

Mr Hasan Ariff contended that there has been jurisdiction error in the decision of the Appellate Tribunal in that the Appellate Tribunal had failed to consider the relevant and valid document in order to arrive at a conclusion in respect of the valuation and therefore the Tribunal acted beyond its jurisdiction in which case the decision of the Tribunal is liable to be reviewed by this Court. He has, however sought reliance from several decisions of the Indian jurisdiction viz. AIR 1968 (SC) 1186. AIR 1962.(SC) 1621 Para 15, AIR 1980 (SC) 1986. We have considered the cited decisions and we are of the opinion that those decisions have no relevance at all the facts are quite distinguishable from those of the present case.

<u>10. Lastly, it has been contended by Mr Hasan Ariff that the record of the relevant letter of credit and the CRF on the basis of which the valuation should have been fixed was transmitted to this Court for deciding the issue and having regard to relevant letter of credit and CRF the matter may be remanded to the Appellate Tribunal for reconsideration of the valuation of the goods imported by the petitioner. We have already stated and observed that no step f44 been taken by the petitioner either before the Review Committee or before the Appellate Tribunal to bring those papers for their consideration and the Tribunal had exercised its discretionary power as contemplated under sub-section (3) of section 193C as aforesaid fairly and reasonably and not arbitrarily the justice ability of the decision cannot be questioned under the process of judicial review as the Tribunal has not acted outside its jurisdiction and we do not find any justification to remand the case to the Appellate Tribunal again for reconsideration as to the valuation of the goods in question.</u>

<u>In the above view, this Rule is discharged. We do not award any cost having regard to the facts and circumstances of the case.</u>

End.

Vs.
