case_source: (From the Judgment and order dated November 2, 2000 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No.5399 of 2000).
full_judgment:
Md. Ruhul Amin, J: The appeal, by leave, is by the plaintiff of Money Suit No. 74 of 1999 (previously numbered 40 of 1997 of the 4th Court of Artha Rin Adalat) of the Court of Sub-Judge and Additional Artha Rin Adalat No.2, Dhaka against the judgment and order dated November 2, 2000 of a Division Bench of the High Court Division. The Division Bench summarily rejected the Writ Petition No. 5399 of 2000.

2. The writ petition was filed impugning the order dated August 17, 2000 of the Court of Subordinate Judge and Additional Artha Rin Adalat No.2 passed in the aforesaid Money Suit making direction to the pawnee (plaintiff) to sell the pawned goods and thereupon to adjust the sale proceeds of the pawned goods against the claim of the pawnee and then to frame the suit upon amending the plaint in respect of the amount, if any, due from the pawner. The Artha Rin Adalat, hereinafter in brief, the Adalat, made the aforesaid direction upon observing that in the absence of selling the hypothecated goods pawnee is not entitled to file the suit for realisation of his claim due from the pawner.

3. Plaintiff-appellant filed aforementioned money suit stating, inter alia, that respondent Nos. 2 and 3 availed loan facilities from the plaintiff and that respondent No. 4 stood guarantor for the repayment of the loan amount due from the respondent Nos. 2 and 3. The defendant No.2 failed to pay the loan amount due against the hypothecated goods kept in the godown of the bank and thereupon, plaintiff filed the aforementioned money suit for realisation of Taka 31,30,699 impleading the respondent Nos. 2-4 as defendants.

4. The respondent No.4 (defendant No.3) entered appearance and filed application seeking adjournment for filing written statement. The said defendant filed written statement. Examination of witnesses from the side of the plaintiff was closed and examination-in-chief of DW 1 was held in part. At that stage of hearing of the suit the contesting defendant filed an application under Order XIV rule 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The application was rejected. The respondent No. 4 challenged legality of the said order of rejection by filing Writ Petition No. 785 of 2000. A Division Bench of the High Court Division disposed of the writ petition upon making direction to the Adalat "to dispose of the issues of law first and postponed settlement of facts until the issues of law have been determined", Thereafter, the Adalat by the order dated August 17, 2000 disposed of the petition filed under Order XIV rule 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure and made direction to the plaintiff to sell the hypothecated goods and to adjust the sale proceeds against the total claim and that thereafter, if any amount remains due then to frame the suit for the said amount upon amending the plaint. The aforesaid direction was made by the Adalat upon observing “তবে উচ্চতর আদালতের সিদ্ধান্ত মতেই দেখা যায় যে হাইপোথিককেটেড গুড বিক্রয় না করিয়া বাদী তাহার পাওনার দাবী পেশ করিতে অধিকারী নহে” This finding of the Adalat was totally wrong.

5. Plaintiff challenged legality of the order dated August 17, 2000 by filing Writ Petition No. 5399 of 2000. A Division Bench of the High Court Division summarily rejected the said writ petition. Thereupon, leave has been obtained for examination of the contention that as per provision of section 176 of the Contract Act upon retaining the pledged goods as collateral security the pawnee can proceed with the suit for realisation of the amount due from the pawner and that to sell or not to sell the pledged goods is the option of pawnee and, as such, neither the pawner is competent to come before the Court with the prayer to direct the pawnee to sell the hypothecated goods and that to make his prayer to the court to direct the pawnee to proceed with the suit for the balance amount of the debt that remained due on adjustment of the sale proceeds, nor the court is competent to make direction to the pawnee to sell the hypothecated goods and that to proceed with the suit upon amendment of the plaint as regard the amount, if any, remains due after adjustment of the sale proceeds of the hypothecated goods.

6. Pawnee's right against the defaulting pawner is provided in section 176 of the Contract Act and the same reads as:

Section 176: "If the pawner makes default in payment of the debt, or performance, at the stipulated time of the promise, in respect of which the goods were pledged, the pawnee may bring a suit against the pawner upon the debt or promise, and retain the goods pledged as a collateral security; or he may sell the thing pledged, on" giving the pawner reasonable notice of the sale.

If the proceeds of such sale are less than the amount due in respect of the debt or promise, the pawner is still liable to pay the balance. If the proceeds of the sale are greater than the amount so due, the pawnee shall pay over the surplus to the pawner."

7. The learned Counsel for the appellant, upon referring to the provision of section 176 of the Contract Act, has submitted that the option either to file a suit for realisation of the amount due from the pawner retaining the pawned goods as collateral security or that to sell the pawned goods for realisation of debt is of the pawnee alone. The learned Counsel submits that the pawnee may either file suit for realisation of the amount due retaining the pawned goods as collateral security or may sell the pawned goods and then file suit for realisation of the amount, if any, remains due after adjustment of the sale proceeds. He continues that the pawner has no right either to call upon the pawnee first to sell the hypothecated goods and to adjust the amount realised by such sale against the amount due and then to file the suit, if any, remained outstanding and that the court can also not make any direction in a suit to the pawnee for realisation of the outstanding debt amount against the pawned goods to sell the same first and that upon adjustment of the sale proceeds to proceed with the suit upon amendment of the plaint for the balance amount, if any, remains due after adjustment.

8. The learned Counsel, in support of his submissions that it is the pawnee's sale option either to file the suit for the amount due from the pawner or to sell the pawned goods for realisation of the outstanding debt and then for the debt, if remains unsatisfied, to file suit, has referred to the case of AM Burq and another vs Central Exchange Bank Ltd and others reported in PLD 1966 Lahore 1. In the reported case it has been observed "It is a right of the pawnee-pledgee either to bring a suit upon the debt or to sell the things pledged upon giving a reasonable notice of sale. Both these rights are concurrent and they are provided in section 176 of the Contract Act.... a pledger cannot compel the pledgee to exercise the power of sale or its adjustment as a means of discharging or satisfying the amount due to him. The pledgee, therefore, is competent in law to sue for his debt without selling the pledged property and adjusting its price towards the payment of the debt. He has, however, to keep the property pledged intact so that he may be able to hand over the security to the pledger on payment of the debt by him". The learned Counsel has also referred to the case of Haridas Mundra vs National & Grindlays Bank Ltd. reported in AIR 1963 Cal., 132 wherein it has been observed "in a case where the pawner makes default, the right of the pawnee to sue upon the debt or promise does not exclude or destroy his right to sell the pawn. The pawnee's rights to sue upon the debt or the promise or to sell the pawn are concurrent, and not alternative, rights". He has also referred to the case of Jiwan Das and another vs Sahu Sarju Prasad and others reported in AIR 1945 Allahabad. 299 wherein it has been observed "the personal rights of the pledgee of goods arising out of his special property in them conferred by the pledge, but I should be most reluctant to hold that there is any implication that the Contract Act, by defining his personal rights, cuts down in any way any remedy he may have through the Courts. The truth appears to me to be that the Court always has an inherent jurisdiction to administer, by sale or otherwise, the property of which it has seisin in any suit which is, in effect, an administration suit. I do not think that a suit on a mortgage or pledge is in its essential characteristics anything but an administration suit of the same kind as a suit for the execution of a trust, for the administration of the estate of a deceased person, for the administration of partnership assets in a partnership suit or any other suit of the same kind. All such suits are in substance suits to ascertain and declare the rights of some person having an interest in specified property and asking the Court, in its administrative jurisdiction to ascertain and give practical effect to his rights......This, however, serves as no reason for supposing that, where a man has an additional remedy outside the Court, but prefers to come to the Court, he should be prevented from doing so ....... a pawnee had a right to seek his remedies through the Court and was not bound to rely upon his personal remedies". The learned Counsel in support of his contention has referred to the case of SL Ramaswamy Chetty and another vs MSAPL Palaniappa Chettiar reported in AIR 1930 Madras. 364 and therein it has been observed "The respondent could not compel the appellants to exercise the power of sale as a means of discharging or satisfying the decree. His only rights were (1) in case the appellants exercised the power, to insist that it should be honestly and properly done and the sale proceeds applied to the debt; (2) in case the appellants did not exercise the power, to redeem the pledges on payment of the debt or so much of it as remained otherwise unpaid and (3) in case the sale was improperly exercised, to get damages caused thereby".

9. As against the contention of the appellant that a pawnee can proceed with his suit for realisation of the amount due from the pawner keeping the pawned goods as collateral security, the learned Counsel appearing for the pawner in support of his contention that the pawnee cannot proceed with the suit against the pawner without selling the pawned goods has referred to the case of Pubali Bank Ltd vs Sultana Oil Mills and Soap Factory and others reported in 51 DLR 323 wherein it has been observed "the provision of sections 176 and 177 of the Contract Act further provide that sale of pledged goods is a condition precedent before the institution of the suit". Provision of section 176 of the Contract Act relates to right of the pawnee and section 177 of the said Act relates to right of the defaulting pawner.

10. From the reading of section 176 of the Contract Act it is seen that pawnee in case of default by the pawner in payment of debt, or performance, at the stipulated time of the promise in respect of which the goods were pledged, is left with the option either to bring a suit against the pawner upon the debt or promise, and retain the goods pledged as a collateral security; or he may sell the goods pledged on giving the pawner reasonable notice of sale. After the sale if the debt is not fully covered, the pawnee has the right to file the suit for realisation of the amount due from the pawner and that after adjustment of the sale proceed against the debt of the pawnee if there remains any surplus, the pawnee shall pay the surplus to the pawner. The first portion of section 176 of the Contract Act relates to the remedy of the pawnee, that is, either to file the suit for realisation of the amount due from the pawner or to sell the pledged goods. These rights are two distinct kinds of rights. The pawnee is not precluded from exercising the first category of right i.e. institution of the suit for realisation of the debt due from the pawner keeping the pawned goods as collateral security without exercising the second category of right ie to sell the hypothecated goods at first and then upon adjustment of the sale proceeds is to go for realisation of the balance, if any, by instituting a suit. The rights of the pawnee are distinct and independent of each other and the exercise of the first one is not conditioned by the second one. The rights as have been given to the pawnee by the provision of section 176 of the Contract Act are two separate rights and different from each other. In that view of the matter we are of the opinion that High Court Division in the case reported in 51 DLR 323 was in error in observing "that sale of pledged goods is a condition precedent before institution of the suit". We are of the opinion that High Court Division totally misread as well as misinterpreted the provision of section 176 of the Contract Act in observing that a pawnee before filing the suit for realisation of the amount due from the pawner against the debt would be required to sell the pledged goods first. The High Court Division in observing that without selling the pledged goods pawnee cannot file the suit for realisation of the amount due from the pawner because of his default in the payment of the debt or performance at the stipulated time of the promise was not correct, in that the material fact is that the options left to the pawnee in the aforesaid situation are disjunctive. The legislature in making available to the pawnee the remedies in case of default on the part of the pawner has provided two (2) options ie for realisation of the debt amount to file the suit keeping the pledged goods as a collateral security or to sell the pawned goods. These rights are two distinct and separate rights and independent of each other is evidenced by the use of the word. 'or'. In that view of the matter one right is not conditioned by the other and, as such, position of law in the light of provision of section 176 of the Contract Act spelt out by the High Court Division in the case reported in 51 DLR that right to file the suit for realisation of the debt amount from the pawner is to be proceeded by the sale of the pawned goods is not the correct exposition of law.

11. In the background of the discussions made hereinover, in our opinion, the provision of section 176 of the Contract Act in the case reported in 51 DLR has not been correctly considered and interpreted and, as such, proposition of law laid down therein is not correct. Rather the decision of the High Court Division is against the provision of law as in section 176 of the Contract Act. The learned Counsel for the appellant at one stage of hearing has also referred to the case of Bengal Metro Engineering Co and others vs Agrani Bank reported in 46 DLR 68 wherein it has been observed "From a plain reading of the above section of the Contract Act, it appears that for the realisation of payment of any debt or pawn from the defaulter pawner, there is no bar in the institution of a proper suit by the pawnee and at the same time to retain the pledged goods, if any, in his custody as a collateral security".

<u>12. Upon the reading of section 176 of the Contract Act and in the background of the observation in the cases referred to from the side of the appellant, we are of the view that High Court Division was in error in affirming the order of the Adalat dated August 17, 2000 passed in Money Suit No. 74 of 1999 directing the plaintiff-appellant to sell the pawned goods and that to adjust the sale proceed against his claim and that thereupon, if any amount remains due against the pawner-defendant then to proceed with the suit upon amendment of the plaint for the amount so remained due against the pawner, in that law relating to the right of the pawnee does not require him to sell the pawned goods first and thereafter, if any amount remains due from the pawner then to file the suit for the realisation thereof. While the law does not require the pawnee to sell the pawned goods first and then to file the suit for the amount, if any remains due from the pawner, the court is not competent to make an order in a suit filed by the pawnee directing him to sell the pawned goods and that upon adjustment of the sale proceeds, if any amount remains due then to proceed with the suit for the balance amount.</u>

13. In the background of our discussions we find merit in the appeal.

14. Accordingly, the appeal is allowed.

There is no order as to costs.

End.

Dr M Zahir, Senior Advocate and Akhter Imam, Senior Advocate  ----- For Respondent Nos. 3 and 4

full_judgment:
ABM Khairul Haque J: This appeal arises out of the order dated 8-4-2001 passed by the Subordinate Judge, Fifth Court, Dhaka, in Title Suit No. 232 of 1999 in rejecting the plaint under Order VII rule 11 of Code of Civil Procedure.

2. The facts leading to the filing of the suit out of which this appeal arises, in brief, are that one Shafi A Chowdhury, instituted the instant suit for declaration and injunction against Pubali Bank Ltd., Bangladesh Bank and others contending, inter alia, that 6,35,980 shares out of 6,56,000 shares of Albert David (Bangladesh) Ltd. (the company') proforma-defendant No.8, belonged to non-Bangladeshi nationals, as such, they said company was declared abandoned and those shares stood vested in the Government represented by the Ministry of Industries under the provisions of Bangladesh Industrial Enterprises (Nationalisation) Order 1972 (President's Order No. 27 of 1972). In pursuance of the policy of the Government those shares were disinvested and the plaintiff purchased those shares in public auction followed by an agreement dated 7-4-1984 by and between the defendant No. 7, Bangladesh Chemical Industries Corporation and the plaintiff and the liabilities of the defendant company owed to the Pubali Bank Ltd. to the extent of Taka 1.15 crore was accepted by the plaintiff who became the Chairman and the Managing Director of the company, but in spite of his payments towards the price of the shares of the Company the defendant No. 5, Government, failed to transfer the said shares in his favour and six others. As such, the plaintiff filed a suit for specific performance of contract, declaration and injunction being Title Suit No. 101 of 1998 before the Third Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka, which was renumbered as Title Suit No. 161 of 1999, on being transferred to the Second Commercial Court at Dhaka. The plaintiff further stated that during the period from June, 1992 to December, 1992, he repeatedly requested the defendant Pubali Bank Ltd to make an audit in the accounts of the company in order to find out the actual dues outstanding against the company and also asked them not to charge interest during the audit period but the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 delayed the matter in calculating the interest by nearly three years although he wanted to clear his dues as he was at that time a director of the Pubali Bank Ltd. The further case of the plaintiff that suddenly by a letter dated 11-8-1997, issued by Bangladesh Bank, defendant No. 3, enclosing a notice dated 7-81997 of the defendant No. 1, Pubali Bank Ltd, issued under section 17 of the Bank Companies Act, 1991 ('the Act') demanding payment of Taka 2,25,03,408.62 within a period of two months from the date of receipt of the said notice, failing which, the notice further stated, the plaintiffs post as a director of Pubali Bank Ltd would stand vacated. On receipt of the said notice, the plaintiff issued a notice upon the Bangladesh Bank, demanding withdrawal of the said notice, but without waiting for a period of 15 days which Bangladesh Bank was required to give a decision, under section 17(3) of the Act, a writ petition under Article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, being Writ Petition No. 5358 of 1997, was filed before the High Court Division on behalf of the plaintiff challenging the legality and the propriety of the notice dated 11-8-1997. Subsequently, after hearing, the Rule was discharged. His appeal before the Appellate Division being Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 851 of 1999 was also dismissed. Thereafter, the plaintiff filed another representation on 25-8-1999 before the Bangladesh Bank stating, inter alia, that he was neither a borrower nor a defaulter or a guarantor for the alleged liability of the Company and prayed for withdrawal of the notices dated 7-8-1997 and dated 11-8-1997 issued under section 17 of the Act but this was refused by the reply dated 3-10-1999, made on behalf of Bangladesh Bank but asked the plaintiff that he was at liberty to see the General Manager of Bangladesh Bank in this' respect. It was also stated in the plaint that on an earlier occasion the defendant Nos. 3 and 4 by their orders dated 19-8-1995, removed the plaintiff from the post of directorship of the Pubali Bank Ltd. under section 46 of the Act. The plaintiff challenged his such removal in Writ Petition No. 211 of 1998 but after hearing the Rule, the said writ petition was discharged by a judgment and order dated 17-5-1999. Against the said judgment and order he went in appeal before the Appellate Division being Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 646 of 1999 and also obtained an order of stay for a period of six months till 12-1-2000. The further case of the plaintiff is that although he took over the management of the company since 7-4-1984 and was acting as its Chairman and Managing Director but since he is not holding any share, he is running the management of the company as its authorised agent and he himself is neither a borrower nor a defaulter of the defendant No.1, as such, is not liable to repay any dues on behalf of the Company because no shares have yet been transferred in his favour. That Pubali Bank Ltd., the defendant No.1, by its letter dated 5-9-1995, informed the company that its liability stood at 1,15,03,916.25 but illegally referred the matter to Bangladesh Bank for its approval although the plaintiff was a director of the defendant No. 1 and the company never applied for remission of any interest, rather, he already paid Taka 11, 50,391 to the defendant No. 1 on behalf of the Company. Since his case was not considered on merit either by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 5358 of 1997 or in appeal, by the Appellate Division and since some incorrect statements were made in the writ petition due to inadvertence, the plaintiff on 24-8-1999 and on 25- 8-1999 gave elaborate replies to the notice dated 11-8-1997 of Bangladesh Bank, the defendant No. 3 but was regretted by them by their letter dated 3-10-1999. As such, the plaintiff filed the instant suit for declaration and injunction on 14-10-1999, for redress of his grievances and made the following prayers.

a)	decree of declaration declaring that the plaintiff is neither a borrower or loanee nor a defaulter of Pubali Bank Ltd the defendant Nos. 1 & 2 and, as such, he is not a defaulter within the meaning of the Bank Companies Act, 1991 and not liable to pay the debt of Albert David (Bangladesh) Ltd, the proforma defendant No. 8.

b)	To declare that the letter No. PU. Bank/Proka/78/97 dated 7-8-97 issued by Pubali Bank Ltd. the defendant No.1 and letter No. BRPD(P) 651/9(8)99-1353 dated 3- 10-99 issued by the Bangladesh Bank, the defendant Nos. 3 and 4 and the contents thereof are unlawful, malafide, void without jurisdiction and not binding upon the plaintiff.

c)	To restrain the defendant Nos. 1 to 4 from giving effect to letter No. PU. Bank/Proka/78/97 dated 7-8-97 issued by Pubali Bank Ltd the defendant No. 1 and letter No BRPD (P) 651/9/97-749 dated 11-8-97 and Letter No. BRPD (P) 651/9/(8)99-1353 dated 3-10-99 issued by the Bangladesh Bank the defendant Nos. 3 and 4 regarding directorship or Pubali Bank Ltd., and also restrain the defendants from interfering with the functioning of the plaintiff as Director of Pubali Bank Ltd.

d)	To declare that the plaintiff is still a Director of the Pubali Bank Ltd the defendant No. 1.

e)	a decree declaring that outstanding liabilities of Albert David (Bangladesh) Ltd. determined at Taka 1,15,03,916.25 out of which 10% of the said amount Taka 11,50,391.63 already being paid the balance of Taka 1,03,53,524.62 only is payable.

f)	All costs of the suit in favour of the plaintiff,

g)	Any other relief or reliefs to which the plaintiff is entitled under the law and equity.

3.	The defendant No. 3, Bangladesh Bank appeared in the suit and filed an application on 8-5-2000 under Order VII rule 11 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure, praying for rejection of the plaint. In the said petition it was contended on behalf of Bangladeshi Bank that since the plaintiff had already unsuccessfully challenged the notice dated 11-8-1997 issued under section 17 of the Bank Companies Act before the Supreme Court, High Court Division, in Writ Petition No. 5358 of 1997 and since his writ petition was dismissed which was upheld by the Appellant Division, the present suit holding that the notice dated 11-8-1997 was validly issued and the letter dated 3-10-1999, filed on the self-same ground, challenging his removal as a director of Pubali Bank Ltd in pursuance of the said notice dated 11-8-1997, is not maintainable. Since both the High Court Division as well as the Appellate Division .held that the plaintiff was responsible for the loan to Albert David (Bangladesh) Ltd., that the letter dated 3-10-1997 was a mere follow-up of the earlier letter dated 11-8-1997 in reply to the representation of the plaintiff, the suit is barred by law and the plaintiff has got no cause of action for the suit. On these facts arid circumstances, the Bangladesh Bank, (the defendant No.3) prays for rejection of the plaint in limini. On a subsequent occasion in January, 2001, another supplementary petition was filed in the suit on behalf of the Pubali Bank Ltd., disclosing that the plaintiff failed to get himself re-elected in the last Annual General Meeting of the Bank held on 30-9-2000 and was no longer a Director of the said Bank.

4. In due course the petition under Order VII rule 11 of the Code was taken up for hearing on 8-4-2001 in presence of both the parties and after hearing, the learned Judge, considering the supplementary petition, by his order dated 8-4-2001, rejected the plaint on the ground that there was no cause of action for the suit as prayed for by the defendant and that it was barred by law. Being aggrieved the plaintiff filed the instant appeal against the said order dated 8-4-2001 rejecting the plaint and also the decree thereon.

5. Mr Rokanuddin Mahmud, Senior Advocate, appears with Mr Raziur Rahman Chowdhury, Advocate, on behalf of the appellant while Dr. M Zahir and Mr Akhtar Imam, Senior Advocates, appear on behalf of the Bangladesh Bank and Pubali Bank Ltd and Mr Tufailur Rahman, Advocate, appears with AKM Mohiuddin and Ms Sufia Ahmed, Advocates, on behalf of the respondent No. 7.

6. We have heard at length both Mr Rokanuddin Mahmud and also Mr Md Raziur Rahman Chowdhury on behalf of the appellant.

7. Mr Rokanuddin Mahmud, the learned Advocate submits that a plaint may be rejected under Order VII rule 11 of the Code but only if at least one of the conditions stated therein is satisfied on a plane reading of the plaint but in this case, he submits, the order dated 8-4-2001 by which the learned judge rejected the plaint, does not show that he at all considered the plaint, rather, the learned Judge illegally considered the matters extraneous to the plaint, such as, the decisions of the High Court Division in its writ jurisdiction and on appeal, the decision of the Appellate Division but failed to consider that the plaintiff himself never took any loan from the defendant No. 1 or anybody else but without appreciating the decisions of the High Court Division as well as the decision of the Appellate Division where only the notice dated 11-8-2001 issued by one of the defendants was challenged, wrongly and illegally rejected the plaint on a vague ground that there was no cause of action for the suit or it was barred by law, without any discussion on the plaint as to why there was no cause of action or how it was barred by law and specially under which law the suit was barred. The learned Advocate further submits that in disposing of a petition for rejection of a plaint under Order VII rule 11 of the Code, the learned Judge ought not to have considered the supplementary affidavit filed on behalf of the Pubali Bank Ltd. stating that the plaintiff was no longer a director as he failed to get himself elected in the Annual General Meeting of the said Banking Company held on 30-9-2000, rather, he ought to have confined himself in the four comers to the plaint and the plaint alone. Besides, he submits further the judgment and order in rejecting the plaint is not at all a speaking order, rather, was written in a most perfunctory manner without discussing either the necessary facts or the principles based on which he rejected the plaint. As such, he prays for setting aside the order rejecting the plaint and for allowing the appeal.

8. In reply Dr M Zahir, the learned Advocate, appearing on behalf of the defendant Nos. 1 to 4 while submitting that on a plain reading of the plaint and the facts and circumstances, wound around it, fully justifies the rejection of the plaint but he did not attempt at all to support the order of the learned Subordinate Judge. He frankly concedes that the order of the learned Judge in rejecting the plaint is rather shabby and does not reflect either the facts necessary for rejecting the plaint nor the necessary legal implications involved in this matter but he submits that this Court in first appeal, under section 107 of the Code of Civil Procedure. has got all the powers and duties of the Court of the original jurisdiction including the power to consider the question as to whether this plaint can be allowed to stand as it is and or to decide whether the suit is at all maintainable in its present form and manner although it was not so done by the trial Court. This was also conceded to by Mr Rokanuddin Mahmud that under section 107 of the Code, this Court has got all the powers, in proper case, to adjudicate the question of rejecting a plaint and the question of maintainability of the suit if the situation so demands.

<u>9. There is hardly any doubt that section 107 of the Code clothes the Appellate Court with all the powers of the Court of original jurisdiction. Reliance in this respect may be made in the decisions reported in AIR 1924 Nagpur 80, AIR 1942 Cal 539, AIR 1951 All 64 FB, AIR 1969 (SC) 1349. The appellate Court can also take into consideration subsequent events and even the change in law (Ref. AIR 1928 Cal 43, AIR 1931 Bom 280, AIR 1974 (SC) 2068).</u>

<u>10. It appears that this provision of the Code amply empowers a Court in its first appellate jurisdiction to consider all and each question of fact as well as the law including the question relating to the rejection of a plaint and also the maintainability of the suit.</u>

11. Mr Rokanuddin Mahmud, the learned Advocate, then took us through the entire plaint, a certified copy which was supplied on behalf of the appellant, and also the prayers made thereon. He submits that the plaintiff was constrained to file the instant suit for declaration under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act since he has got both legal status as Chairman and Managing Director of the Company and also right to property which was threatened in all respect by the defendants, as such, he has got cause of action for the suit which is stated in his paragraph 48 of his plaint. Under such circumstances, the plaint which satisfies the provisions of Order VII of the Code of Civil Procedure and also the suit filed under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act being legal and valid the question of rejection of the plaint does not arise. Besides, the question of maintainability of the suit cannot be decided at this stage without the written statement filed on behalf of the defendant and only after framing of the issue, this question can be considered at the time of hearing of the suit. As such, he prays that the appeal should be allowed and the order of rejection of the plaint be set aside, so that the suit may proceed in accordance with law with all the opportunities to the defendant to defend their case in filing written statement and in giving evidence at the trial.

12. Dr M Zahir, the learned Advocate, on behalf of both of the Bangladesh Bank and Pubali Bank Ltd. firstly, submits that the plaint can be rejected under anyone of the provisions mentioned in Order VII rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure and it is not even necessary to write the various grounds and facts in details in the petition for rejection of the plaint, however, the relevant provisions should be brought to the notice of the Court that the plaint is liable to be rejected because of the reason as it comes within the ambit of rule 11, such as, the plaint does not disclose a cause of action or that relief claimed is undervalued or the plaint is written upon paper insufficiently stamped or the suit appears from the statement in the plaint to be barred by any law and if any of the above mentioned grounds is raised at any stage of the suit, it is incumbent on the Court to consider whether the plaint is liable to be rejected under any of the provisions of rule 11. He submits specifically that in this case the plaint is liable to be rejected because it is barred by law, such as, res judicata and there was no cause of action for the suit.

13. So far the question of res judicata is concerned he submits that the Appellate Division not only considered the legality of the notice dated 11-8-1997, issued by the Bangladesh Bank but also considered the merit of the claims of the defendants No. 1 against the plaintiff and dismissed the appeal upholding the decision of the High Court Division. The said notice, issued under section 17 of the Act, giving details of the liabilities of the plaintiff in respect of the company owed to the defendant, having been finally decided by the highest Court of the country, the learned Advocate submits, the self-same issue of liability of the plaintiff as narrated in the said notice cannot now be again re-opened in this suit as the same is barred under section 11 of the Code by being res judicata because the said notice gave the details of the liabilities of the plaintiff and that his position as a director of the defendant No.1 would also be vacated if he would fail to clear up his dues within a period of two months from the date of the said notice.

14. Mr Akhter Imam, the learned Advocate, also appearing on behalf of Bangladesh Bank, submits in this respect that a finding and a decision given by the High Court Division even in its writ jurisdiction can operate as res judicata in a subsequently filed suit between the same parties. In support of his contention he cites the case of Ashok Kumar Srivastav vs National Insurance Co Ltd AIR 1998 (SC) 2046 and submits that the finding of facts arrived at by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 5358 of 1997 by its judgment dated 14-6-1999 which was upheld by the Appellate Division by its judgment dated 16-8-1999, operate as res judicata in this subsequently filed suit on 14-10-1999, as such, the plaint was justifiably rejected under clause (d) of rule 11 under Order VII of the Code, the suit being barred by law.

<u>15. The wisdom of the aforesaid decision is not disputed. It is now well settled that if an issue was finally decided on merit in an earlier suit or even in a writ petition by the High Court Division, the same issue shall operate as res judicata in view of the provision of section 11 of the Code, in a subsequently filed suit .on the same issue. Reliance in this regard can be made in the decision in the cases of Daryao vs State of UP AIR 1961 (SC) 1457, Amalgamated. Coalfields Ltd vs Janapada Sabha, Chhindwara, 1964 (SC) 1013, YB Patil vs YL Patil AIR 1977 (SC) 392, GK Sharma SD Sharma 1986 Suppl SCC 239 and also the case reported in AIR 1998 (SC) 2046 .</u>

<u>16. But the question is, whether an. issue of res judicata can be resolved in disposing of a petition under clause (d) of rule 11 of Order VII of the Code. Generally, it cannot be d.one, because in rejecting a plaint under the said provision, the Court cannot travel beyond the four corners of the plaint. Even assuming that all the averments made in the plaint is correct, if the Court finds that still there is no cause of action for the suit or the suit is barred by law, only then the plaint may be rejected, otherwise not, Even in any of the decisions mentioned above, the issue of res judicata was not decided in a petition under Order VII rule 11 of the Code but at the time of hearing of the suit.</u>

<u>17. Theoretically however, it is still possible to reject a plaint on the ground of res judicata in an exceptional circumstance, if it is so found on a meaningful reading of the plaint. The case of Islami Bank Bangladesh Ltd vs Abdul Jalil 2000 BLD 508 = 52 DLR 571, provides such an example, where the plaint was rejected under Order VII rule 11 of the Code by the High Court Division, predominantly on the ground of res judicata, which was also upheld by the Appellate Division in 2000 BLD (AD) 278. Mahmudul Amin Choudhury, J (as his Lordship then was) held in that case as follows at para 9:</u>

<u>"It is well settled now that a plaint may be rejected under Order 7 rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure merely on a plain reading of the plaint but in exceptional circumstances the court may invoke its inherent jurisdiction and can throw the plaint out in limini. It is also well settled that the plea of implied bar should be decided on evidence unless the facts disclosed in the plaint clearly indicate that the suit is not maintainable. In exceptional cases recourse may be taken even under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure."</u>

<u>His Lordship further reiterated at para 12:</u>

<u>"It is well settled that where a plaint cannot be rejected under Order VII rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure the Court may invoke its inherent jurisdiction and reject the plaint taking recourse to section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure."</u>

<u>18. Ordinarily, a plaint should not be rejected under Order VII rule 11 of the Code on the ground of res judicata unless it is so palpably clear and obvious from a meaningful reading of the plaint that no further evidence is required, in such circumstances without subjecting the defendant from further ordeal of a suit, the plaint may be rejected in limini, if it is not so definite and obvious, then in that circumstances, it is always prudent that the issue of res judicata should be considered at the time of hearing of the suit. In any view of the matter, a learned Judge in disposing of a petition to reject a plaint under Order VII rule 11 of the Code must apply his judicial mind and act very cautiously before throwing out the plaint and must not deal with the question hastily or in a slipshod manner. He can certainly do so if he is so satisfied that it has come within the ambit of rule lion a meaningful reading of the plaint alone and assuming all the statements made in the plaint to be correct, still it answers the conditions set out in rule 11, but his order must also clearly and without ambiguity reflect his such satisfaction that it has really come within the ambit of rule 11, otherwise not.</u>

19. We have gone through the plaint and found that in paragraphs 20-21 of the plaint the plaintiff categorically referred to Writ Petition No. 5853 of 1999 filed before the High Court Division and that the Rule was discharged and on appeal before the Appellate Division the Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 815 of 1999 was also dismissed. Since the judgments in the writ petition as well as in the leave to appeal before the Appellate Division was specifically mentioned and referred to in the plaint and was also read over and discussed before us, we can certainly refer to those decisions which were produced before us on behalf of the respondents as in the case of Abdul Jalil mentioned above. On perusal of the judgments of the Writ Petition No. 5853 of 1997 and CPLA No. 815 of 1999, it appears that the question of illegality and propriety of the notice dated 11-8-1997 issued under section 17 of the Act was considered. Although the High Court Division as well as the Appellate Division considered the facts leading to the issuance of that notice but it appears to us that both the Divisions of the Supreme Court considered only the legality of the issuance of the notice dated 11-8-1997, not the quantum of liabilities of the plaintiff. It is true that both the High Court Division as well as the Appellate Division made discussions on the liabilities of the Company and also of the plaintiff but such discussion of facts was required only to decide the question of legality of the notice dated 11-8-1997. It is true that the letter dated 7-8-1997 of the defendant No. 1, which was enclosed with the notice dated 11-8-1997, stated the liabilities of the plaintiff in respect of the company but the purpose of such discussion of facts was certainly not to decide the liability of the company or the plaintiff but only such of the facts which was required to dispose of the writ petition and the appeal thereon. In that view of the matter, the decisions of the High Court Division and the Appellate Division, although would operate as res judicata so far as the prayers 'b', 'c' and 'd' made in paragraph 50 of the plaint is concerned, but not the rest of the prayers. As such, we are unable to accept the contention raised by Dr M Zahir and Mr Akhtar Imam that the decisions taken in the writ petition as well as in the appeal operate as res judicata in respect of the entire suit.

20. The next point raised by Dr M Zahir and Mr Akhter Imam is with regard to the cause of action and maintainability of the suit. They refer to the decision in the case of Burmah Eastern Ltd vs Burmah Eastern Employees Union PLD 1967 Dacca 190 = 18 DLR 709 and also refer to the decision of Chowmuhani College vs Md Ismail Hossain 26 DLR 10 and submit that if on a plane reading of the plaint, if it appears to the Court that there is no cause of action for the suit or that the suit is incompetent, the plaint is liabile to be rejected outright. In this .case, they submit, firstly, the laibilities of the Company as well as that of the plaintiff having already been finally decided by both the Divisions of the Supreme Court while considering the notice dated 11-8-1997 enclosing the accounts of the liabilities in the latter dated 7-8-1997, there is nothing further for the learned Subordinate Judge to consider. Secondly, since admittedly, the plaintiff could not get himself elected as one of the directors of the Pubali Bank Ltd (the defendant No. 1), he is not entitled to any declaration as to his legal character or status as such director. Thirdly, the plaintiff is not entitled to any declaration which is based on his contractual or financial/pecuniary relationship with the defendant No. 1 as contained in prayer C in his plaint, as such, they submit, instead of unnecessarily subjecting the defendants to the circuitous course of the suit till pre-emptory hearing, the plaint should be rejected in limini, even if not under Order VII rule 11 of the Code, but under the inherent jurisdiction of the Court as propounded by SM Murshed, CJ in the case of Bunnah Eastern Ltd and also in the case of Abdul Jalil (20 BLD (AD) 278). They further submit that the plaint can be rejected at any stage of the suit if it comes within the ambit of Order VII rule 11 of the Code or if it is found to be incompetent or not maintainable, as was found to be so by the learned Subordinate Judge and rightly rejected the plaint, although he could not substantiate his such finding by proper readings which he ought to have done. In this manner both of them assiduously submit that the facts even as stated in the plaint itself show that there was no cause of action for the suit and since the suit is incompetent, the order rejecting the plaint should be upheld, they conclude.

21. As this stage when asked specifically as to whether the plaintiff is still a director of the defendant No. 1 or not, both Mr Rokanuddin Mahmud and Mr Raziur Rahman Chowdhury, Advocates, specifically concede that the plaintiff did not contest in the last Annual General Meeting of the defendant Pubali Bank Ltd. held in month of September, 2000, as such, he is no longer a director of the Pubali Bank Ltd and it was verbally conceded so when the petition by way of supplementary affidavit was filed on behalf of the defendant No. 1 in January, 2001, before the Court of Subordinate Judge. Both the learned Advocates concede before us that since the plaintiff was not a director of the Pubali Bank Ltd. his prayers in the plaint as stated in sub-paragraph Nos. b, c and d of paragraph 50 became infructuous. They also submit that their memorandum of appeal refers only to the prayers A and C which is equivalent to the prayers 'a' and 'e' respectively made in the plaint but they maintain that the plaint as well as their prayers for declaration as made out in paragraph 'a' as well as 'e' are proper, legal and comes within the four comers of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. They also submit that if strictly speaking, even assuming but not admitting that their prayers for the decree for declarations as made in sub-paragraph 'a' and 'e' of the plaint do not strictly come within the purview of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act but certainly come under Order VII rule 7 read with section 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure independent of the Specific Relief Act and, in that view of the matter, they submit that the plaint cannot be rejected in limini since the suit is maintainable.

22. We have heard the learned Advocates of both the sides at length and also went through the plaint. The plaint gives a resume of the disputes between the parties which was narrated earlier. This is a suit for declaration. Paragraph 48 specifically describes the cause of action while paragraph 50 embodies five specific prayers for declaration with two other general prayers. It is a cardinal principle of law, well settled by the decisions of the superior Courts of the sub-continent that for deciding a question whether a plaint should be rejected under Order VII rule 11 of the Code, the Court should confine itself to the averments made in the plaint and plaint alone and cannot ordinarily travel beyond it. The Court cannot consider the written statement or any other document or paper in this connection; rather, assume that all the statements made in the plaint are correct. But in spite of such assumption, if the Court finds that the plaint does not disclose a cause of action or it is undervalued, or it is insufficiently stamped or it is barred by any law, then it becomes incumbent on the Court to reject the plaint outright. There is a long line of decisions establishing this point of law and the wisdom of those decisions is unquestionable. But in this case a special situation arose. One of the prayers made in the plaint is for a declaration that the plaintiff is still a director of the Pubali Bank Ltd., subsequent to the filing of the suit, in pursuance of an Annual General Meeting held in due course on 30-9-2000, he was not elected as a director of the defendant No. 1. This fact was brought to the notice of the Court at the earliest opportunity in January, 2000, by the defendant No. 1 and conceded to by the plaintiff himself so much so that he subsequently forget his such prayer for declaration as director of Pubali Bank Ltd. The question raised before us is as to whether the said petition divulging the fact that the plaintiff could not get himself elected as a director can be taken into consideration in deciding the prayer for rejection of the plaint under Order VII rule 11 of the Code. We have already held that in considering the question of rejection of a plaint the court cannot ordinarily travel beyond the four corners of the plaint but if a document comes before the Court which is conceded to by the plaintiff himself in such circumstances, what useful purpose would be served by proceeding with the suit and thereafter to dismiss such a prayer for declaration after raising a contested issue to that effect when such a prayer had already been abandoned by the plaintiff himself. In such a situation, we are of the view that the Court should not be that much naive or astute to keep its eyes closed and ignore the facts brought before it which will ultimately prejudice not only the defendant but also the plaintiff who will have a chance to retrace his steps, at the earliest possible moment, so that if permissible under law, he may found a properly constituted case.

<u>23. In such circumstances where a certain fact is brought to the notice of the Court, though not specifically mentioned in the plaint or crops up subsequent to the filing of the suit and accepted as true by both the parties including the plaintiff then such a fact, though not referred to in the plaint, can be taken into consideration by the Court in considering the question of rejection of a plaint under Order VII rule 11 of the Code. It would have been otherwise had it been objected to by the plaintiff. In that case, however sacrosanct the document may be, it ought to be duly proved on evidence, before it is accepted and acted upon by the Court in deciding an issue before it. That was not the case here, it was rather conceded by the plaintiff. In that view of the matter we shall take into account and consider the petition filed on behalf of Pubali Bank Ltd in January, 2001 that since 30-9-2000 the plaintiff was no longer the director of Pubali Bank Ltd.</u>

24. Now let us see how far the suit is maintainable and whether the plaint is liable to be rejected under Order VII rule 11 of the Code or the suit is liable to be dismissed as not maintainable, not filed properly as a declaratory suit.

25. Now let us first consider the legal position in this respect. The particulars of a plaint are contained in rule I under Order VII containing the details of the plaint. Order VII rule 2 envisages a suit for movable property. A declaratory suit is envisaged under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act but there may be other forms of suit also as envisaged under section 9 of the Code read with Order VII rule 7 of the Code. Order VII rule 5 requires that the plaint must state the defendant's liability and Order VII rule 9 describes the procedure for admitting the plaint.

26. In this appeal, Mr Rokanuddin Mahmud, Advocate, firstly, argues that his suit definitely comes within the ambit of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act.

27. The ingredients of section 42 as decided in different decisions of this sub-continent that the plaintiff must establish that (i) the plaintiff at the time of institution of the suit is entitled to a legal character and or a right to any property, (ii) the defendant has denied such character or title of the plaintiff, (iii) declaration asked for is a declaration that the plaintiff is entitled to such a right to property and in certain cases the plaintiff is in such a position that he does not require any consequential relief.

28. This is an equitable principle of law originally evolved from Scotch action of declaration. In England, a mere decree for declaration is an innovation. Originally, a declaration was not given except as an introductory to the relief which the Court proceeded to allow. This kind of decree for mere declaration was first accorded authorative sanction in England by section 50 of the Chancery Procedure Act, 1852. The said provision was made applicable to the Supreme Courts in India by section 19 of Act VI of 1854. This relief of mere declaration was adopted in India by section 15 of the Code of Civil Procedure of 1859. In 1862, when the Supreme Courts in India were abolished and the High Courts were established, the provisions of the Civil Procedure Code of 1859 were extended to the Courts established by Charters. In 1877 by Act X, a new Code of Civil Procedure was enacted repealing the earlier Code but the new Code did not contain any provision like that of the section of the earlier Code because in 1877 by Act I, a new Act, namely, Specific Relief Act, was enacted which contains Section 42. The provision further widened the scope of the relief with regard to declaration. However, this provision does not provide or contemplate all kinds of declarations, rather, what is provided for in the section itself, such as, only a declaration that the plaintiff is entitled to any legal character or any right to any property. In this connection, it would be pertinent to refer how Jenkins CJ viewed section 42 in the case of Musstt Deokali Koer vs Babu Kedar Nath 16 CWN 838.

"The section does not sanction every form of declaration, but only a declaration that the plaintiff is entitled to "any legal character or to any right as to any property" it is the disregard to this that accounts for the multiform and at times eccentric declarations which find a place in Indian plaints.

If the Courts were astute-as I think they should be-to see that the plaints presented, conformed to the terms of section 42, the difficulties that are to be found in this class of cases, would no longer arise. Nor would plaintiffs be unduly hampered if the provisions of section 42 were enforced, for it would be easy to form a declaration in such terms as would comply with the provisions of the section where the claim was one within its policy."

His Lordship further held as follows:

"I would only add this, that the limit imposed by section 42 is on decrees which are merely declaratory, and does not expressly extend to decrees in which relief is administered, and declarations are embodied as introductory to that relief. For such declarations legislative sanction is not required; they rest on long established practice. But for all that the Court should be circumspect and even chary as to the declarations it makes; it is ordinarily enough that relief should be granted without the declaration. "

Similarly, in the case of Sheoparsan Singh vs Ramnandan Prasad Singh AIR 1916 PC 78 a suit praying for a declaration that the plaintiffs were the next reversioners to the estate of one Rup Narayan, alias Bachu Singh, deceased and, as such, were entitled to obtain revocation of probate granted earlier by the District Judge where they also-raised their such claim. On behalf of the Board, Sir Lawrence Jenkins, J, held:

" .....the suit fails at the very outset, for the plaintiffs, while the will stands, as stand it must for the purposes of this suit, are not clothed with a legal character or title which would authorise them to ask for the declaratory decree sought by their plaint. The suit, therefore, should be dismissed because it is misconceived and incompetent."

29. Similarly, declaration that the defendant is liable to pay the plaintiff such money as he is liable to pay under a decree is not maintainable in the case of Sripatrao Sada Shiv Upre vs Shankarrao Sarnaik AIR 1930 Bom 331 so also in a similar circumstances in the case of Nathu Ram vs Mula AIR 1937 Lal 25. or that a suit for declaration in respect of rights arising out of a contract which would affect only the pecuniary relationship, between the parties to the contract was held to be not maintainable in the case of Ramkrishna vs Narayana (1915) ILR 39 Madras.

30. In the case of Krishnaveni Ammal vs Soundararajan, AIR 1945 Mad 53 a suit for declaration that certain transfers made by the defendant were made for the purpose of defrauding the creditors, Mockett offg, CJ held:

"It is true, as laid down in the various decisions to which I have referred, that the general view is that section 42, Specific Relief Act, is not exhaustive, but there is no authority for the proposition that a suit for a declaratory decree will lie when the plaintiff is neither entitled to any legal character nor to any right in the suit property."

31. But there may be cases where the plaintiff was not suing as a person entitled to any legal character or to any right as to any property and, as such, the suit was barred under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act.

32. In the case of Fischer vs Secretary of State for India in Council 26 IA 16, Lord Macnaghten, for the Judicial Council, explained section 42 in this manner at page 27:

"Now, in the first place it is at least open to doubt whether the present suit is within the purview of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. There can be no doubt as to the origin and purpose of that section. It was intended to introduce the provision of section 50 of the Chancery Procedure Act of 1852 (15 & 16 Vict, c 86) as interpreted by judicial decision. Before the Act of 1852 it was not the practice of the Court in ordinary suits to make a declaration of right except as introductory to relief which it proceeded to administer. But the present suit is one to which no objection could have been taken before the Act of 1852. It is in substance a suit to have the true construction of a statute declared, and to have an act done in contravention of the statute rightly understood pronounced void and of no effect. That is not the sort of declaratory decree which the framers of the Act had in their mind."

In the case of Partab Singh vs Bhabuti Shing (1913) 40 IA 182 Sir John Edge on behalf of the Judicial Council while holding that section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877 did not apply held as follows at page 192:

" .....that the appellants, Partab Singh and Ahbaran Singh, should have a decree setting aside the decree of December 15, 1899, in their suit, and declaring that the agreement of compromise and the decree of December 15, 1899, in the suit of Bhabuti Singh are not binding upon them or either of them, and that they are entitled to such rights as they had before their suit was dismissed on December 15, 1899."

Similarly, the provisions of section 42, Specific Relief Act, are not exhaustive is well established in a long line of decisions, such as a suit which did not come within the purview of section 42 but declaration was given that the plaintiff was a Mohal Rajput in the case of Ghulam Rasul Khan vs Secretary of State for India (1925) 6 ILR (Lah) 269. an order debarring one from acting as vakil for another in a Village Court was held to be maintainable in the case of Ramchandra Rao vs Secretary of State AIR 1916 (Mad) 1061.

33. The Supreme Court of India in the case of Ramaraghaba Reddi vs Seshu Reddi, considered the scope of section 42 and held that the said provision is not exhaustive. In that case a suit was instituted for a declaration that the provision in the earlier compromise decree that the lands mentioned in the schedule were the personal properties of certain defendants and binding on the temple. Ramaswami, J, on consideration of a long line of decisions, held:

"In our opinion, section 42 of the Specific Relief Act is not exhaustive of the cases in which a declaratory decree may be made and the courts have power to grant such a decree independently of the requirements of the section. It follows, therefore, in the present case that the suit of the plaintiff for a declaration that the compromise decree is not binding on the deity is maintainable as falling outside the purview of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act."

This principle was also followed in the case of M/s Supreme General Films Exchange Ltd vs His Highness Maharaja Sir Brijnath Singhji Deo of Maihar AIR 1975 (SC) 1810 and also in the case of Ashok Kumar Srivastav vs National Insurance Co Ltd AIR 1998 (SC) 2046.

34. Keeping this legal position in view let us now consider the question of maintainability of the present suit under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. We have already found that among the reliefs prayed for in the plaint, some of those are already stated to be infructuous due to events over-running the plaintiff. The learned Advocates for the appellant frankly concede to this and candidly submits that they would only press their prayers 'a' and 'e' in the plaint which are mentioned as paragraph 'A' and 'C' in their Memorandum of Appeal. Both of them specifically stated that they would not press other prayers in the plaint.

35. Let us reiterate the facts described by the plaintiff in the plaint by way of cause of action to file the instant suit for declaration. Firstly, the plaintiff described himself to be a private person, a businessman by vocation. He narrated that in auction he and 6(six) others purchased 6,35,900 shares of Albert David (Bangladesh) Ltd. but could not yet get those shares transferred to him by the Government defendant No. 5, for which he had already filed another suit. Secondly, although the shares were not transferred in his name and 6(six) others but he was acting as chairman and managing director of the concerned company. Thirdly, in the year 1992 he raised certain objections on the calculation of interest in respect of the loan of Albert David (Bangladesh) Ltd but the Pubali Bank Ltd. took nearly 3 years to furnish the audited accounts of the said company. Fourthly, the legality of the notice dated 11 "8-1991, issued by the defendant No. 3 which he challenged in his Writ Petition. Fifthly, after dismissal of the writ petition, the reply of Bangladesh Bank dated 3-10-1999 refusing to withdraw their notice dated 11-8-1997. Since notice was issued by the Bangladesh Bank enclosing a letter of the defendant No.1 Pubali Bank Ltd dated 7-8-1997 stating his alleged liability to be Taka 2,25,03,408.62, according to the plaintiff, that demand raised by the Pubali Bank Ltd., endorsed by the Bangladesh Bank, gave rise to the cause of action, amongst others, for the suit. As such, he prayed for declarations, inter alia, that the plaintiff is neither a borrower nor a loanee as mentioned in prayer 'a', as such, not a defaulter within the meaning of the Bank Companies Act, 1991 and also prayed for a declaration that after payment of Taka 11,50,391:63, the balance of Taka 1,03,53,524.62 only is payable as mentioned in prayer 'e' of the plaint which were also mentioned in prayers A and C respectively in the Memorandum of Appeal in this Court.

<u>36. Now we have to examine whether the plaint as a whole with those two prayers is maintainable under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, in view of the legal position discussed above. On a plain reading of the plaint, it would show that the plaintiff is not praying for any declaration as to his legal character or any right as to any property which is the basis for a suit for a declaration under section 42 so well propounded by Jenkins, CJ. He is claiming that he is not a borrower or a loanee or a defaulter. He personally may not be the borrower but he was found to be a defaulter within the meaning of section 17 of the Bank Companies Act, by the Appellate Division. Besides, his claim that he is required to pay Taka 1,03,53,524.62 only and not Taka 2,25,03,408.62 as demanded by the defendant No.1 depends on the contractual relationship between the parties. This kind of declaration involving pecuniary relationship of the concerned parties does not come within ambit of declaratory suit under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. What the plaintiff is claiming is not a declaration of his legal character or as to his any right but the extent of his contractual obligations involving his financial liabilities. The above noted decisions would unmistakably show that a declaration with a regard to the contractual or financial obligation involved or transacted between the parties cannot come within the ambit of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. Besides, such a declaration may tend to oust the jurisdiction of the Artha Rin Adalat established under the Artha Rin Adalat Act, 1990 because if such a declaration is given that the plaintiff is not a defaulter or he is not a borrower or he is not a loanee the Pubali Bank Ltd., as a creditor, may be prejudiced in filing a suit against the plaintiff claiming repayment of loan before any court. As such, we would hold that this prayer on the basis of the averments made in the plaint that the plaintiff is not a borrower or a defaulter is not maintainable, simply because this pecuniary relationship or financial transaction between the two parties might be the subject matter of a properly framed suit either by the creditor or even by the debtor but declaration in respect of such claims cannot stand under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. In view of the above facts and circumstances, we would hold that this suit for declaration as mentioned in prayer 'a' and prayer 'e' in paragraph 50 of the plaint is not maintainable under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act.</u>

37. Let us now consider whether the suit is maintainable under section 9 read with Order VII rule 7 of the Code of Civil Procedure. From the decision of Fischer vs Secretary for India, 26 Indian Appeals 716 it appears that a suit for declaration even beyond section 42 of the Specific Relief Act is also possible and section 42 is not exhaustive. The Supreme Court of India in the case of Veareddi Rantaraghava Raddy vs Kondun Seshe Raddy AIR 1967 (SC) 436 in consideration of the decisions from various High Courts of that country with special reference to 26 IA 16 PC, 40 lA 182 PC, AIR 1960 PC; AIR 1964 Andhra Pradesh 118. finally held that section 42 is not exhaustive and. declaratory suits independent of section 42 is permissible as referred to above.

38. True it is that a suit is possible independent of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, or even under section 9 read with Order VII rule 7 of the Code of Civil Procedure but that would not give a go-by to the requirements of law necessary for filing a suit. It is not the law that any busybody or any stranger, who has no locus standi or Cause of action for the suit, can maintain a suit for anything or for everything. Even in filing a suit under section 9 he must have locus standi as well as legal right, in order to claim a relief against a defendant. In this case, it appears from the plaint itself that no shares in Albert David (Bangladesh) Ltd have yet been transferred in favour of the plaintiff. This fact as mentioned in his own plaint shows that he has got no interest in the said company and cannot file a suit on its behalf without any specific and tangible interest in the said company. A question may arise and is rightly raised on behalf of the appellant that in the face of the notice issued by the Bangladesh Bank dated 11-8-1997 enclosing a letter dated 7-8-1997of Pubali Bank claiming more than two crore takas what relief the plaintiff may have. True it is that the notice dated 11-8-1997 demanded payment of Taka 2,25,03,408.62 but the main purpose of the said notice was that if he fails to pay the said amount claimed, he would lose his office of directorship in the Pubali Bank Ltd within the period of next two months. Such purpose of the said notice was also noted with approval by the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court. The said notice is not a notice demanding recovery of loan, for recovery of its dues; the Pubali Bank Ltd. has to file a properly framed suit against the plaintiff. As such, we are of the view that the plaintiff has got no cause of action for the suit based on the aforesaid notice. But if he wants to resolve his own liability then he can file it properly framed suit but not a suit for declaration that he is not a defaulter or a borrower. As a matter of fact at the far end of the hearing of the appeal, Mr Raziur Rahman Chowdhury, the learned Advocate, on behalf of the appellant, submits that the prayers made in the plaint were not for declaration although written in that manner but as a matter of fact the prayers are actually for decree for accounts between the plaintiff and the defendant No. 1. But plain reading of the plaint would show that the instant suit is not a suit for accounts but is framed as a suit for declaration.

39. Another point is raised on behalf of the appellant. Referring to the last portion of the prayer 'a' in the plaint that (the plaintiff) 'not liable to pay the debt of Albert David (Bangladesh) Ltd., the learned Advocate of the appellant citing several decisions submits that a negative declaration is permissible. In support of his contention he refers to the decisions reported in 37 DLR 49, 40 DLR 226, 42 DLR 211. The decisions reported in 40 and 42 DLR and decisions reported in 37 DLR relied on three other decisions of the Indian jurisdiction namely, 45 CWN 470, lLR 1944 Lahore 168 and the other decision has got no citation, as such, could not be considered. Those two decisions reported in lLR 1944 Lah 168 and 45 CWN 470, although negative declarations, were entertained but the learned Judges held that although the prayers were made in a negative form but as a matter of fact declaration of their own status was prayed for.

40. Be that as it may, although section 42 of the Specific Relief Act is not exhaustive and declarations independent of that provision is even permissible but a suit for declaration, however would not lie when the plaintiff is neither entitled to any legal character or status nor clothed with any right.

41. Under such circumstances we are of the view that the relief as claimed in prayer 'a' and prayer 'e' to the plaint cannot be maintainable either under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act or even under section 9 read with Order VII rule 7 of the Code of Civil Procedure. So far we have discussed regarding maintainability of the suit, as we have already referred to the decision reported in PLD 1967 Dacca 190 that the maintainability of the suit goes to the root of the matter which was upheld in many a later decisions (e.g. 26 DLR 10). We are also of the view that this suit cannot proceed as not maintainable for reasons stated above and is liable to be dismissed in limini. In this connection we would repeat the warnings so forcefully sounded by Sir Barnes Peacock, in the case of Sree Narain Mitter vs Sreemutty Kishen Soondory Dassee (1872) LRIA Sup Vol. 149, at page 162, which is still true even six and half score years later.

"There is so much more danger in India than here of harassing and vexatious litigation that the Courts in India ought to be most careful that mere declaratory suits be not converted into a new and mischievous source of litigation."

<u>42. Now let us consider the second branch of the argument advanced on behalf of the respondent that the suit is not only maintainable but the plaint is also liable to be rejected on the ground that there was no cause of action for the suit as stated in clause I of Order VII rule 11 of the Code. We have gone through the plaint and found that the grievances of the plaintiff as stated in the plaint firstly that the defendant No. 5 did not yet transfer his share in his favour this is not the subject matter of the suit in this case but in another suit pending before another Court. Since on his own showing that he does not have the shares of Albert David (Bangladesh) Ltd. he is not a share-holder of the said company as such, the question of filing a suit on behalf of the Albert David (Bangladesh) Ltd does not arise because, on one hand, he cannot say that he is not the shareholder of the company but, on the other hand, he has interest in it, cannot be accepted. Even if he is assumed to be a share-holder, strictly speaking, he has no right in the assets of the company or cannot normally represent it. The right of a share-holder is only to the extent of dividends if declared. The contention on behalf of the appellant is that since the notice was issued on him he has a legal right to file the suit. The notice dated 11-8-1997, as we have already found, was in respect of his holding of this office of directorship in the Pubali Bank Ltd., the question of liabilities, as such, is irrelevant. In this connection, it should be remembered that it is not the relief which is claimed rather it is the relief which can be given to the plaintiff, that has to be looked into and considered in a plaint. Mere issuance of a notice by the Bangladesh Bank who is not a creditor, enclosing a letter of Pubali Bank Ltd., for the purpose of removing him from the post of its directorship, will not clothe the plaintiff with the necessary legal right to file this suit for declaration with regard to his liabilities, which is an entirely different matter. Under such circumstances we are of the view that there is no cause of action to file the instant suit. In that account also the plaint is liable to be rejected under rule 11 of Order VII of the Code.</u>

43. Under such circumstances the appeal is dismissed but without any order as to costs.

44. Before parting with the case I would like to observe that whenever a learned Judge is confronted with a petition to reject a plaint he must first assume that the plaint was legally filed, unless the defendant persuades him to hold that the plaint is liable to be rejected in limini under Order VII rule 11 of the Code. In dealing with such a petition he should not be unnecessarily hasty, rather act judiciously in considering the plaint.

45. Unfortunately, in the instant case, the learned Subordinate Judge failed to substantiate his order with reasons in rejecting the plaint. His order is perfunctory and lacks application of his judicial mind.

46. Let a copy of this judgment be forwarded to the learned Subordinate Judge wherever he is posted now for his guidance.

Send down the records forthwith.

End.
