full_judgment:
This Rule was issued calling upon the opposite party to show cause as to why the judgment and decree passed on 8.7.91 in SCC Suit No. 24 of 1982 by the Subordinate Judge, Bogra should not be set aside.

2. The facts for the disposal of the Rule are:

The petitioner Md. Mukbul Hosain Khandkar was a defendant in the said SCC Suit No. 24 of 1982 instituted by the opposite party Mst. Jahada Khatun as plaintiff for eviction of the petitioner from the suit land and for a decree for Taka 360.00 being arrear rent for the term. The case of the opposite party as plaintiff in the aforesaid suit was that she took lease of the land of dag No. 1414 consisting 28 decimals of land appertaining to khatian No. 125 of Sutrapur Mouza, Police Station Kotwali, District Bogra on. 28.11.55 by a registered deed under the care and initiative of her husband M. Rafiq Khan and constructed some stalls by wood and CI sheets and proposed to give them on rent to the people and called it Rafiq Khan Market. The defendant petitioner entered into a registered tenancy agreement with the opposite party plaintiff on 6.10.65 to be effective for 5 years from 1.11.65. It was stipulated in the tenancy agreement that the defendant petitioner would pay monthly rent in the first week of the following month. It was further stipulated that the defendant petitioner would not sub-let the premises or make any pucca construction. Later it was also agreed that if the plaintiff opposite party wished to make pucca construction she should let it be known to defendant petitioner and if such construction was undertaken the defendant petitioner would continue to remain a tenant on the same of the registered agreement. Towards the end of 1970 the plaintiffs’ husband purchased bricks worth Taka 90,000.00 and 50 cubit feet of sand and kept it in open space next to the market for construction. It was contended that defendant petitioner was habitual defaulter in payment of rent. He did not pay the rent in time and sometimes kept 2/3 month’s rent arrear and paid rent only on persuasion. The defendant paid rent till February, 1971. In 1971 the said Rafiq Khan Market was set on fire and parts of some of the stalls including that occupied by the petitioner were destroyed. The plaintiff opposite party's husband was a member of political party Muslim League and in 1971 he was Secretary of Bogra Peace Committee. He was a candidate for membership of parliament. Being afraid of his life after the liberation of Bangladesh he went into hiding at different places at different times. Taking advantages of his absence the defendant petitioner with the building materials left by the plaintiff opposite party, without approval, constructed a two-storied building which was depicted in the sketch map as No.9 on the ground floor, 9/1 on the 1st floor and 13 on the ground follow and 13/1 on the 1st floor, After a general amnesty was declared by the Government of Bangladesh in 1974 the plaintiffs husband returned to his place of residence and wanted to know from the defendant under what authority he had constructed the pucca building and demanded rent. But the defendant avoided the plaintiff on some pretext or other. The defendant being a habitual defaulter the plaintiff opposite party served notice through his lawyer under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act and demanded vacant possession of the premises by 31st December, 1991 which was refused by the defendant petitioner. In the circumstances, the plaintiff opposite party was constrained to file an eviction suit under the Premises Rent Control Ordinance and claimed 3 years' arrear rent. It was contended by the plaintiff opposite party that he remained busy and because of financial constraint he could not file the suit earlier. The defendant petitioner contested the suit by filing a written statement. It was, inter alia, contended by the defendant petitioner that the relationship of landlord and tenant did not exist between the plaintiff opposite party and the defendant petitioner and, therefore, the SCC Suit was not maintainable. After denying the material allegation of the plaintiff the defendant petitioner stated that the suit premises originally belonged to one Akram Hossain Tarafdar. The premises having remained vacant and fallow for a long time a market in the name of Badruddin New Market was started in the western side of the premises. After partition of the Sub-continent business in Bogra town developed and moveable shops made of tin and wood were created on both sides of the road near the suit premises. On promulgation of Martial Law in 1958 the moveable’s stalls were removed from both sides of the road. In the meantime the plaintiff claimed title over the suit premises and the shop owners approached the plaintiff to carry on their business which was allowed by the plaintiffs’ husband and accordingly, the owners of the stalls created their respective shops and carried on business. It was claimed by the defendant that the suit plot 15/14 was vacant and so he constructed a stall there and carried on cloth business. Actually the said suit plot became a market and in the beginning of October, 1965 the husband of the plaintiff demanded from the defendant and one Afzal Hossain Pramanik and other owners of the stalls for written permission to use the premises in order to avoid future complication. It was agreed that for permission to use the shops they would pay Taka 2.00 per foot as licence fee for the respective shops. Accordingly, an agreement to this effect was entered into and registered. It was stated the agreement was not written according to the agreement nor it was read out to the defendant. It was claimed that the plaintiffs’ husband managed to write the agreement according to his wishes and got it registered. It was later discovered by the defendant that the registered agreement was not a licence agreement for use but was tenancy agreement. In fact the agreement was to be a licence agreement. It was further stated that in 1969 some of the users of the stalls namely, Munsur Rahman, Zahirul Islam, Nasiruddin were purchased by the defendant. Stall No.6 was sold by defendant petitioner to defendant Muslimuddin Khondker who carried on cloth business there. Subsequently this was also purchased by the defendant and these stalls are as deposited in the map. Stalls Nos. 9 & 9/1, 13 & 13/1 belonging to one Matius Rahman were claimed to have been purchased by the defendant. These stalls were set on fire in 1971 by the Pakistan Army which were completely destroyed as a result of which the possession of the premises of the plaintiff opposite party came to end. After the emergence of Bangladesh the Government directed the defendants and others to carry on their usual business, In the meantime, the suit land was declared as abandoned property and the Management Committee of the abandoned property verbally directed the owners of the stalls to construct shops at their own costs and continue their business. Accordingly, the owners constructed shops in 1972 and have been in possession of their respective shops. In these circumstances it was stated by the defendant petitioner that the plaintiff opposite party had no right, title or interest in the suit premises. The property was abandoned property under President's Order No. 16 of 1972.

3. The plaintiff opposite party made a prayer before the see Judge to try the aforesaid suit as a regular one. But the learned Subordinate Judge refused the said prayer. The plaintiff thereafter moved the District Judge Bogra under section 24 of the Code of Civil Procedure but the District Judge rejected the said prayer and directed that the aforesaid suit be tried by the see Judge on the basis as to whether there was a relationship of landlord and tenant between the plaintiff and the defendant.

4. The plaintiff examined 7 witnesses and the defendant examined two.

5. After considering the facts and circumstances of the case and evidence on record the learned see Judge decreed the suit by the impugned judgment and decree passed on 8.7.91 in see Suit No. 24 of 1982 against which the defendant petitioner has obtained the present Rule.

6. It has been submitted on behalf of the petitioner that he did not accept the plaintiff as his landlord after the expiry of the agreement dated 1.1 1.65, that he has built two sets of shops on the aforesaid suit land after the original stall was gutted by fire by the Pakistan Army, that he has not accepted the plaintiff either orally or by written document as his landlord after the liberation of Bangladesh when he built the aforementioned shops. It was submitted that the original agreement having expired in November, 1970 and there being no proof of renewal the landlord and tenant relationship ended. It is also contended that the original shops taken on tenancy in 1975 having been completely destroyed by fire set by Pakistan Army in 1971 the tenancy was frustrated. It has been argued that the see Judge misconceived the provision of holding over and wrongly found relationship of landlord and tenant between the parties on misconception of aforesaid principle of law. The see Judge failed to notice that on expiry of original lease agreement and the destruction of the stall by fire there was no evidence on record to hold that the landlord accepted the rent from the defendant or asserted to his continuing in the original shop as tenant.

7. The plaintiff opposite party by evidence passed Ext 1 which is a registered deed of settlement signed on 19.11.55 and registered on 28.11.55. This deed of permanent settlement was made in favour of the plaintiff opposite party. Her name was recorded in Mr. RR Khatian which was proved by Ext. VI Exts.5 (d) to 5(ka) showed payment of revenue. The holding tax receipts were proved by Ext. 5 to 5(c). The defendant in his cross-examination admitted the plaintiff to be the owner of the suit premises. It is on evidence that the see court was satisfied that the plaintiff had proved his right, title and interest in the suit land. The se court then next considered whether the defendant was a tenant of the plaintiff or not. He found from Ext. 8 which is a registered lease deed dated 8.10.65 whereby the defendant by signing the same accepted the plaintiff as the owner and agreed to pay rent on the basis of the agreement. The see court was, therefore satisfied that the defendant was undoubtedly a tenant of the plaintiff. It was further found that rent receipts were issued by the defendant in favour of the plaintiff which are marked Exts.4, 4(a) 4(b) & (c). It was found from evidence that the defendant continued to pay rent to the plaintiff until February 1971. The se court was, therefore, satisfied that there could not be any question that there did not exist a landlord-tenant relationship between the plaintiff and the defendants. The next question that SC Court took up was whether the defendant petitioner was a habitual defaulter or not. It was the case of the plaintiff that the defendant continued to pay rent up to February, 1971 but did not pay the rent in time as stipulated in the agreement. After operation of Bangladesh the plaintiff went into hiding and after general amnesty was declared by the Government he returned to his home in 1974 and demanded arrear rent from the defendant which was refused. The plaintiff therefore, served notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act to deliver vacant possession of the suit premises by December, 1981 and hand over the possession of the same to the plaintiff. As the defendant did not pay the arrear rent nor vacated the premises the plaintiff filed the present suit. As a part of the arrear rent became barred by limitation, the plaintiff claimed 36 month’s rent from 1979 to 1981 at the rate of Taka 10.00 per month which is Taka 360.00. The SC Court having believed Ext. 9 which was the deed of tenancy and the rent receipt Ext. 4 it was satisfied that the suit was maintainable in its present form in the SC Court. The SC Court further held that the defendant had admitted that the plaintiff was her landlord, and thereafter the tenant could not raise question of plaintiffs’ title and for this the court relied on the case reported in 36 DLR (AD) 93. The SC Court found that it was admitted that the stall was gutted by fire when the Pakistan army set fire to the stalls in 1971. The defendants had argued that as the subject matter of the tenancy was completely destroyed the tenant-landlord relationship ended with it. However, the SC Court held that although the stall was destroyed by fire it was agreed that if the plaintiff constructed new pucca building the old tenancy would continue and the defendant would continue to pay the rent on old terms of the written agreement. Having made such an agreement the SC Court held that the defendant could say that the tenancy had come to an end because the stalls were destroyed by fire. That there was an oral agreement was stated in the plaint. In cross examination PW.2 stated that the plaintiff told him that there was an oral agreement. The SCC Judge further held that according to section 108 of the Transfer of Property Act, so long as the tenant does not leave or abandon the premises after it is destroyed by fire, the relationship of landlord and tenant is not destroyed. In the instant case the defendant did not hand over the premises to the plaintiff. Thereafter the landlord-tenant relationship was not broken simply on the ground that the premises was destroyed by fire It was also found by the SC Court that the plaintiff was a Bangladeshi national and that his property could be declared abandoned under President's Order No. 16 of 1972. Further, that the suit premises was an abandoned property, was not notified in the Gazette as required under law and then on the representation made by the plaintiff the relevant authority held that it was not an abandoned property. The SC Court then discussed the evidence of PW 3 who deposed that the suit premises and other stalls were constructed by the plaintiff and that the evidence of PW 3 was corroborated by PWs 4 and 5. Court had no reason to disbelieve their evidence as the defendant did not have any evidence to contradict them. Thus relying on the evidence of the PW 5 the court believed that the stalls were originally constructed by the plaintiff and did not believe story of the defendant that the stalls were moved across the road by the defendant. PW 4 Saiful Islam also stated that he had seen the plaintiff to take and keep the bricks and sand next to the suit premises and PW 6 Abdul Majid deposed that he supplied the bricks to the plaintiff from his own brick field. Placing reliance on these evidence the court found the claim of the defendant that he had later constructed the pucca stall with his bricks, sand and cement after the original stalls were gutted by fire to be false. It was stated by the defendant that after emergence of Bangladesh one Matiur Rahman along with others constructed pucca buildings. Matiur Rahman who carried on business in the suit stall Nos. 13/1 died. Upon his death his wife and sons continued business and on 30.4.77 sold the stall to Ataur Rahman Talukder from whom the defendant purchased the suit stalls by deed on 17.11.77 in the name of his son Rafiqul Islam and carried on business. The court below held that since the defendant and others who carried on business in the suit premises had no title or interest they could not claim the suit property nor transfer them.

8. It was submitted that the original agreement having expired in 1970 and there being no proof that there was renewal of the said agreement, the landlord tenancy relationship between the plaintiff and the defendant ended. The mere expiry of a registered lease deed will not bring an end to the tenancy. Thus, if the tenant continues to occupy the premises and the landlord continues to receive rent after the expiry such tenancy is a tenancy by holding over. In the instant case it is the case of the plaintiff that the tenant petitioner continued to pay rent which was accepted by the landlord till February, 1971. The SC Court had found that the tenant petitioner had paid rent to the plaintiff until February 1971 and therefore, the assertion that the tenancy ended in November, 1970 with the completion of 5 years cannot be accepted. There is nothing to show that the tenant after the expiry of the lease period of 5 years did not continue as a tenant or refused to accept the plaintiff as his landlord.

9. In the case of Siddik Ali being dead his heirs Afia Rahman and others vs. Nurun Nessa Khatun and others reported in 43 VLR (AD) 3 it was held by the Appellate Division:

"Tenant's continuous possession with landlord's assent creates an implied contract constituting a tenancy by holding over. Such a tenancy cannot be created by tenant's continuance of possession alone-there must also be the assent of the landlord, which may be expressed or implied. It may be evidenced by acceptance of rent or by other circumstances. Where the lessor dissents there cannot be any holding over. Absence of dissent will not necessarily imply assent, but from the tenant's continuous possession for a long period, without contrary indication from the landlord may constitute an implied assent. Implied assent is a question of fact inferable from the length of possession and other circumstances excluding an inference of landlord's dissent".

<u>10. I have said that in the instant case after the expiry of the registered agreement in February, 1970 there is no evidence that the tenant dissented or that the plaintiff did not give assent to the tenancy, In the circumstances it cannot be said that with the expiry of the lease after 5 years the relationship of landlord and tenant ceased to exist between the plaintiff and the defendants. A similar view was taken in the case of Nakul Das Mridha vs. Bangladesh and others reported in 1986 BLD 331 where it was held that:</u>

<u>Holding over means retaining possession It does not necessarily create any tenancy after the expiration of the stipulated term. The common law rule is that if a lessee remains in possession after the expiry of the terms, he is tenant by sufferance. A distinction is however, made between a tenant continuing in possession after the determination of the lease with the consent of the landlord, and the tenant remaining so without his consent. In common law the former is called a tenant holding over or a tenant at-will and the latter is called a tenant by sufferance. "</u>

<u>In the instant case we have seen that there has been no dissent either by the tenant or by the landlord on the expiry of the written agreement and therefore, the tenancy continued by holding over.</u>

11. It was next submitted that the lease premises having been gutted by fire and the suit premises being completely destroyed the tenancy between the plaintiff and the defendant petitioner came to an and as it rendered the tenancy agreement void.

12. Mr. SR Paul, the learned Advocate for the petitioner has argued at length that under section 56 of the Contract Act the tenancy between the plaintiff and the defendant was frustrated as the whole suit property was completely destroyed. In this connection he has relied on the case of Azizur Rahman & others vs. Abdus Sakur and others reported in 36 DLR (AD) 195. In that case several cases were referred to and discussed. While discussing whether the doctrine of frustration as embodied in section 56 of the Contract Act is applicable to leases of immovable property the Appellate Division discussed the case of Khitish Chandra Mondal VS. Shiba Rani Debi and others reported in AIR 1950 Cal. 441. In that case the plaintiff erected a thatched shed and which was rented out to a monthly tenant was burnt by fire. The tenant raised another structure on the land in spite of the landlord's protest and claimed to be a tenant. It was held:

(1) That section 108(c) did not in term apply as B neither elected to walk out even after total destruction nor was willing to spend payment for rent and give up possession. (2) that the doctrine of frustration applied to leases. The contract between A and B became impossible of performance through no negligence on the part of A and he was entitled to claim that the lease had come to an end by destruction by fire.

(3) that under the tenancy B had no right to raise structures of his own, treating the lease as the lease of the land only."

13.  Whether the doctrine of frustration as contained in section 56 of the Contract Act and applied to leases was considered in Jiwaulal & Co. Ltd. vs Manat & Co. Ltd. 64 CWN 932. In the opinion of the Court, the entire law of the doctrine of frustration which may be applied to leases is to be found in section 108(c) of the Transfer of Property Act. It was accordingly held:

"If a house is destroyed wholly, even then the lease does not determine unless the lessees so chooses. In other words, by the demolition of an entire house the lease would not be destroyed or determined.

Then on the question of whether the doctrine of frustration under section 56 of the Contract Act applied to leases and exceeded contract or not the Appellate Division referred to the case of National Carriers Ltd. vs. Panalpina (Northern) Ltd. (1981) 2 WLR 45 where it was observed by Lord Russell:

"The law should not be compartmentalized. In principle a common law doctrine ought not to be held capable of applying only in one field of contract but not in another. To preserve the dichotomy between leases on the one hand and other types of contract on the other can undoubtedly create anomalies. Thus if a ship is demise-chartered for the purpose of storing oil and explodes without fault of either party, the demise charter would clearly be frustrated. If the same demise charterer also leases an adjacent shore installation for the same purpose and the same explosion destroys that installation along with the demise chartered ship rent for that storage installation would remain payable in full for the unexpired period of the lease though liability for demise charter jore had ceased upon the frustration of the demise charter party."

After considering these decisions among others the Appellate Division in Azizur Rahman's case held; that the doctrine of frustration as embodied in section 56 of the Contract Act is applicable to leases of immovable property. In that case the subject matter of the tenancy was destroyed by fire. The said premises however, remained vacant and in possession of the plaintiffs. The defendant appellant in collusion with each other and ignoring plaintiffs and also lawyer's notice wrongfully constructed new huts and houses on the premises and refused to deliver possession of the land. The landlord plaintiff instituted suit for declaration of title and recovery of possession after removal or the structures by the defendant. The contention of the defendant, inter alia, was that some kutcha houses were only partly damaged by fire which were repaired by the defendant and made habitable and, therefore, there was no extinction of the subject matter of tenancy due to conflagration as alleged by the plaintiff. The Appellate Division held that frustration in the present case was apparent from the facts proved and, therefore, the defendant appellant's contention failed.

14. Mr. SR Paul has argued that the instant case was similar in that the subject matter of the tenancy having been completely destroyed by the Pakistan Army by setting fire to it the tenancy was frustrated and the plaintiff, therefore, could not file the present suit under the Rent Control Ordinance for eviction of the defendant petitioner as no landlord-tenant relationship existed between them.

Section 56 of the Contract Act provides as follows:

"Agreement to do impossible act. An agreement to do an act impossible in itself is void.

Contract to do act afterwards becoming impossible for or unlawful. A contract to do an act which, after the contract is made, becomes impossible or, by reason of some event which the promisor could not prevent, unlawful, becomes void when the act becomes impossible or unlawful.

It has been argued that in the instant case that as the suit premise was completely destroyed by fire it became impossible for either party to act under the tenancy agreement. Therefore, it is a question of fact whether it became impossible by reason of some event (in present case the suit premise being gutted by fire) to do the act under the contract.

<u>15. Where plea of frustration is raised on the happening of a certain event the real question is whether the event which has accrued is such and whether its relation to the contract is such that in considering the contract and the surrounding circumstances it must be held that it would not be just and reasonable to hold the parties any longer to the terms of the contract. To attract the doctrine of frustration of contract the performance of the contract must become absolutely impossible due to the event, where in spite of intervention even subsequent to the making of the agreement which are not in contemplation of the parties and which could not be foreseen with reasonable diligence, the contract could still be performed in substance then it could not be said that the contract has become impossible of performance within the meaning of section 56 of the Contract, Act.</u>

16. Keeping this in mind, let us now see whether as a result of the suit premise being gutted by fire it did become impossible for the parties to perform their act under the tenancy. Admittedly the suit premise was gutted by fire by the Pakistan Army in 1971. It is also admitted that the tenant defendants did not leave the premises or hand over possession of the suit premises to the plaintiff landlord. Puce a shops were construed and the tenant continued to do business an usual. Although the defendant has claimed that his construction was made by him from bricks, cement and both at his own cost, the evidence is otherwise. I have seen while narrating the judgment of the SC Court that PW 4 Saiful Islam had deposed that he had seen the plaintiff keep cement and bricks and sand on the vacant land next to the suit premises in 1970 prior to the destruction and demolition of the suit premises. These materials were brought by the plaintiff with the intention to construct pucca building on the suit land in place of the tin shed. PW.6 deposed that the bricks were supplied to the plaintiff from his own brick field. It is also in evidence that it was agreed between the plaintiff landlord and the defendant tenant that in the event of the plaintiff making pucca construction the defendants would continue to occupy the premises as a tenant on the old terms and conditions. Therefore, although the old huts were destroyed by fire, by subsequent construction of pucca building and continuous occupation of the premises by the defendant it appears to me that the tenancy was not completely frustrated making the parties impossible to act under the agreement. It is true that the tenant did not pay any rent to the landlord after the suit premises were destroyed but the mere non-payment of rent does not mean that the tenancy had come to an end. The plaintiff had accepted the defendant to be his tenant and there is no evidence that there was dissent from either parties I have already said that there was finding by the SC Court that there was an oral agreement that in the event of construction of pucca shops the tenant would continue to occupy the premises as a tenant on the same terms and condition therefore from the facts and circumstances discussed above, I find that the tenancy had not been completely frustrated as a result of the fire but continued with the construction of pucca house as per oral agreement.

17. In the facts and circumstances, I find that if would not be just and reasonable not to hold the parties any longer to the terms of the contract i.e. the tenancy agreement between the plaintiff and the defendant. As the contract could be still performed in substance it cannot be said that the agreement had become impossible of performance within the meaning of section 56 of the Contract Act.

18. In the instant case the facts are different from the facts in the case of Azizur Rahman vs. Abdus Sakur and others reported in 36 DLR (AD) 195 where after the premise was destroyed by fire the plaintiff landlord took up possession of the premise and the defendant collusively with others put up structures at his own costs and claimed to be a tenant which was not recognized by the Appellate Division. In the present case the defendant was inducted as a tenant who did not leave the premises when it was destroyed by fire and instead constructed pucca building with the material brought by the plaintiff for the purpose and continued to occupy it as a tenant on term agreement and orally. In such circumstance the defendant cannot say that he is not a tenant and claim title.

19. A point was taken by the plaintiff by opposite party that the defendant petitioner not having opposed the application made by the plaintiff under section 28A of the SCC Act and having not preferred any revisional application against the order passed in Misc. Case No. 28 of 1982, thereby accepted the finding of the District Judge, Bogra that the dispute was between the landlord and tenant. The defendant was therefore now estopped by the said judgment from taking a different stand that there existed no landlord-tenant relationship, and therefore the matter could not be decided by the SC Court.

20. Mr. SR Paul submits that there was no scope for the defendant to prefer revisional application against the order passed under section 28A of the SCC Act as it is barred under the said Act. In this connection he has referred to the case of Abdul Khalek Mia vs. Maya Bibi and others reported in 35 DLR (AD) 310 where it was held as follows:

"Prior to the amendment in 1962 transfer of Small Causes suit could be made under section 24 (4) of the Code of Civil Procedure and the law says the transferred court will be deemed to be Court of Small Causes." The effect was that the suit must be tried under the Small Causes Court procedure without any right of appeal although the transferred Court does not possess SCC power inasmuch as by the deeming provision the transferred court would be Small Cause Court for the purpose of the suit. No revision lay from such order (vide Kesho vs. Geyal and Company AIR 1938 Lahore 95). But the position was changed in 1962 and 28A (2) provides; where a suit is so withdrawn, the District Court or the Court to which such suit is transferred shall try and dispose of the same as if such suits were not cognizable by a Court of Small Causes. Thus the position was altered sharply. In section 24 CPC the transferred court would not be deemed to be Court of Small Causes but under section 28A (2) when a suit is so withdrawn the court shall try and dispose of the same "as if such suits were not cognizable by a court of Small Causes. Thus the procedure is also altered and the procedures laid down in the Small Causes Courts Act are no longer applicable. This independent and new remedy provided for by section 28A has not been made revisable under section 25 of the Small Cause Courts Act. It has been held in R. vs. Judge of Essex County Court (1887) 18 QBD 704 that in the case of an Act which creates a new jurisdiction, a new proceeding, new forums or new remedies the procedure, forums or remedies there prescribed and no others must be followed until altered by subsequent legislation. The reason is obvious. A revision has been provided by the legislature mainly under section 25 of the Small Causes Courts Act and there is scope for revision in the exercise of jurisdiction conferred by any other because the enactment is of a special nature. The learned single Judge had passed his opinion without giving any reason. It is imperative that all judgments must contain the reasons for the decisions. Order 20 rule 4 CPC says that a judgment shall contain, amongst others, the decision thereon and the reason for such decision. In this case we have the decision but no reason. The decisions of the learned single Judge must be set aside. As order under section 28A is not revisable under section 25 of the Small Cause Courts Act because the effect of an order under section 28A is to take out the case from the ambit of Small Causes Courts Act since it cannot be "adequately" tried by such court."

21. Mr. Abdur Rahim, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff opposite party, on the other hand, submits that by this decision no representation would lie under section 25 of the Small Causes Courts Act where the suit is transferred to be tried as the transferred court is not a SC Court. He has further submitted that where an application under section 28A of the SC Court is rejected there is no bar to prefer revisional application under section 25 of the Small Causes Courts Act.

22. Mr. Abdur Rahim further argued that the District Court while acting under the SCC Act is not a persona designata but a District Court under the High Court and, therefore, a revisional application lay under section 115 CPC against the judgment passed by the District Court. Section 28A provides:

"Power of District Court to withdraw and transfer suit (1) where a District Court is satisfied that any particular suit cannot be adequately tried by a Court of Small Causes it may withdraw such suit from that court and

(i) try or dispose of the suit itself or

(ii) transfer such suit to another court subordinate to the District Court.

23. In support of this contention he has referred to the case of AKM Ruhul Amin vs. District Judge and Election Tribunal, Bhola and others reported in 38 DLR (AD) 172 where the Appellate Division considered as to what procedure was available to a person for challenging the order passed by District Judge under article 29(4) of the Local Government (Union Parishad) Ordinance 1983. In that case it was held that:

"An election dispute relates to a right to office. The dispute is civil in nature, judicial officers who decide civil disputes have been empowered to decide election disputes. Procedure for holding the trial of such disputes is the same as that of an ordinary civil Court being constituted by Munsifs and empowered to decide election disputes relating to right to office, after taking evidence and hearing arguments, both on facts and law, are definitely exercising judicial powers, and not administrative powers, though it may be that they are constituted by the Election Commission, an executive authority-

24. Having regard to these considerations, it would appear that District Judge as held in Article 29(4) of the Ordinance does not mean persona designata that is his private or personal capacity but clearly indicated his office, that is, District Court of which he is the presiding Judge.

25. Court of District Judge is subject to both appellate and revisional jurisdiction of High Court Division.

26. In exercising revisional powers under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure against the decision of any election appellate Tribunal, High Court Division can grant any relief to which any aggrieved party is entitled to under the Ordinance.

27. Without going into the question whether any revisional application can be made under section 25 of the see Act against an order passed under section 28A of the Small Causes Courts Act the matter may be disposed of on the merit of the cases to whether there existed a landlord-tenant relationship between the plaintiff and the defendant. Having found that there exists a landlord-tenant relationship between the plaintiff opposite party and the defendant petitioner I must hold that the SCC Judge acted within his jurisdiction in adjudicating the matter and passing the decree in favour of the plaintiff opposite party.

28. In these facts and circumstances, I find no reason to interfere with the judgment and decree passed by the SC Court in SCC Suit No. 24 of 1982 on 8.7.91.

29. In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs.

The stay order granted earlier by this Court is hereby vacated.

End.

parties:
Mantu Faraji alias Jamal Faraji and others ------ Petitioners
vs.  
Mahiuddin Khan ------ Opposite Party
full_judgment:
Syed Amirul Islam, J: This Rule obtained on an application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure is directed against the Judgment and Order dated 19-11-1990 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Kushtia in Miscellaneous Appeal No.84 of 1987 dismissing the appeal and modifying the judgment and order dated 31-1-1987 passed in Miscellaneous Case No.597 of 1974 by the. Assistant Judge, Additional Court Kushtia to the effect that appellant No. 1 will not get the cost of removing his house from the disputed land.

2. The opposite party No.1 filed an application under section 96 of the Slate Acquisition and Tenancy Act against the present petitioners and others to pre-empt the case land as co-sharer of the case holding. The case was resisted by the pre-emptee petitioners denying the material allegations made in the petition and contending, inter alia that the pre-emptor opposite party NO.1 is not a co-sharer.

3. The trial Court on a review of the evidence allowed the miscellaneous case and directed the pre-emptor to pay Taka 4,000.00 as improvement cost and Taka 1,000.00 for removing the structures from the case land. Being aggrieved by the said judgment and order passed by the trial Court the present petitioners preferred an appeal before the learned District Judge, Kushtia which was registered as Miscellaneous Appeal No.84 of 1987 and the said appeal on transfer was heard and disposed of by the Additional District Judge, Kushtia who vide the impugned judgment and order dismissed the appeal and modified the judgment and order passed by the. trial Court to the effect that the pre-emptee petitioner is not entitled to get the cost of Taka 1,000.00 for removing the structures standing on the case land. Being aggrieved by the judgment and order of affirmance and modification the pre-emptee petitioner preferred this revisional application and obtained the present Rule.

4. Mr Abu Siddique, the learned Advocate appearing for the pre-emptee petitioners, urges only one poit before this court. His only submission is that the case land is a homestead land although situated in the rural area and, as such, it is not an agricultural land but a non-agricultural land and, as such, an application under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act (hereinafter referred to as the Act) is misconceived and not maintainable in law but both the courts below overlooking this legal aspect of the case allowed the case illegally and the same has caused an. error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. In support of his contention the learned Advocate refers to the following decisions namely, 20 DLR 562 and 1197 and 21 DLR 633. To fortify his contention he submits that the pre-emption in respect of non-agricultural land is governed by section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act whereas a pre-emption in respect of agricultural land is governed by section 96 of the Act irrespective of the location of the land.

5. Mr Hasan Foiz Siddiqui, the learned Advocate appearing for the pre-emptor opposite party, on the other hand, submits that it is now well settled that a homestead land situated in the rural area is governed by the provisions of section 96 of the Act and not by section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act and in support of his contention he relies on the decision reported 1 MLR (H.C.) 1996 page 70 wherein it has been held that homestead situated in the rural area is an agricultural land and section 96 of the Act is attracted in pre-empting such land.

6. In the instant case unfortunately, the point which has been urged by the pre-emptee petitioner before this Court was neither taken in the written objection before the trial Court nor the same was argued before the appellate Court below. Be that as it may, it is an important question of law and, as such, I allowed the learned Advocate to agitate the point before me. His only submission is that since the case land is homestead land it is not agricultural land and it must be governed by the provision of section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act and the pre-emption application ought to have been filed under section 24 of that Act and not under section 96 of the Act

7. Thus the question falling to be determined in this case is whether the homestead land situated in rural area is an agricultural land within the meaning of section 96 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act (hereinafter called the Act) or is a non-agricultural land within the meaning of section 2(4) of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act.

8. Here it should also be remembered that the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act came into operation when Bengal Tenancy Act, 1885 was in force and governed the agricultural land and that is why homesteads which were within the ambit of section 182 of, the BT Act were kept outside the ambit of Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. Such a homestead land is not a non-agricultural land as defined in section 2(4) of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. Thereafter came the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950.

9. The Act came into operation in 1951 and prior to that the BT Act was operative in the field and section 182 of the BT Act applied to the homestead lands situated in the rural areas.

10. After the promulgation of the Act the question arose as to which of the laws will govern the right of pre-emption in respect of homestead lands in the villages: is it section 96 of the Act or section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act? The question came up before the Pakistan Supreme Court for consideration in Civil Appeal No.47-D of 1963 dated 22-1-1965. In that case the question involved was as to whether an application for pre-emption under section 96 of the SAT Act could be entertained in respect of Non-Agricultural land, The Supreme Court, proceeding on the admitted basis that the dispute was as to non-agricultural homestead land within the municipality, observed and found as under:

"Because section 96 occurs in Chapter XIII the trial Court held that the right of pre-emption can be claimed in respect of non-agricultural land. The court, however, overlooked the fact that this chapter which regulated the right and liabilities of a raiyat was made applicable to tenants of non-agricultural land but it does not enlarge the content of the right as given in section 96 or introduce any change in the incidents of the right. In other words, it does not materially affect the character of the land in respect of which the right of pre-emption can be claimed"

11. Section 96, in clear terms, lays down that this right of pre-emption will be available only in respect of a 'holding. In view of the definition of 'holding' as given in section 2(13) of the Act, it can not be said that the right of pre-emption can be exercised in respect of non-agricultural land. Here it may be mentioned that there is specific provision for pre-emption of non-agricultural land in the East Bengal Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act (XXIII of 1949). Under that Act a contiguous owner can not claim a right of pre-emption. After review of relevant provisions of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act we think that section 96 is confined to agricultural land and therefore, a right of pre-emption under this section can not be claimed in respect of homestead land within a Municipality.

12. This interpretation of section 96 has been followed by the then Dacca High Court in the case reported in 20 DLR 562 and 21 DLR 633. But these decisions were given when the original section 81 was in force and section 81-A was not added to the Act. But subsequently, by amending the Act sub-sections (2) and (3) of section 81 was omitted and a new section 81A was inserted by the State Acquisition and Tenancy (Amendment) Ordinance, 1967 and after the amendment of 1967 difference of opinion arose as to whether the law enunciated by the Pakistani Supreme Court in Civil Appeal No.47-D of 1963 is still good law. In Noor Jahan Begum vs. Md Tabarak Ali (Civil Revision No.639 of 1969) a Single Bench of the High Court Division held as follows:

"By the new provisions, the entire part V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act has been made applicable to a holder of non-agricultural land. The simple test is as to whether the holder of non-agricultural land has become a tenant under the Provincial Government is respect of such land by virtue of the acquisition of the superior rights in such land. If the holder of non-agricultural land has become a tenant directly under the Provincial Government his rights and liabilities will be governed by the provisions of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act subject to the provisions contained in Part V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. It comes to this that for the purpose of pre-emption relating to non-agricultural land if the holder of the holding has become tenant directly under the government by virtue of acquisition of the superior rights in such land, section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act will be applicable in preference to section 24 of the East Bengal Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. Section 81-A(2) makes provision for other non-agricultural tenants."

13. After the pronouncement of the said judgment the same law came up for consideration in First Miscellaneous Appeal No.15 of 1975 and a Division Bench of the High Court Division after considering the provisions of law containing in the two Acts, observed that "Under section 24, only the co-sharer tenants of non-agricultural land, which is the subject of the transfer, can make an application. This distinction has been maintained in the two Acts even after the omission of sub-sections (2) and (3) from section 81 and insertion of section 81A to the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Thus, we find that insofar as an application for pre-emption is concerned section 96 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act will have their application in their respective areas, namely, section 96 shall be applicable to agricultural lands beyond the Municipal area whereas section 24 will be applicable to all classes of lands within the Municipal area and this view that we have taken is supported by the said unreported decision of the Supreme Court of Pakistan in Civil Appeal No.47-D of 1963".

14. This divergence of judicial opinion has been finally resolved by the Appellate Division in the case reported in 33 DLR (AD) 323. In that case the Appellate Division after considering the relevant provisions of both the Acts and the conflicting decisions finally came to the decision that in spite of the omission of sub-sections (2) and (3) of section 81 and insertion of section 81 A., section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act has not been rendered ineffective nor impliedly repealed so as to compel the owner of any land falling within the Municipal area to prefer an application under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Thus, the law is now well settled that section 96 of the Act shall be applicable to agricultural lands beyond the Municipal area and section 24 of the Non- Agricultural Tenancy Act will be attracted to all classes of lands within the Municipal area.

15. Now the pertinent question that calls for determination in the instant Rule is, as to whether the homestead land situated in rural area is an agricultural land or non-agricultural land. Non-Agricultural land has not been defined in the Act but it has been defined in the Non Agricultural Tenancy Act. Section 2(4) of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act reads as under:

"Non-Agricultural land" means land which is used for purposes not connected with agriculture or horticulture and includes any land which is held on lease for purpose not connected with agriculture or horticulture irrespective of whether it is used for any such purposes or not, but does not include: (a) a homestead to which the provisions of

section 182 of the Bengal Tenancy Act, 1885 (V1lI of 1885) apply Section 182 of the BT Act reads as follows:

"Where a raiyat or an under-raiyat holds his homestead otherwise than as part of his holding within the same village or any village contiguous to that village, his status in respect of his homestead shall be that of a raiyat or an under-raiyat according to the status of the landlord of the homestead, and the incidents of his tenancy of such homestead shall be governed by the provisions of this Act applicable to raiyats or under-raiyats, as the case may be."

<u>16. The term home stead is not used in that section as a generic term descriptive of a particular kind of land, but was intended to denote any, land used by the raiyat of under-raiyat for residential purposes, The scheme of that section was to divide homestead lands into two classes, (1) those comprised in the raiyati-holding, and (2) those outside the raiyat holding. Thus a homestead land held by a raiyat otherwise than as a raiyati holding and the homestead land held by a raiyat were governed by that section and those homestead lands were kept outside the definition of Non-Agricultural land as contained in section 2(4) of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. At the time of enactment of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act the BT Act was in operation and the homestead lands governed by the BT Act were kept outside the ambit of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. In 1950 the parliament passed the East Bengal Estate Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 and from the date of coming into force of the whole of Part V in any area, the BT Act stands repealed in that area. By 1964 the Part V was enforced throughout country so, BT Act stands repealed entirely in Bangladesh from that period. Even after the repeal of BT Act by the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, there has been no corresponding change in section 2(4) of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act although the provisions of BT Act have been repealed and replaced by the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. Thus in interpreting section 2(4) of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act today one must read section 2(4)(a) as a homestead to which the provisions of section 182 of the Bengal Tenancy Act, 1885, (VIII of 1985) would have applied instead of the word 'apply'. Thus, from the scheme and  definition of 'non-agricultural land' as given in the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, it is crystal clear that homestead land outside the raiyati-holding Situated in the village are not non-agricultural land ie they are agricultural land or land of raiyati holding. So, a transfer of homestead land by a raiyat beyond the Municipality is attracted by section 96 of the Act and not by section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. Pre-emption in respect of non-agricultural land can be claimed only under the provisions of section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act and pre-emption in respect of raiyati holding ie agricultural land can only be claimed under section 96 of the Act. The view taken by me gets support from the decision reported in 30 DLR 75, wherein it has been held that homestead being part of the holding of a raiyat is not excluded from the operation of section 96 of the Act. Similarly, in a recent decision reported in 1 MLR 72, another Single Bench of this Division has held that suit holding being homestead situated in the rural area is an agricultural land and section 96 of the Act is only available. It thus, appears that the correct legal position is that a homestead situated in a village shall be governed by the provisions of section 96 of the Act, be it held by a raiyat as a raiyati-holding or independently of a raiyati holding whereas section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act will be applicable to all classes of lands within the Municipal areas. In the instant case there is no dispute that the case land although a homestead is situated in a village and, as such, is a raiyati land within a village and so section 96 of the Act is attracted.</u>

In the result the Rule is discharged without cost.

End.

vs

full_judgment: Anwarul Hoque J: This is an application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure and is directed against an order dated 14.11.93 passed by Judge in charge, 1st. Additional District and Sessions Judge, Chittagong in Election Tribunal Case No. 3 of 1991. 2. It is the case of the petitioner that he is a sitting member of Parliament duly elected in last General Election held on 27.2.91. The opposite party No. 1 as petitioner, instituted an election case being Election Tribunal Case No. 3 of 1991 before the Election Commissioner, Sher-e-Banglanagar, Dhaka which was referred to the learned District Judge, Chittagong for trial in his capacity as the Election Tribunal for Chittagong District. In that election petition relief was sought in the form of a declaration to declare that the election of the present petitioner as member of Parliament from Constituency No. 290 Chittagong 12 (Anwara-West Patiya) is invalid, illegal and also for a further declaration that the petitioner should be declared as member of the parliament on the allegations that the petitioner adopted illegal means and corrupt practices and spent huge amounts by constructing several gates, election officers using number of transports to carry the voters to the polling stations and also influenced the opposite party No. 12, the Assistant Returning Officer. It is also the case that he hired anti-social and armed miscreants who being armed with cocktails firearms created terror and coerced the voters to vote for him in different polling stations mentioned in the election petition. It is also the allegation that the re-election held in seven centres were also vitiated due to illegal activities of the present petitioner and in the premises he prayed for the declaration as mentioned above. 3. The present petitioner who is the sitting member of the parliament as opposite party No. 1 submitted his written objection denying all the allegations mentioned in the election petition contending that the election was fair, free and without any violation of the election rules. The petitioner did not adopt any illegal or corrupt practice and because of his popularity and social welfare activities in local areas and being a known philanthropist in the district he was elected twice as a member of parliament from the same constituency before and raising other legal question, he prayed for the dismissal of the election petition. 4. The learned Judge of the Election Tribunal who is the District Judge, Chittagong appointed by the Election Commission under Article 53(1) of the Representation of People Order 1972 (President's Order 155 of 1972) for the trial of election petition, after examination of the election petition and the deposition of the opposite party No. 1 as PW 1 by an order dated 11.4.93, transferred the election petition to the court of Mr. M. Ismail Mia, the Additional District and Sessions Judge, First Court, Chittagong but in spite of the objection by the petitioner about the locus standi and jurisdiction to try the election petition as it had not been transferred in accordance with the provision of Article 54(1) of the Representation on the People Order, 1972, the court proceeded with the trial and completed examination of PW 1 and examined some other witnesses on behalf of the election petitioner rejecting the contention of the petitioner about locus standi and jurisdiction vide order No. 48 dated 24.4.93 and by the same order also rejected the prayer of the opposite party No. 1 for personal appearance of the petitioner. 5. On transfer of the learned Judge Mr. Md. Ismail Mia to First Court of Additional District and Sessions Judge, the case was being taken up by the judge-in-charge of that court acting also as judge-in-charge, relating to Election Tribunal Md. Syed Enayetullah who in spite of petitioner's prayer to adjourn the hearing till the Election Commission legally appoints a judge as Election Tribunal to dispose of election petitions including the election petition in which the petitioner is the opposite party No. 1, the judge in-charge rejected the contention of the petitioner by an order dated 17.10.93 and proceeded with the hearing of the election case filed against the petitioner by examining the witnesses of the opposite Party No. 1. Thereafter the opposite party No. 1 namely, the election petitioner on 14.11.93 after intimating the court that he had concluded the examination of his witnesses prayed for personal appearance of the petitioner under Article 56 of the Representation of the People Order, 1972 and pursuant to that the learned judge in-charge directed the petitioner to appear in person by 17.11.93. The present petitioner namely, Alhaj Aktaruzzaman Chowdhury (Babu) filed an application to examine the witnesses on his behalf and also prayed for the examination of the petitioner's duly constituted attorney and other witnesses. The learned Judge agreed only to examine the petitioner's constituted attorney and then to strike off the defence and to give an ex parte decision on petitioner's failure for personal appearance. The court adjourned the case to 4.1.94 after examining the attorney of the petitioner as PW fixing the next date on 9.1.94 keeping the matter of personal appearance of the petitioner open. After conclusion of the evidence of DW 1 expressing reluctance to examine further witnesses on behalf of the petitioner unless the petitioner appears in person and gives evidence in the election case, he passed the order which is challenged before this court. 6. It is the contention of the learned Advocate Mr. M. Nurullah that the Tribunal committed error of law in ordering personal appearance of the petitioner keeping in view the real purport of Article 56 of the Representation of People Order, 1972 without any legal consideration to the conditions to be adhered to for personal appearance as contemplated. Order 3 rule 1, Order 5 rule 3 and Order 10 rule 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure which as procedure matter have been made applicable in case of trial of election petitions and, as such, there is an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. It is the further case of the learned Advocate that the judge in charge now dealing with the Election Case No. 3 of 1991 having no locus standi and jurisdiction in respect of hearing of the election case as a persona designata, the matter having assigned to the District Judge only, the order passed has occasioned a failure of justice making the impugned order as wholly illegal and unsustainable in law. Since the learned Judge in charge has allowed the petitioner to represent him in the case through his constituted attorney, the impugned order concerning personal appearance of the petitioner is contradictory and is the result of non application of judicial mind and the same having occasioned failure of justice, the impugned order is bad in law as well as in fact. 7. We have examined the submissions of the learned Advocate and examined the relevant provision of law. The relevant provision as to the jurisdiction of the Tribunal, is referable to the Representation of People Order, 1972 and also the Notification made thereunder namely, Notification dated 6th March, 1991 issued by the Election Commission, Secretariate, Sher-e-Bangla Nagar, Dhaka. Under Article 49 of the Order no election shall be called in question except by an election petition made by a candidate for that election. An election petition shall be presented to the Commission within such time as may be prescribed and shall be accompanied by a receipt showing that the petitioner has deposited at any Bank or at any government Treasury or Sub-Treasury in favour of the Commission as security for the costs of the petition a sum of Taka one thousand. The petitioner shall join as respondent to his election petition all contesting candidates and any other candidates against whom any allegation, if any, of any corrupt or illegal practice is made. Illegal and corrupt practice has also been defined in the Act and it has been also provided in Article 52 that every election petition shall contain a precise statement of any corrupt or illegal practice or other illegal act alleged to have been committed, including as full a statement as possible of the names of the parties alleged to have committed such corrupt or illegal practice or illegal act and the place of the commission of such practice or act. Under Article 53 of the Order for the trial of election petition under this Order the Commission shall appoint as many Election Tribunals, as may be necessary. Under sub-article 2 of Article 53 a tribunal shall consist of a person who is or has been or is or at the time of his retirement as a District and Sessions Judge was qualified to be a judge of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh. Under Article 54, the commission either on its own motion or on application made in this behalf by any of the parties may at any stage transfer an election petition from the Tribunal to another Tribunal and the Tribunal to which the election petition is so transferred shall proceed with the trial of the petition from the stage at which it is transferred provided that the Tribunal to which an election petition is so transferred may, if it thinks fit, recall and examine any of witnesses already examined. Under Article 56 any appearance application or act before a Tribunal may be made or done by a party in person or by an Advocate or any other person entitled or allowed to plead in any civil Court and duly appointed to act on his behalf. It further provided that the Tribunal may where it considers necessary direct any party to appear in person. 8. It thus, appears that all election petitions must be tried by the Election Tribunal to be constituted by an order of the Commission. Under Article 53 and sub-article 2 of Article 53 a Tribunal shall consist of a person who is, or has been, or is or at the time of his retirement as a District Judge and Sessions Judge was qualified to be a judge of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh. From notification dated March, 1991 it appears that the Secretary of the Election Commission in exercise of the power as under Article 53 of the Order appointed election Tribunal in various electoral areas and it is seen from the notification that District and Sessions Judge of the various Sessions areas have been mentioned. 9. It is the case of the petitioner before this court that the Notification having appointed District and Sessions Judge of each Sessions Division of different areas to be the Election Commission, only the said person could constitute the Tribunal and the said power and function cannot be delegated by the District and Sessions Judge to Additional District Judge, as was done in the instant case and therefore the continuation of the trial of the instant petition case before a Judge-in-charge of the District and Sessions Judge and Additional District Judge and Sessions Judge is illegal, without jurisdiction. It is an exercise of power by usurpation of jurisdiction and therefore a nullity. 10. We have already referred to the various provisions of the law which are relevant in order to examine the contention of the petitioner. It has been provided in sub-article 2 of Article 53 that a tribunal shall consist of a person who is or has been or is as the time of his retirement as a District and Sessions Judge was qualified to be a judge of the Supreme Court. It has not totally prohibited the Additional District Judge or Judge-in-charge for acting as Tribunal. When the Notification of the Commission refers to the District Judges and Sessions Judge to be Election Tribunal it need be read along with Article 152(1) of the Constitution in the definition clause which defines District Judges to include an Additional District Judge. This is the Constitutional definition of the expression of District Judge and need be so understood as to include an Additional District Judge and a Judge-in-charge of that court of Additional or District Judge. Therefore, an exercise of power of an Election Tribunal by an Additional District Judge and or Judge-in-charge of that court or District Judge is. not an usurpation of jurisdiction. It can be tried by the District Judge or by an Additional District Judge, or by a Judge-in-charge of those courts when so required. We further find that this jurisdictional point has not been taken in the instant case specifically. The earlier petition challenging jurisdiction has been long rejected and accepted by the parties as such, as the matter has proceeded in the Additional District Judge Court acting as Tribunal who has ordered for the personal appearance of the present petitioner when only the petitioner rushed to this court. In the instant case we find that there is no absence of jurisdiction of the Tribunal. 11. Coming back to the order of personal appearance which is the impugned order in the instant case, it is seen that the Representation of People Order clearly provided that the Tribunal, if it thinks fit, may order personal appearance of the party before the court and it is in the proviso to Article 56 which provided that the Tribunal may, where it considers necessary, direct any party to appear in person. This order therefore can be passed by the Tribunal if it considers it necessary to do so. This question of necessity therefore need be a consideration to be considered objectively before passing such an order. When we look at the order we find that there is no absence of such objective consideration of the necessity for personal appearance. The Tribunal while ordering personal appearance had referred to the provision of Article 56 of the Order and proceeded to find that as there are personal allegation of corrupt and illegal practice alleged to have been committed by Alhaj Aktaruzaman Chowdhury, the Court considers that as there are witnesses to depose against him and in order to controvert those it needs his personal attendance and it is so necessary for ends of justice. Considering so the Tribunal directed the petitioner Alhaj Aktaruzzaman Chowdhury to appear in person and depose in Court on 17.11.93. That date is however over because we are now in January, 1994. The personal appearance before that Court on that day and even today had not been complied with. If Alhaj Aktaruzzaman Chowdhury has personal inconvenience to be present on that or any other future day he may make a prayer before the court for time after going to the court on subsequent day but the order need be complied with. The time may be allowed if he can prove to the satisfaction of the court that he is unable to move. This however is between Aktaruzzaman Chowdhury and the court to which we do not want to make any comment but so far this petition is concerned we find no substance, which is summarily rejected. End.

Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed, Senior Advocate, instructed by Md Nawab Ali, Advocate-on-Record -----For the Respondents (In Civil Appeal No.50 of 1993). CP 244/93 
Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed, Senior Advocate, (Mahmudul Islam Senior Advocate with him), instructed by Md Nawab Ali, Advocate-on-Record -----For the Petitioner (In Civil Petition No.244 of 1993)
Not represented -----The Respondents (In Civil Petition No. 244 of 1993).
