Because in view of the provisions of Part III (Sections 38 to 51 A) and section 79 of the Town Improvement Act, 1953 and the fact that the respondents have not pleaded sanction or notification of sanction in either of the two cases of acquisition (LA Case No. 4/86-87 and LA Case No. 2/87-88) the alleged acquisition proceedings are all without lawful authority and no vesting has taken place as urged on behalf of the respondents. II. Because in view of the provisions of section 79 of the Town Improvement Act, 1953 and section 15 of the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982 and the fact that the respondents have not pleaded or proved any agreement required to be entered into under section 15(1) of the Ordinance which is a mandatory provision, the acquisition proceeding in the two LA cases are without lawful authority and no vesting of the lands in question had taken place as submitted by the respondents." The appellant cannot be permitted to assail the acquisition proceedings raising new grounds on facts at this stage, particularly because there was no challenge in the writ petition regarding the said proceedings. The grounds are not only beyond the leave order but beyond the writ petition also. However, in order to meet the aforesaid grounds the respondents have supplied copies of letters showing respondent No. 2's proposal for acquisition of 393 acres of land for extension of Uttara Township and Government’s sanction for the said acquisition. A copy of the agreement dated 10 June 1988 in connection with LA Case No. 2 of 1987-88 as required under section 15 of the Ordinance has also been supplied. From these papers it appears that there was no procedural illegality in the acquisition proceeding. 31. It is on record that the land shown in the layout plan of the appellant was included in the original Uttara township project. The Central Land Allocation Committee allotted 3300.00 acres of land in 1960 for the project. But the DIT because of financial constraint acquired only 951.00 acres before. It is evident that the acquisition of 393 acres in LA Cases No. 2 of 1987-88 was for the same purpose and it is incongruous that a small area inside the big public project will be in private hands doing the same job. Of necessity, the public facilities like, roads, bridges, schools, parks, etc. will be provided in the public project and the private entrepreneur will have the benefit of those facilities without making any investment in that behalf at all. From H and H1 it appears that the appellant and the Capital Housing Society have been allowed to retain 21.09 acres of land on the basis of documents produced by them subject to verification. They will thus be able to make allotments of their own lands without taking any responsibility for the public facilities as are required to be provided in a housing project. For example, the Ranabhola link road which runs across the appellant's layout plan lands was constructed by the respondent but the benefit of the same will be squarely drawn by the private allottees of the appellant. Considering the public interest and the contents of the impugned orders by which the appellant has not been wholly deprived and at least it has been allowed to retain those lands for which it has been able to produce documents, it appears that substantial justice has been done to it. In view of the discussion above, I find no merit in this appeal which is accordingly dismissed without any order as to costs. Mustafa Kamal J: With regret I am unable to agree with the judgment and order passed by my learned brother, A TM Afzal, J. 34. This appeal by leave by the writ petitioner is from the judgment and order dated 13.2.92 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No.1539 of 1991 discharging the Rule Nisi. 35. The appellant filed the writ petition calling into question three Orders passed by respondent No. 1 Ministry of Public Works and Urban Development dated 13.8.90 (Annexure-H), 6.9.90 (Annexure-H1) and 27.9.90 (Annexure-H2) relating to acquisition of land in LA Case No.4 of 1986-87 and LA Case No.2 of 1987-88. The appellant is a Private Limited Company incorporated on 3.6.75 for the purpose, inter alia, of acquiring land, constructing houses and buildings, dealing with and improving property, undertaking housing projects, transacting business of real estate agent, etc. The appellant selected an area of about 300 bighas of land at Mouza Biljuri, JL No. 201, under PS Uttara and prepared a housing project named "Mahua". It submitted an application on 28.3.78 to the then Dhaka Improvement Trust (now Rajdhani Unnayan Kartripakkha), shortly the Kartripakkha, respondent No. 2, for a no objection certificate. It wanted to develop the area as a housing project in association with the owners of the land with a view to selling plots of land therefrom to intending purchasers among the members of the public. The Board of Trustees of respondent No. 2, the highest decision-making body of the Kartripakkha, in its meeting held on 4.10.78 (Annexure-A) approved of the said project in the following terms: “১৫। মহুয়া গৃহায়ন সমিতির জমি হুকুম দখলের আবেদন। মেসার্স মহুয়া গৃহায়ন সমিতির আবেদন বিবেচনা করিয়া বোর্ড এই মতামত ব্যক্ত করেন যে, উক্ত সমিতির নিজস্ব দখলে যতটুকু জমি আছে তাহার উপর তাহাদের প্রস্তাবিত গৃহায়ন প্রকল্প বাস্তবায়নের ব্যাপারে ডি,আই,টি,র আপত্তি থাকিবে না। তবে ডি, আই,টির উত্তা উপ-শহরে রাস্তাঘাট এর সাথে তাহাদের প্রস্তাবিত গৃহায়ন প্রকল্পের লেআউট এ প্রদর্শিত রাস্তাঘাটের সহিত সমজ্ঞাস্য থাকিতে হইবে এবং উক্ত লেআউট ডি,আই, টি শহর পরিকল্পনাকারী সাহেব কর্তৃক অনুরোধ (ংরপ) করাইয়া নিতে হইবে। 36. After repeated rejection of the appellant's layout plan and after a detailed discussion with the appellant stretching over four years, the Kartripakkha finally approved of the appellant's layout plan involving, according to the appellant, more or less 300 bighas of land, by Memo. No. PT/ DIT/6.21 121-STHA dated 27.2.83 (Annexure- B), adding four further conditions: "1. No deviation of the layout plan be made without the approval of DIT. 2, That you will have no objection to future acquisition of land by DIT for construction of bridge or culverts and their approaches to Ranabhola for extension of Uttara Scheme of DIT. 3. Individual building plan within your housing scheme will be required to be approved by DIT. 4. That all the internal roads within your housing scheme have to be built in conformity with the layout plan of the Uttara Model Town of DIT so that a uniform movement of traffic is ensured." 37. The layout plan shows a 100 feet wide road from Uttara to Ranabhola to be built in future by the Kartripakkha the width and alignment of which were inserted in the layout plan in apparent consultation with the agreement of the Kartipakkha. The appellant thereafter started survey, clearance of trees and shrubs, earth cutting, earth filling, levelling, demarcating and plotting in phases at huge expenses as the area consisted generally of low and marshy land. The appellant claims to have purchased so far by registered deeds 65 bighas of land more or less and has claimed to have taken possession of another 150 big has of land by entering into contracts of purchase with the owners. It has already allotted 250 plots and committed allotment of another 413 plots to the members of the public. The Kartripakkha has sanctioned house building plans on several plots of land allotted by the appellant. While in the midst of developing the housing project the appellant was surprised to learn that respondent No. 2 proposed to acquire land for the said Uttara-Ranabhola link road the width of which had been increased to 300 feet without informing and consulting the appellant and had changed the road alignment piercing through the heart of the appellant's housing project. The said deviation will spoil 60 developed and 137 allotted plots of the appellant. It submitted a detailed representation to the Chairman of the Kartripakkha by a letter dated 17.11.86 (Annexures-C and C 1) objecting to the proposed deviation, with no answer. The Managing Director of the appellant met the Chairman of respondent No. 2 and following the meeting sent him another letter dated 17.6.87 requesting him to cancel the proposed disastrous deviation from the approved layout plan and the Chairman promised to do so, but the Kartripakkha, on the contrary, proposed to the Government to acquire land of Bailjuri Mouza for extension of their Uttara Housing Project wherein the entire lands of approved layout plan of the appellant had also been included. The Kartripakkha got their proposal for acquisition approved by the Government and proceeded with the acquisition of land in LA Case No. 2 of 1987-88. The appellant approached the President on 2.10.89 for redress of its grievances and also sent a detailed representation dated 30.10.89 to the Secretary, Ministry or Land Administration and Land Reforms to keep the appellant's housing project out of the Kartripakkha's acquisition. Upon receipt of the President's remark on the appellant's application the Ministry of Works, respondent No.1, asked for a detailed report on the matter from the Chairman of the Kartripakkha who sent a report on 12.11.89 (Annexure-D) to the Ministry stating, inter alia, that for the establishment of Uttara Model Town the former Dhaka Improvement Trust obtained an allotment of 3,300 acres of land in 1960 from the Central Land Allocation Committee, but for paucity of fund only 951 acres were acquired initially. Taking into account the pressing problem of housing the former Trust requested the Government to acquire a further area of 393.00 acres of land of Bailjuri Mouza by Memo dated 16.9.87. The Ministry of Works and the Ministry of Land approved or the proposal on 29.12.87 and 4.5.88 respectively. It was further stated in the report that at the time of making the proposal on 16.9.87 the former Trust should have left out 200 bighas of land for which the appellant had an approved layout plan. After receiving the said report the Ministry of Works, respondent No.1, by a Memo dated 27.1.90 (Annexure-E) gave a decision that the area for which clearance has been given by the Kartripakkha to the appellant by their letter dated 27.2.83 (Annexure-B) is to be left out of acquisition and requested to issue necessary orders immediately to all concerned including the Ministry of Land, the acquiring authority. A copy of this Memo dated 27.1.90 was also forwarded to the appellant. The Memo contains a map and plot index to be excluded from acquisition. 38. It is the appellant's case that the then Chairman of the Kartripakkha and some Officials of the Ministry of Works who were not well-disposed towards' the appellant were determined to spoil its housing project and by asking the appellant to submit the deeds of all the lands purchased by it to prove Its ownership of lands diverted the real issue. Even then the appellant submitted details of its purchased lands and lands in possession by letter dated 20.6.90. The appellant addressed several letters to give effect to Annexure-E and after some inconclusive meetings with the appellant, respondent No. 1 suddenly issued the first impugned Memo dated 13.8.90 (Annexure-H) purporting to cancel the order dated 27.1.90 (Annexure E) and requesting all authorities to keep out of acquisition only those lands of the appellants, over which the appellants acquired full title to the complete satisfaction of the authority and also which will be found to have contained 3 or more acres in a block. There will be no re-opening of LA Case No. 4/86-87 for which land had already been acquired. Respondent No. 1 issued the second impugned Memo dated 6.9.90 Annexure H1, asking all authorities to keep out of acquisition those lands or the appellant for which it has submitted valid documents of title. The third impugned Memo was issued on 27.9.90 (Annexure H2) the ultimate outcome of which is that the entire LA Case No. 2 of 1987-88 was kept intact keeping out of acquisition only 21.09 acres of land of the appellant, which, the appellant says, will entirely sabotage its housing project. Both respondent No. 1 and respondent No. 2 filed separate affidavits-in-opposition, the first one stating that the appellant was given a no objection certificate "on its own possessed land" and the second one Slating that the project was approved "only on land owned" by the appellant and both of them commonly stating that the appellant did not fulfill the conditions on which the approval to its project and layout plan was given. In particular it was denied that the appellant improved any land. They also stated that at the time of "requisition" of land under the two LA Cases the appellant did not raise any objection with the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka, under the provisions of Ordinance No. II of 1982. The appellant petitioned to respondent No. 1 only after acquisition of the land. The acquisition process under the two LA cases rightly proceeded and culminated in the payment of compensation to the owners of the land, except the appellant and, as such, the property now vests in the Government In spite of repeated requests the appellant failed to furnish its documents of title and papers showing mutation of any land in its favour. 39. In its affidavits-in-reply the appellant denied the material allegations stating that the order as to payment of compensation was made after the Government's impugned decision dated 13.8.90 (Annexure-H), that the payment of compensation to the owners has not yet taken place and that the Government changed their decision at Annexure E at the instance of the Kartripakkha which acted with the intention to sabotage the appellant's housing project. Mouja Bailuri has over 2000 bighas of land and the Kartripakkha's housing project can very well be achieved by excluding the appellant's sanctioned lay-out area, of 300 bighas. The appellant also filed a supplementary affidavit-in-reply during hearing of the case before the High Court Division specifically to counter the allegation of respondent No. 1 that the appellant failed to produce its documents of title. The appellant's letter dated 20.6.90 to respondent No. 1 showing details of its purchased lands and lands in its possession under contract of purchase is contained in Annexure-L. 40. In discharging the Rule Nisi the High Court Division held that mere inclusion of certain land owned by others in the layout plan expecting to acquire this land by way of purchase or otherwise in future cannot create any vested right in anyone and by including such land in the layout plan the appellant cannot claim to estop the Kartripakkha to act contrary to the layout plan and the principle of estoppel does not apply. The appellant acquired valid title to only 65 bighas of land and it has not acquired title by contract of purchase of another 150 bighas under section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act. The High Court Division also held that compensation had already been paid to the original owners and therefore the land has already vested in the Government. It was of opinion that the layout plan was approved by the Kartripakkha in exercise of its power under section 3 of the Building Constructions Act, 1952 and, as such, section 21 of the General Clauses Act will apply. The High Court Division also repelled the submission of the appellant that the impugned three Memos and the consequence thereof are violative of Articles 40 and 42 of the Constitution. 41. Leave was granted to consider the appellant's submission that the High Court Division erred in law in taking the view that the respondents changed their earlier decision for non-fulfillment of conditions on which the layout plan was approved, that is, the appellant did not acquire title to the land, that there was no such condition at all for the approval of the layout plan as well as for the exemption under Annexure-E. that for the development of housing projects prior acquisition of title to the land is not necessary, vide section 74(3) of the Town Improvement Act, 1953 under which the appellant's layout plan was approved, that the High Court Division was confused as to the provisions of the Town Improvement Act and the Building Constructions Act; that the respondents took extraneous matters into consideration while changing their earlier decision and that the appellant's fundamental right to enter into and carry on any lawful trade and business under Article 40 of the Constitution has been infringed by the impugned orders. 42. I have no disagreement with the submissions of Mr. A W Bhuiyan, learned Additional Attorney-General appearing for respondent No.1 that if the acquisition of 393 acres of land is complete under section 11 of Ordinance No. II of 1982 then it is no use crying over the spilt milk and that the transaction is a past and closed one; but I do not agree upon the facts presented to us that acquisition is fait accompli in this case. Under section 11 of the Ordinance, the property shall stand acquired and vested absolutely in the Government free from all encumbrances when the compensation mentioned in the award under section 7 has been paid or is deemed to have been paid in pursuance of section 10. Section 11 also provides that immediately after the acquisition of the property a declaration by the Deputy Commissioner in the prescribed form to that effect shall be published in the Official Gazelle. All that has been shown to us is a photocopy of a chalan in LA Case No. 2 of 1987 -88 dated 25.11.89 by which the Deputy Commissioner deposited a sum of Taka 92,61,36,586.77 in the public account for payment of compensation for acquisition of land in the said LA case. There has been a simple assertion in the affidavits-in-opposition of respondent Nos. 1 and 2 that the owners of the land, except the appellant, have since taken payment of the compensation, which the appellant stoutly denied in its affidavits-in-reply. Nothing else has been shown before the High Court Division or to us to induce any amount of assurance in our mind that after depositing the compensation money in the public account the Deputy Commissioner actually completed disbursement of the same among the owners. On the contrary it appears from Annexure G to the writ petition that several writ petitions have been filed in 1993 against the acquisition in LA Case No. 2 of 1987-88 by several owners which are still pending in the High Court Division and on perusal of the records of which I find that neither the Kartripakkha nor the Government have yet filed any affidavit-in-opposition to the same. The appellant has asserted that it has received no notice of acquisition in respect of any land under its ownership and possession and there has been no denial to this categorical assertion. How then is the acquisition a completed transaction? When we asked the learned Additional Attorney-General to produce the Gazette Notification under section 11 (2) of the Ordinance, he submitted that no Gazette Notification has yet been made. Not a single case of disbursement of compensation money has been brought to our notice. A photocopy of the Memo dated 16.9.87 by which the Kartripakkha requested respondent No.1 to acquire 393 acres of land of Mouza Bailjuri has been made available to/us by the learned Counsel for respondent No. 2. This Memo shows that the Central Land Allocation Committee allotted 3450 acres of land to the former Dhaka Improvement Trust for its Uttara Satellite Town Project in 1965, but for financial difficulties only 950 acres of land was decided to be acquired as a first block of the project. About the present stage of that project of 1965 it is stated in the said Memo that the acquisition of land for the said project is in its final stage. When that is the position with regard to the first block of Uttara Satellite Town Project, it is difficult for us to be assured by a mere statement in the affidavits-in-opposition that full compensation money has already been paid in LA Case No. 2 of 1987-88. Besides, if the acquisition of 393 acres of land is complete, then how can respondent No. 1 pass the various impugned orders in Annexure-H series, making a freelance exercise of excluding some lands from acquisition, then again including it? Is this exercise a conclusive evidence of vesting of property in the Government? The learned Additional Attorney-General's argument is therefore thoroughly unacceptable to me. 43. True it is that the appellant has not challenged the acquisition proceedings in the two LA cases involved, but there is no denial to its assertion that it has not received any notice of acquisition in respect of lands under its ownership and possession and therefore its failure to challenge the acquisition proceeding, especially when the acquisition process is not yet complete, will not be fatal to it. The appellant's intention in filing the writ petition was to restore the order of respondent No. 1 dated 27.1.90 (Annexure E) and, with respect, I differ from my learned brother ATM Afzal J. that Annexure E has no legal basis and I will give my reasons later on. 44. The Town Improvement Act, 1953, shortly the Act, makes provisions for the development, improvement and expansion of the Capital of the Republic and Narayanganj and Tongi Municipalities and certain areas in their vicinity. The Kartripakkha is empowered under sections 38-42 to frame an improvement scheme or a rehousing scheme in respect of any area (which means that it is its discretion to frame or not to frame such a scheme) and after preparing a notice stating that a scheme has been framed and giving some particulars and the map of the area comprised in the scheme shall cause a notice to be published weekly for three consecutive weeks in the Official Gazette and in local newspapers and also send a copy of the notice to the Mayor of the Corporation or Chairman of the Pourashava under section 45. Thereafter within 30 days every person whose name appears in the Municipal Assessment List and the occupiers of the land have to be served with a notice under section 48. Considering any objection, representation and statement of dissent received thereunder and after hearing all persons making such objection, etc. the Kartripakkha may either abandon the scheme or apply to the Government for sanction of the scheme with or without modification under section 49 and the Government may sanction with or without modification or may refuse to sanction any improvement scheme under section 50. When the Government sanctions an improvement scheme it shall announce the fact by Notification and the publication of a Notification shall be conclusive evidence that the scheme has been duly framed and sanctioned under section 51. Similar provisions are there in section 51A in respect of schemes of Taka 5 lakh or more outside the City or Municipal limit. Mr. Khandkar Mahbubuddin Ahmed, learned Counsel for the appellant, has additionally assailed the impugned orders on the ground that sections 38-51A of the said Act and section 15 of Ordinance No. II of 1982 have not been followed and I concur with my learned brother A TM Afzal, J. that these new allegations and grounds are not available to the appellant for the reasons given by him. 45. But I have outlined the provisions of sections 38-51A of the said Act to show the scheme of the act. The said Act also provides that the Kartripakkha shall prepare a Master Plan for the area within its jurisdiction indicating the manner in which it proposes that land should be used and the stages by which any such development should be carried out. The Government shall within 1 month from the receipt of the Master Plan from the Kartripakkha publish the same in the official Gazette. Then comes section 74(3) which provides as follows: "74(3). All future developments and: constructions, both public and private, shall be in conformity with the Master Plan or with the amendment thereof." 46. When a land developer wishes to acquire by purchase a block of land for a housing project it applies for a no objection certificate from the Kartripakkha for a number of reasons. First, the developer's project may not be in accord with the Master Plan and its enterprise may be nipped in the bud by the kartripakkha by passing on this simple information, sparing the developer from pursuing a fruitless course. Secondly, the Kartripakkha may have an improvement or re-housing scheme of its own in the area chosen by the developer and the Kartripakkha may also thus save the developer from its efforts. Thirdly, even if the Kartripakkha does not have any scheme of its own, it may require the developer to keep its plan in conformity with the layout plan of the Kartripakkha's own adjoining the developer's proposed project area so as to achieve a uniformity and harmony in the development and to ensure uniform movement of traffic. Fourthly, the Kartripakkha may not have any improvement scheme of its own but it may have a future plan to build a highway or a wide road to connect its adjoining housing project with a distant area so as to facilitate future urban extension and the developer may be warned well ahead of the Kartripakkha's future plan. Section 74(3) is therefore the right section in the said Act under which a developer may ask the Kartripakkha to issue a 'no objection certificate'. 47. When a developer approaches the Kartripakkha for a no objection certificate with a scheme of its own it is absolutely not necessary that it should own any or all of the area covered by its plan. It approaches the Kartripakkha for an assurance that after the layout plan is approved it will be kept outside of any other developer's or the Kartripakkha's own improvement scheme or acquisition plan, subject of course to the fulfilment of conditions that the Kartripakkha may impose upon the approval. 48. I have quoted earlier in full the terms under which the Board of Trustees of the Kartripakkha approved of the appellant's project on 4.10.78 (Annexure A) and the further conditions under which the appellant's layout plan was approved by the Town Planner on 27.2.83 (Annexure B). It will be noticed that 110 time-limit was given within which the appellant was required to complete its project. However that is not fatal to the Kartripakkha, because in the absence of a time-limit the Kartripakkha can wait for a reasonable period to see whether the developer has made any progress with his project and if no progress or an insignificant progress has been made it is free to take such decision as it may think fit, namely, cancel the no objection certificate or acquire the land for its own project. The approval of the project stating “উক্ত সমিতির নিজস্ব দখলে যতটুকু জমি আছে তাহার উপর তাহাদের প্রস্তাবিত গৃহায়ন প্রকল্প বাস্তবায়নের ব্যাপারে ডি, আই,টির আপত্তি থাকিবে না।” does not mean and can never mean that on the day of sanction, i.e. on 4.10.78 all the lands proposed to be covered by the developer will have to be in the developer's possession, Nor does the approval of the layout plan on 27.2.83 mean that on the dole of approval the area covered by the layout plan should be already in possession of the developer. Both the approval dated 4.10.78 and the sanction dated 27.2.83 are in the nature of a go-ahead signal to the developer to go on acquiring land by private purchase and negotiation and to implement its project within the terms of approval. A developer will indeed be a foolish investor if after acquiring 300 bighas of land by private purchase it applies to the Kartripakkha for a no objection certificate only to learn that his project is contrary to Master Plan or that the Kartripakkha has a project of its own on the same land or that the project could be sanctioned only on fulfilment of some impossible conditions imposed by the Kartripakkha. The approval and sanction are a developer's permit to operate within a certain area, rendered harmless by any intervention of the Kartripakkha in future. 49. The layout plan was not sanctioned under section 3 of the Building Constructions Act, 1952 as held by the High Court Division. It was a sanctioned layout plan within the meaning of section 74(3) of the said Act. The approval and sanction cannot be said to be bereft of creating any legal relationship between the Kartripakkha and the developer. Nor can it be said that it is an ultra vires act of the Kartripakkha. Under the said Act the Kartripakkha has been given an enabling power to make and execute an improvement in a re-housing scheme, but it is not statutorily bound to do so in respect of each and every inch of land within or outside the Capital and Narayanganj and Tongi Municipalities. It is also within the legal competence of the Kartripakkha not to frame any improvement scheme in respect of a particular area. Acting completely within its jurisdiction, namely, to frame or not to frame any improvement or re-housing scheme in respect of any area, the Kartripakkha decided in the present ease not to have an improvement scheme of its own within the area of the layout plan of the appellant. By the approval and sanction therefore the Kartripakkha gave the following statutory promises to the appellant: (1) The appellant's project is in conformity with the Master Plan. (2) The Kartripakkha itself has no scheme of its own in respect of the area covered by the layout plan. No other developer will be given a parallel approval and sanction in respect of the area. Therefore the appellant is free to implement its project on the terms and conditions set down by the Kartripakkha. (3) If the appellant violates any terms and conditions of the approval and sanction it will be entitled to a show cause notice as to why its approval and sanction will not be cancelled. (4) In the absence of a time limit the Kartripakkha will wait for a reasonable period to see if the appellant has made any progress with its project and after being satisfied that the appellant has made no progress or an insignificant progress cancel the approval and sanction by a prior notice and may frame a scheme of its own following the procedure laid down in the said Act. It may then submit to the Government its own scheme for sanction. 50. Respondent No. 2 has not made any averment nor placed any material to show that before submitting its own scheme for acquisition on 16.9.87 any enquiry was made by the Kartripakkha as to how far the appellant had proceeded with its housing project. It did not cancel the appellant's approval and sanction before sending its own proposal for acquisition and hence reliance upon section 21 of the General Clauses Act by the High Court Division and its renewed plea by the learned Additional Attorney-General are thoroughly misplaced. The Kartripakkha did not even wait for a reasonable period before it framed its own scheme. Acquisition of land by private purchase often involves litigation and it is a time-consuming process. The Kartripakkha's own Uttara Block Statellite Town Project, undertaken in 1965 for acquisition of 950 acres of land is still, on its own admission, at the stage of final acquisition. To expect that within four years of the sanctioning of a layout plan the appellant will be able to achieve what the Kartripakkha with the coercive machinery of Ordinance No. 11 of 1982 has not been able to achieve within three decades is to ask for the moon. The Kartripakkha acted completely behind the back and without the knowledge of the appellant in changing the width and alignment of Uttara-Ranabhola Link Road and in forwarding its acquisition proposal on 16.9.87, without even caring to inquire how much progress the appellant had made and what expenses it had incurred in the meanwhile. Both the respondents are now claiming in their respective affidavits-in-opposition that the appellant did not fulfill the terms and conditions of approval, but there is little doubt that this allegation, besides being vague, is an afterthought aired for the first time to make out a case against the appellant. It is also now being alleged by the respondents that the appellant did not make any improvement as it claims to have made, and this allegation too is an afterthought, as respondent No. 2 did not even allege and never produced any materia to show that it framed its own scheme as the appellant failed to improve the land. 51. I am quite aware of the possibility that unscrupulous land speculators by obtaining an approval and sanction from the Katripakkha can with impunity continue to hoard land without doing any improvement work or without implementing any housing project. In some countries land hoarding charges are imposed on such land speculator. In our country in the absence of any such legislation it will be wise for the Kartripakkha while according approval to a private housing project to make provisions for periodical review of the project and to set up a time-limit for its completion. 52. Under such circumstances as detailed above I do not think why the principle of promissory estoppel, on which Mr. Khandkar Mahbubuddin Ahmed rests his main submission, will not apply in this case. As HWR Wade in his book Administrative Law, 5th Edition says. "The basic principle of estoppel is that a person who by some statement or representation of fact causes another to act to his detriment in reliance on the truth of it is not allowed to deny it later, even though it is wrong. Justice here prevails over truth. An estoppel is often described as a rule of evidence, but more correctly it is a principle of law. (Canada and Dominion Sugar Company Ltd. vs. Canadian National (West Indies) Steamship Ltd. (1947) AC 46 (56) (P. 232)'. 53. The principle of promissory estoppel is applicable to public authorities as well and in this particular case there is no escape from the fact that the Kartripakkha is estopped from resiling from the promises I already mentioned that it has made to the appellant. 54. Now for the representation that the appellant submitted to the President culminating in the order of respondent No. 1 dated 27.1.90 (Annexure-E). With regret I am unable to concur with my learned brother ATM Afzal, J that the appellant's application to the President and all the orders that followed (Annexures E and H series) have no foundation in law. From Annexure-H it is found that LA Case No. 4 of 1986-87 was started for acquiring land for "approaches" to Ranabhola Link Road, not for the link road itself. Presumably, the appellant's layout area was not affected thereby, but the appellant was alarmed because the width of the road was increased to 300 feet and the road alignment was changed so as to pierce through the appellant's housing project. The appellant sent its first representation to the Chairman of the Kartripakkha on 17.11.86 (Annexures C and C 1) objecting to the proposed deviation in LA Case No. 4 of 1986-87, with no answer. Much has been made of the fact that instead of filing an objection to the Deputy Commissioner under Ordinance No. II of 1982, the appellant was running to the President and the Chairman of the Kartripakkha, apparently to achieve an end by non-legal means. The appellant's representation to the Chairman is fully covered by section 52 of said Act which is as follows: "52. At any time after any improvement scheme or re-housing scheme has been sanctioned by the Government and before it has been carried into execution, the Kartripakkha may alter it : Provided as follows: (a) if any alteration is estimated to increase the estimated net cost of executing a scheme by more than five per cent of such cost, such alteration shall not be made without the previous sanction of the Government; (b) if any alteration involves the acquisition, otherwise than by agreement, of any land the acquisition of which has not been sanctioned by the Government the procedure prescribed in the foregoing sections of this Chapter shall, so far as applicable, be followed as if the alteration were a separate scheme; (c) if owing to the changes made, in the course of a scheme any land not previously liable under the scheme to the payment of a betterment free, becomes liable to such payment, the provisions of sections 45, 48 and 49 shall, so far as they are applicable, be followed in any such case." 55. There is nothing to show that the Ranabhola approach scheme for which lands were acquired in LA Case No. 4 of 1986-87 had been carried into execution before the appellant addressed its representation to the Chairman on 17.11.86. In fact LA Case No. 4 of 1986-87 was still in its infancy at that stage. There is also nothing to show that while addressing its subsequent representations to the President on 2.10.89 and to the Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms on 30.10.89, the Kartripakkha's scheme in respect of LA Case No. 2 of 1987-88 had already been carried into execution. LA Case No. 2 of 1987-88 for 393 acres was started, according to the affidavit-in-opposition of respondent No. 1 (para 5) and according to the affidavit-in-opposition of respondent No. 2 (para 7), for the purpose of Uttara-Ranabhola road proper (and not its approach from the Uttara end) as well as for the Kartripakkha's housing project. This last LA case hit the appellant in real terms and before the scheme even got off to a start it moved the President this time so that the Kartripakkha may retrace its steps under section 52. The President himself did not take any action, but respondent No. 1 in pursuance of a noting from the President asked for a report from the Chairman. In his report dated 12.11.89 (Annexure-D) the Chairman did not state that its Uttara-Ranabhola approach road in LA Case No. 4 of 1986-87 or the road itself or the housing project in LA Case No.2 of 1987-88 had been carried into execution and, in fact, suggested some alternative including exclusion of the appellant's layout plan from its scheme and it was perfectly within his statutory power under section 52 of the said Act to do so. The Ministry of Works by Memo dated 27.1.90 (Annexure-E), in fact, took a decision excluding the appellant's layout plan area, thus accepting the suggestion of the Kartripakkha and acting in exercise of its powers under section 191A Of the said Act which is as follows: "191 A. The government shall exercise general control and supervision over the Kartripakkha as well as its Chairman and other members and may give direction to them, as may be necessary for ensuring that their activities conform to the purposes of the Act; and the Kartripakkha, the Chairman and the other members shall exercise their powers and perform their functions in accordance with such direction." 56. Respondent No. 1, the controlling Ministry of the Kartripakkha, after applying its mind, found that it was reasonable to exclude the appellant's land covered by the layout plan from the proposed acquisition and its decision, in view of the promises made to the appellant, was taken for ensuring that the activities of the Kartripakkha conform to the purposes of the Act. In Annexure-E, respondent No. 1 never indicated that the lands covered by the appellant's layout plan must be owned by the appellant. There was neither any absence of power nor any lack of legal cover in giving this decision. The order of respondent No. 1 dated 27.1.90 (Annexure-E) was sabotaged by Annexure-H series on completely extraneous considerations. The appellant was not clamouring for compensation for acquisition of its land in the LA proceedings. It was only stating that it was given a promise to operate within a certain area which should be kept out of acquisition. Respondent No. 1 diverted the real issue by asking the appellant to produce its title deeds and mutation papers. This diversionary manoeuvre was aimed at establishing the proposition that either on the date of approval of the project (4.10.78) or on the date of the approval of the layout plan (27.2.83) the appellant must either own or possess the entire land of layout area or else its right is only limited to receipt of compensation for acquisition of land. What the Kartripakkha truly understood to be the appellant's main bone of contention (Annexure-D) and what respondent No. 1 rightly comprehended to be the main issue (Annexure-E) were now misdirected towards non-issues, namely, how much land the appellant owns and possesses now. And the entire Annexure-H series is a product of asking a wrong question and giving a wrong answer. 57. Although Mr. Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed could not lay his hands on any persuasive material to bring home the appellant's allegation of collusion between the Chairman of the Kartripakkha and a high official of respondent No. 1, it is quite apparent from the quixotic turn of decisions from Annexure-H to H2 that some malicious hands were operating behind the scene to divert the real issue, taking one decision at one time, revising the same by the next breath, taking another decision the next and taking irrelevant matters into consideration. For example, Chairman by his report dated 12.11.89 (Annexure-D) mentioned and annexed various approvals given to various developers within the 393 acres proposed to be acquired for the Kartripakkha, and the decision of respondent No. 1 dated 27.1.90 (Annexure-E) was taken in full consideration of the same. Yet by the first impugned Memo dated 13.8.90 (Annexure-H), Annexure-E was cancelled on the ground inter alia, that it was not brought to the notice of respondent No. 1 whether one Capital Housing Society had a housing project within the appellant's project area and whether the said Capital Housing Society had an approved housing project from the Kartripakkha. These information’s were apparently already supplied when the decision in Annexure-E was taken. 58. It is contended by the respondents that the appellant did not act to his detriment following any promise, it did not improve any land and it suffered no damages. I have already held that this allegation, made for the first time in the affidavits-in- opposition, is an afterthought, and deserves no serious consideration. The appellant's progress with its project was never inquired into by any of the respondents at any time. In any view of the matter, the following observations by the Indian Supreme Court in the case of MP Sugar Mills Co. Ltd. vs. The State of Uttar Pradesh, AIR 1979 (SC) 651) is a complete answer to the respondents' submission: We do not think that in order to invoke the doctrine of promissory estoppel it is necessary for the promisee to show that he suffered detriment as a result of acting in reliance on the promisee. But we may make it clear that if by detriment we mean injustice to the promisee which would result if the promisor were to recede from his promise, then detriment would certainly come in as a necessary ingredient. The detriment in such a case is not some prejudice suffered by the promisee by acting on the promise, but the prejudice which would be caused to the promisee, if the promissor were allowed to go back on the promises." 59. It is accepted by the respondents that the appellant purchased some lands at least in its layout area and that is enough to say that it has altered its position as a result of the promise. The respondents' assertion that it had released from acquisition all the 65 bighas of land purchased by the appellant by Annexure-H2 is also palpably incorrect. The appellant purchased 32.86 acres of land, but by Annexure-H2 only 21.09 acres of land purchased by it have been released from acquisition. Its possession of another 150 bighas of land by contract of purchase has not been considered at all. 60. The learned Additional Attorney-General has also placed his reliance upon some observations made by the Indian Supreme Court in the said MP Sugar Mills case (Supra) at P. 644 which has been quoted by my learned brother ATM Afzal, J., Respectfully, I say, the quotation is incomplete, for the Indian Supreme Court proceeds to say, "It would not be enough for the Government just to say that public interest requires that the Government should not be compelled to carry out the promise or that the public interest would suffer if the Government were required to honor it. The Government cannot, as Shah, J, pointed out in the Indo-Afgahan Agencies case, claim to be exempt from the liability to carry out the promise "on some indefinite and undisclosed ground of necessity or expediency", nor can the Government claim to be the sole judge of its liability and repudiate it "on an ex parte appraisement of the circumstances". If the government wants to resist the liability, it will have to disclose to the Court what are the subsequent events on account of which the Government claims to be exempt from the liability and it would be for the Court to decide whether those events are such as to render it inequitable to enforce the liability against the Government. Mere claim of change of policy would not be sufficient to exonerate the Government from the liability. The Government would have to show what precisely is the changed policy and also its reason and justification so the Court can judge for itself which way the public interest lies and what the equity of the case demands. It is only if the Court is satisfied, on proper and adequate material placed by the Government, that overriding public interest requires that the Government should not be held bound by the promise but should be free to act unfettered by it, that the Court should refuse to enforce the promise against the Government. The Court would not act on the mere ipse dixit of the Government, for it is the Court which has to decide and not the Government whether the Government should be held exempt from liability. This is the essence of the rule of law. The burden would be upon the Government to show that the public interest in the Government acting otherwise than in accordance with the promise is so overwhelming that it would be inequitable to hold the Government bound by the promise and the Court would insist on a highly rigorous standard of proof in the discharge of this burden, but even where there is no such overriding public interest, it may still be competent to the Government to resile from the promise "on giving reasonable notice, which need not be a formal notice, giving the promisee a reasonable opportunity of resuming his position" provided of course it is possible for the promisee to restore status quo ante. If, however, the promisee cannot resume his position, the promise could become final and irrevocable. Vide Ajayi vs. Briscoe (1964) 3 ALL Er 556." 61. The respondents have neither placed any material nor any copy of a prior notice to the appellant to show that they had acted in an overriding public interest or that events that have subsequently transpired justify denial of an equity in favour of the appellant. There is nothing to show from the record, that a large part of the appellant's layout area was acquired in LA Case No. 4 of 1986-87 and the appellant merely stood by, sending only two representations to the Chairman. LA Case No. 4 of 1986-87 was started for an approach to Uttara-Ranabhola Road and it presumably did not affect the appellant's layout area. But the LA Case alarmed the appellant which found that the proposed road alignment would spoil its 60 developed and 137 allotted plots. So it requested the Kartripakkha to retrace its steps under section 52 of the said Act. There is also nothing to show that in 1986 the Kartripakkha started construction of the link road to Ranabhola. It was only constructing the approach road from the Uttara end upon the Kartripakkha's acquired land. Annexure B precluded the appellant from questioning acquisition of land for the Kartripakkha for construction of bridges or culverts and their approaches to Ranabhola (not to Uttara). The width and alignment of the link road had already been settled and finalised between the appellant and the Kartripakkha by a protracted negotiation from 1978 to 1983. The appellant's layout plan contained a provision for 100 feet road. When the Kartripakkha changed the width and alignment of the link road without informing the appellant and behind its back, the appellant certainly had the legal right to object to such unilateral change disastrous to its project. It did so, timely and within the law. It was only when LA Case No. 2 of 1987-88 was started that the link road proper with approach to Ranibhola and the housing project of the Kartripakkha was included in the 393 acres of land which included the appellant's layout area. It is nowhere the respondents case, not a word has been said anywhere, that the 300 feet link road has already been consumed within an unknown area of 300 bighas within the appellant's layout area. In fact, there is no material on record that the link road has at all been constructed. The respondents have not made out any case that within the 300 bighas of the appellant's layout area, provision has been made for public facilities like roads, bridges, schools, parks, etc. The Kartripakkha's layout plan has not been shown to us and we simply do not know what material benefit the residuary allottees of the appellant (as per Annexure-H2) will derive from the Kartripakkha's layout plan. The appellant's sanctioned layout plan contained a number of open spaces with provisions for playground, schools, park, internal roads (some as large as 40 feet wide), shopping centre, Community Centre, Commercial area, etc. How can it be said that the Kartripakkha was offering a better and more comprehensive service within easy access to the appellant's allottees within the layout area? The word 'public interest' is not a mere catchword. The Kartripakkha's scheme of better utility and convenience has to be shown to the Court which it has not. Besides, if all the Government orders (Annexure-E to H series) are not at all in accordance with law, then even Annexure-H2 falls, and the respondents are under no legal obligation to honour the minimum 'grace' granted to the appellant. All its 300 bighas are gone, including 21.09 acre so very graciously released from acquisition by Annexure-H2. The appellant had come to the writ jurisdiction for cancellation of Annexure-H series and the High Court Division refused to grant that prayer. How to say that not only Annexure-H series but also Annexure-E has no legal basis is, I think, a windfall received by the Government without disowning Annexure-E. Upon the facts disclosed in the affidavits-in-opposition I hold therefore that there was no overriding public interest, justified by subsequent events, to deny the equity in favour of the appellant. In the light of the above discussions, I allow this appeal with no costs and declare that the impugned Memos. (Annexures-H, H1 and H2) have been passed without lawful authority and are of no legal effect. Latifur Rahman J: I have gone through the judgments proposed to be delivered by my learned brother ATM Afzal, J. and my learned brother Mustafa Kamal J; I concur with the judgment of my learned brother ATM Afzal J. Order of the Court By the majority decision the appeal is dismissed without any order as to costs. End.

caseno: Appeal From Original Order No. 52 of 1992 with Civil Rule No. 58(fm) of 1992
lawyer:
Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed with SM CI Monir, Advocates ----- For the Appellant. 	 
MA Wahhab Miah with Biswajit Roy and B Chakroborty, Advocates ----- For the Respondents.
parties:
Khalilur Rahman (Md) and others ------ Appellant
vs.
Abdur Rahman Bhuiyan alias Zinnat Ali Bhuiyan & others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Mahmudul Amin Choudhury J: This appeal is directed against the judgment and order dated 9-3-92 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Chandpur in Miscellaneous Case No. 59 of 1990 filed under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act for pre-emption of the case land. 

2. The short fact leading to this appeal is that the respondent as petitioner filed the aforesaid case for pre-emption stating that his father Late Fazlul Huq Bhuiyan was the owner of the case land and the building and the petitioner-respondent lost his father during his minority and he inherited the case land and building along with other co-sharers. It is also the case of the petitioner that opposite parties 1-3 purchased 0.200 acre of land and three annas share of the building thereon from opposite parties 7 and 8 by registered kabala dated 22-3-79 at a consideration  of Taka 30,000.00. The present appellant further purchased 0.08 acre of land and one anna share of the building from Rokeya Begum, the predecessor of  opposite parties 12-20 by registered kabala dated  17-8-79 at a consideration of Taka 15,000.00. Opposite Party No. 1 purchased 0.0270 acre of land and four ann as ten gondas share of the building from opposite party Nos. 9, 10 and Rokeya Begum, the predecessor of opposite parties 12-23, by another registered kabala dated 7-4-79 at a consideration of Taka: 34,000.00 and opposite party No.3 purchased 0123 acre of land and 2 annas share of the building from opposite party No.l1 by a registered kabala dated 11-4-79 at a consideration of Taka 18,000.00. It is also the case of the petitioner that opposite party No.2 purchased .2070 acre of land and 4 annas 10 gandas share of the building from opposite parties 4, 5 and 6 by another registered kabala dated 14-4-79 at a consideration of Taka 34,000.00 and in this way opposite parties 1 and 2 purchased.0953 acre of land and 15 annas share of the building thereon from opposite parties 4-11 .and from Rokeya Begum, the predecessor of opposite parties 12-20, at a total consideration of Taka 1,31,000.00 but for these purchases no notice under section 23 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act was served upon the petitioner-respondent. It is also the case of the petitioner-respondent that he was minor when those kabalas were executed and registered and that he was ignorant about these at the time of transfers. It is also the case of the petitioner-respondent that his father died on 9-9-74 and the petitioner was the youngest son of his father who was born on 16-5-69, and he inherited .0310 acre of land and the share of the building thereon from his father and became a co-sharer in the building by inheritance. He came to know that his share to the extent of 0.0310 acre of land and the share of the building thereon have been transferred by false personation by two forged kabalas collusively and without consideration, which are void ab initio by alleged sale deeds dated 24-3-78 and 19-9- 78 and these were registered in the District Sub-Registrar's Office, Comilla for which Title Suit No. 117 of 1986 was instituted in the Court of the learned Assistant Judge, Sadar Chandpur for a declaration that the alleged deeds are illegal, forged, collusive, without consideration and void. It is also the case of the petitioner that opposite parties 1-3 instituted CR Case Nos. 342 and 346 of 1984 before the Upazila Magistrate, Chandpur Sadar alleging that those deeds were executed and registered by the mother, brother, brother-in-law and sister of the  petitioner by false personation during the minority of   the vendor. It is the' further case of the   petitioner-respondent that he came to know about the deeds for which the present Miscellaneous Case was   filed from Salamatullah Khan and Habibur Rahman   for the first time on 10-5-90 and after getting the   certified copies of the deeds the petitioner deposited the   statutory amount of Taka 1,31,000.00 along with 5%  compensation and prayed for pre-emption under   section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. 

3. Before the trial Court appellant Alhaj Md Khalilur Rahman Miah and opposite party No., 2 Abdul Matin Miah entered appearance and contested the case by filing a written objections and their case  is that, the actual name Of the petitioner-respondent is Zinnat Ali and he was never named as Abdur Rahman and the deeds in question, for which the  pre-emption is sought for were executed and registered in the presence of the petitioner during his majority and the proceeding was not instituted  within time as prescribed under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949. The petition, is therefore, barred by limitation. The petitioner's entire share of the disputed land and building has been transferred by registered kabalas dated 24-3-78 and 19-9-78 and thereby his title to the case land has been extinguished and the petitioner is no longer a co-sharer in the holding. It has also been contended that this petitioner became major at the time of execution of the kabalas, which were done by him, in favour of opposite parties 1-3 and, as such, the I petitioner is not entitled to get an order of pre-emption. 

4. Before the trial Court both the sides produced oral and documentary evidence in support of their respective cases. The learned Subordinate Judge by his impugned judgment dated 9-3-92  allowed the case and ordered that case land and the  share of the building be pre-empted accordingly in  favour of the petitioner-respondent and the right,  title, and interest of the case land and the share in the  building thereon vest in the petitioner-respondent  free from all encumbrances 

5. The contesting opposite party No. 1 on being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the a judgment dated' 9-3-92 passed by the learned 0 Subordinate Judge in the aforesaid Miscellaneous case preferred this appeal. 

6. Mr Khandker: Mahbubuddin Ahmed k appearing with Mr SM Moonir on behalf of the appellant, submits that the petitioner-respondent flied this miscellaneous case for pre-emption of five kabalas of different dates and when the petitioner-respondent sought to pre-empt the case land and building covered by these five kabalas heought to have filed separate case. He submits that the present case is a case of misjoinder of causes of action. He also submits that the five kabalas are not between the same parties and the dates are also different. Placing section 24(1) of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act Mr Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed submits that this section requires the filing of separate cases. There may be a joint trial but five separate cases ought to have been, filed. He submits that this section indicated that for each transfer a separate case is required to be filed. 

7. As against this Mr M Wahhab Miah, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner-respondent, placing section 24(1) of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act submits that .this section clearly indicates that for several documents for pre-emption, one case may be filed and there is no bar in it and in support of his submission he placed reliance in the case of Hajee Majar Ullah Sowdagar vs. Mvi Nurul Haque & ors, 'reported in 23 DLR 68. It is submitted that in this decision a Division Bench of this Court found that one pre-emption case for different kabalas is maintainable. He also relied on another decision, which is of course a Single Benchdecision, reported in 42 DLR 253 (Sree Jitendra Nath Howladervs. Sree Bisweewar Howlader & ors) It is submitted that this decision has followed the principle 'of law enunciated in 23 DLR case. The learned Advocate contends that the facts leading to the decision reported in 23 DLR and the facts of the present case before us are similar though that decision was given in a proceeding filed under section 96 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. 

8. Before proceeding further with other arguments, we intend to dispose of the first objection that has been raised by Mr Khondker Mahbuddin Ahmed on misjoinder of causes of action. For proper appreciation of the whole matter let us look into the provision of section 24(1) of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act."24(1) If a portion- or share of the Non-Agricultural land held by a non-agricultural tenant is transferred, one or more co-sharer tenants of such land may, within four months of the service of notice issued under section 23 and, in case no notice had been issued or served, then within four months from the date of knowledge  of such transfer;' apply to the Court for such  portion or share to be transferred to himself or to themselves, as the case may be." 

9. Mr Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed submits that the words portion or share is singular which indicate that there should be a separate case for each kabala. For proper appreciation of the whole matter let us look into the provision of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act wherein it has been provided as follows: "96(1) If a portion or share of a holding of a raiyat is transferred, one or more co-sharer tenants of the holding may, within four months of the service of the notice given under section 89, or, if no notice has been served under section '89, within four months of the date of the knowledge of the transfer, apply to the Court for the said portion or share to be transferred to himself or themselves." 

10. The language of section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act and section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act are same and similar. The learned Advocate failed to produce any decision of any higher Court on the point that in Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act cases separate applications for different transaction, are to be filed. So, we may profitably derive a sense of direction from the decision given under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 

11. We have gone through the decision reported in 23 DLR 68 wherein one miscellaneous case was filed for pre-emption of three kabalas of three different dates. Parties to the case were also different In one kabala opposite party No. 1 of that case purchased from opposite party No.4 by kabala dated 18-8-66 and he also purchased from opposite party No.3 by another kabala dated 22-8-66 and opposite parties 1 and 2 jointly purchased from opposite party No.5 another portion of land by kabala dated 2-9-66. So, it appears that the vendors are different in these kabalas. In that decision the High Court Division observed that on a careful reading of the provision of section 96 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act it would be found that the transfer shall have to be pre-empted under certain conditions mentioned therein and in this case admittedly there were three independent transfers or sales. It is true that if by the document lands of several holdings are sold the pre-emptor can maintain one application for pre-empting the lands of all the holdings if his claim is not otherwise barred, but if the sales are different and independent then in that case the question is, whether the pre-emptor has to file separate applications for those independent sales or can he maintain one application for a number of independent sales. It has been held that the scheme of section 96 of the Act would show that the intention of the legislature is also not very clear on this point. The learned Judges after consideration of the relevant laws, including the Code Civil Procedure, ultimately came to the decision that an applicant under section 96 for pre-emption can join several causes of section against the defendants in one application arising out of several independent transfers or sales subject to the question of limitation and other conditions relating to maintainability of an application for pre-emption. 

12. In the present case before us admittedly lands and building covered by five kabalas have been sought to be pre-empted in a single case. We have gone through the provision of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act and we find that as there is no clear decision from any higher Courts on section 21 of the said Act we may very well consider the principle of law set forth in the decision reported in 23 DLR 68 which was of course, a case under section 9p of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act the language of both the sections are same and similar. Section 96 relates to a portion or share of holding of a raiyat, whereas section 24 is in respect of a portion or share of the non-agricultural  land held by a non-agricultural tenant. There is no difference in between the two sections. So, relying on the principle of law as set out in 23 DLR 68 and  42 DLR 253 we hold that the petitioner-respondent  can very well maintain the present miscellaneous  case under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural  Tenancy Act even though lands and buildings of five  kabalas have been sought to be pre-empted in a  single pre-emption case and in that view of the  matter we find no force in the argument advanced by Me Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed in this respect So, on consideration of the submissions made by the learned Advocates of both the sides we hold that the present miscellaneous case is maintainable in law. 

13. Mr Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed then submitted that under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act a co-sharer tenant of such land may, within four months of toe service of notice issued under section 23 and, in case no notice has been issued or served, within four month from the date of knowledge of such transfer, apply to the Court for such portion or share for pre-emption. He submits, that here in the present case the miscellaneous case does not come with in these two categories. It is submitted that the case was filed long after the period of limitation. 

14. It is the definite case of the petitioner-respondent that he was born on 16-5-69 and the questioned kabalas were executed and registered in 1979 when he was a minor. Mr Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed submits that even according to the 'admitted date of birth of the respondent he attained majority on 16-5-87 and he filed the suit, that is, Other Class Suit No. 117/86 in the Upazila Munsif Court, Chandpur and he was ordered to remain present in Court on 29-5-88 as according to the present appellant he was a major and when he was so produced the Court found him to be major and he was ordered to prosecute his own case, though that case was filed through his sister. The learned Advocate contends that even in 1988 this petitioner-respondent was a major and he had the knowledge of the disputed transfers and he himself filed a suit for declaration of certain kabalas to be void, illegal, etc. and that indicates his knowledge of the existence of the kabalas to be pre-empted. But the miscellaneous case was not filed within four months or at least 29-5-88. 

15. Before the trial Court the contesting parties adduced evidence, both oral and documentary. According to the petitioner-respondent, he was born on 16-5-69 and there is no evidence to hold otherwise. The School certificates were produced to prove the date of birth of the respondent and he proved that he was born on 16-5-69 and from that date the petitioner became major on 16-5-1987.   Admittedly, the case was filed on 15-5-1990. It is also the case of the petitioner-respondent that he came to know of these kabalas on 10-5-90 and then obtaining certified copies filed the case within 5 days that, is, on 15-5-1990. Excepting the papers of Title Suit No.117 of 1986 nothing has been produced to show that this petitioner-respondent was major in 1979 when the questioned documents were created. Though it is the definite case of the present-appellant that the petitioner attained majority in 1979 but nothing has been produced to prove it.  So, according to the petitioner in 1979 he was a minor and he attained majority on 16-5-198-7: The petitioner examined several witnesses to prove the date of knowledge. He-himself deposed as PW 1 and  stated that he came to know of the transfers from Salamatullah Khan and Habibur Rahman and on  obtaining certified copies of the kabalas on 10-5-90  filed the present miscellaneous case. He deposed that this Habibur Rahman is dead and Salamatullah Khan is alive This Salamatullah Khan deposed as PW 2 and he stated on oath that he came to know of these  kabalas from opposite party No.2 in the month of  April, 1990 and he informed the matter to the  petitioner-respondent and thereafter the present case  was filed. Admittedly, the case land and building are situated in Chandpur and all the kabalas were registered in Comilla by the District Sub-Registrar The kabalas were written by DW 4 Abdus Sattar  Prodhaniya who is admittedly a deed writer of Chandpur Sub-Registry Office. When the parties are from Chandpur and the land sought to be transferred is at Chandpur and when the scribe is also from  Chandpur there was no earthly reason for registering  the deed at Comilla and no explanation has been  given from the side of the defence for such  registration. According to the respondent, this, has been done purposely so that the information relating to the existence of the kabalas may not be leaked out. 

16. Now the question is whether the miscellaneous case has been filed within the stipulated time as provided under section 24 of the  Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. It provides that such cases are to be filed within four months from the date of service of notice or within four months from the date of the knowledge of such transfer. When admittedly no notice has been served upon the petitioner respondent he had to file the case within four months from the date of his knowledge. The kabalas are of the year 1979 and the case was filed on 15-5-1990. It is the definite case of the petitioner-respondent that in 1979 he was minor-and from the evidence en, record we hold that the petitioner-respondent has succeeded in proving that he was a minor in 1979 as he was born in 1969. From the perusal of the record it appears that the respondent earlier instituted a criminal case against the brothers and sisters of the petitioner alleging that knowing fully well that the petitioner-respondent is a minor they have defended him by creating a kabala showing this petitioner as major. This petition of complaint has been marked as Ext 3 before the trial Court wherein it has been categorically stated that the complainant on taking copy of the plaint and written statement of SCC Suit No.3 of 1984 came to know that this petitioner was minor when the kabala was executed and registered by showing him major. So this Ext.3 proved that on the date of filing of the criminal case, that is, on 23-4-84, the present petitioner-respondent was a minor. It is submitted by Me Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed that in this case the pre-emptor entered appearance and he had knowledge of the transfers but nothing has been• produced to show that the pre-emptor entered appearance and contested the case and there is no proof that the pre-emptor was aware of the kabalas. So, from this it cannot be found that the pre-emptor had knowledge of the kabalas from before 16-5-87. Even no evidence was led to prove that the respondent was aware of the kabalas in the later part of 1989 or in the earlier part of 1990 and within time he has not filed the case in question. The learned Advocate for the appellant placing the provision of section 8 of the Limitation Act submits that such pre-emption cases are not maintainable and barred by limitation. He further submits that as the case was filed beyond time the pre-emptor is not entitled to take advantage of the provisions of sections 6 and 7 of the Limitation Act Section 6 provides that where a person entitled to institute a suit or proceeding or make an application for the execution of a decree is, at the time from which the period of limitation is to be reckoned, a minor, or insane, or an idiot, he may institute the suit or proceeding or make the.  application' within the same period after the  disability has ceased, as would otherwise have been  allowed from the time prescribed thereof in the third column of the First Schedule or in section 48 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Section 7 of this Act provides that where one or several persons jointly entitled to Institute a suit or proceeding or make an application for the execution of a decree is under any such disability, and a discharge can be given without   the concurrence of such person, time will run against all, but, where no such discharge can be given, time  will not run as against any of them until one of them becomes capable of giving such discharge  without the concurrence of the others or until the  disability has ceased. The learned Advocate contends that the advantage given to the litigant under sections 6 and 7 of the Limitation Act is not applicable to a pre-emptor in a case for pre-emption as provided under section 8 of the Limitation Act. He argued that as the pre-emptor-respondent cannot take advantage of sections 6 and 7 on the ground that he was a minor the present case is barred by limitation under section 8 of the Limitation Act. Section 8 of this Act provides that nothing in section 8 and 7 applies to suits to enforce rights of pre-emption, or shall be deemed to extend for more than three years from the cessation of the disability or the death of the person affected thereby, the period within which any suit must be instituted or application made. This section clearly indicates that within three years from the date of cessation of tile disability suit or proceeding must be instituted. This cannot be extended beyond the period of three years as provided' in sections 6 and 7 of the Limitation Act. Here in the present case before us the petitioner-pre-emptor-respondent attained majority on 16-5-87 and the miscellaneous case was filed on 15-5-90 which is admittedly within three years and it is in evidence that the petitioner-respondent came to know of the transfers from PW2 SalamatuIIah Khan and Habibur Rahman and thereafter he obtained the certified copies of kabalas from Comilla and filed miscellaneous case within four months as stipulated under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act So, on consideration of the materials on record and the relevant laws we find no force in the argument advanced by Mr Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed on the point of limitation. 

17. Admittedly, the pre-emptor-respondent is a co-sharer in the holding and from the evidence on record it is found that during his minority the lands were transferred in 1979 by five different kabalas without serving any notice upon him or upon his natural guardian and thereafter on getting the information the petitioner-respondent filed the present miscellaneous case for pre-emption within four months from the date of knowledge under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act and the miscellaneous case is not barred by limitation and in that view of the matter, we hold that the learned Subordinate Judge has not committed any wrong or illegality in allowing pre-emption and there is nothing to interfere with the impugned judgment

18. In this appeal the appellant earlier filed an application under Order 41, rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure for taking additional evidence and along with the petition filed three documents which were marked as Annexures-A, Band C to the petition. Annexure A is the certified copy of the plaint of Title Suit No. 117/86 renumbered as Title Suit No. 82 of 1990 pending before the Additional Assistant Judge, Chandpur and Annexure B is the application filed in the said suit by the present appellant under Order 14, rule 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure with a prayer for dismissal of the suit and Annexure C is the order-sheet dated 24-5-88 and 29-5-88. 

19. Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed submits that these documents were earlier taken into evidence by this Court by order dated 26-6-94 and the additional evidence may be considered as could not be taken into evidence before the trial Court. 

20. It is well-settled that under rule 27 of Order 41 of the Code of Civil Procedure the admissibility of the additional evidence is made to depend, not upon the relevancy or materiality to the issue before the Court of the evidence sought to be admitted, or upon the fact whether or not the applicants had an opportunity of adducing evidence at some earlier stage, but upon whether or not the appellate Court requires the evidence to enable it to pronounce judgment or for any other substantial cause. Additional evidence under this Rule should not be taken until the appellate Court has examined the evidence on record and has, after such examination come to the conclusion that the evidence as it stands is inherently defective. Until this is done, the appellate Court has no power to take additional evidence, nor even if the evidence offered be the evidence of new matter discovered after the Court of first instance had pronounced its judgment. It is well-settled that only when the appellate-Court requires it, or finds it needful" additional evidence can be admitted. Here 'In the present case the appellant failed to satisfy any of these conditions for accepting additional evidence. It has been argued by Mr Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed that these Annexures-A, Band C will prove the knowledge of the pre-emptor as regards the existence of the kabalas sought to be pre-empted. But as the matter before us can be disposed of without any additional evidence and as the appellant failed to satisfy the conditions on which the additional evidence may be adduced and as the additional evidence is not required by us for effective disposal of the appeal, we are not inclined to accept this additional evidence. 

21. Mr Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, submits that a Division Bench of this Court on 26-6-94 ordered for acceptance of the additional evidence and on the same date disposed of the appeal on merit which judgment was, of course, subsequently set aside by the same Bench on a review petition filed by the respondent on 16-8-94. It is submitted by Mr Ahmed that by this order dated 16-8-94 only the judgment delivered by the Bench on 26-6-94 was set aside and recalled but not the order accepting additional evidence. From the order dated 16-8-94 it appears that the Bench set aside the order dated 26-6-94 on which date the prayer for additional evidence was accepted and then judgment was delivered. We have also gone through the aforesaid judgment and it appears that in the four corners of the judgment nothing has been mentioned that for effective disposal of the appeal additional evidence was found necessary and accordingly additional evidence was allowed to be adduced, In that view of the matter, we hold that by order dated 16-8-94 the order of acceptance of additional evidence and the judgment have been cancelled and re-called as a whole and it also appears that the Bench has not felt any necessity of taking additional evidence as evident from the judgment itself. 

22. In that view of the matter, we find no force in the argument advanced by Mr Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed.

23. Thus, having given our anxious consideration to the materials on record and after hearing the learned Advocates of both the sides we finds no merit in this appeal and the same is liable to be dismissed.

 24. Court-fees paid are correct. 	

25. The appeal, is accordingly dismissed without any order as to costs. 

26. The judgment and order passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Chandpuri in Miscellaneous Case No. 59 of 1990 is hereby affirmed, 

Send down the lower Court records at once. 

End.

caseno:
Civil Revision No. 3257 of 1991 (Dhaka) 
Civil Revision No. 117 of 1990 (Barisal)
lawyer:
Md. Shamsul Haque, Advocate-----For the Petitioner. 
Syed Ziaul Karim, Advocate----- For the Opposite Party Nos.1 & 2.
parties:
Abdul Goni Kha ----- Petitioner
Vs
Md. Abdul Aziz Azizur Rahman and ors ----- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
