Upazila Revenue Officer, Patiya, Chittagong & others ------ Respondents
full_judgment: Mahmudul Amin Choudhury J: This Rule Nisi was issued calling upon Respondent Nos. 1 and 2 to show cause as to why the decision dated 10.4.85 given by Respondent No.1 in M L Case No. 5 of 1984 (Annexure-F to the petition) should not be declared to have been given without lawful authority and is of no legal effect. 2. Respondent No. 2 as the petitioner earlier filed an application on 3.9.84 under section 95A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act read with President's Order No. 88 of 1982 and President's Order No. 24 of 1972 for restoration of the mortgaged land comprising an area of .50 decimals before the Upazila Revenue Officer, Patiya, Chittagong against the petitioners and other heirs of late Abdus Samad Choudhury and that petition was registered as ML Case No. 5 of 1984-85. Their case is that the land originally belonged to respondent No. 2 and that one Yunus Mia, the predecessor-in-interest of respondent Nos.16 to 21 was the attorney and nephew of late Abdus Samad Choudhury, the predecessor-in-interest of the petitioner and respondent Nos. 3 to 12. Said Abdus Samad Choudhury was a Sub-Inspector of Police and was posted at Barisal and the said attorney and nephew used to manage his affairs and that on 13.12.1949 the said Yunus Mia purchased the scheduled land on behalf of Abdus Samad at a consideration of Taka 2,500 and got a deed in the benami of one Md. Ibrahim Miah, the predecessor of respondent Nos. 13 to 15 who was a close relation of said Abdus Samad Chowdhury and in the same sitting Md. Yunus Mia executed a deed of agreement to reconvey the land in question within three years to respondent No. 2 and that the case land was always in the possession of Abdus Samad Choudhury and after his death, his heirs namely, the present petitioners and respondent Nos. 3 to 12 possessed the same. It is also the case of the petitioners that ML Case was filed before the Upazila Revenue Officer, Chittgaong and that the said Yunus Mia died leaving behind respondent Nos.16 to 21 as his heirs and the said Ibrahim Mia died leaving behind respondent Nos. 13 to 15 who never possessed the land in question. It is also their case that transaction dated 13.12.49 was a mortgage and the petitioners along with respondent Nos.3 to 12 are bound to restore the case land to respondent No.2. After the case was registered before the Upazila Revenue Officer as ML Case No. 5 of 1984-85 notices were issued upon the present petitioners and respondents No. 3 to 21 and petitioner No.1 on receipt of the same filed a written objection on 24.10.84 stating, inter alia, that Md. Yunus Mia was never the attorney of late Abdus Samad Choudhury and neither the said predecessor nor the petitioners are bound by his acts and deeds and the said Yunus Mia was never authorised by any power of attorney, registered or otherwise, to act on behalf of Abdus Samad Choudhury and that the alleged transaction dated 13.12.49 took place long before the promulgation and operation of section. 95A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and President's Order No. 88 of 1972 and President's Order 24 of 1973 and the same does not come within the mischief of that section. Their further case is that Chapter V of the said Acquisition Act which contained section 95A of the Act came into operation in the District of Chittagong on 1.8.63 by Notification No. SR 116-63-609 dated 18.7.1963 while sub-section 1 of section 95 was amended by EP Ordinance XXI of 1969 on 18.11.1969 and the alleged transaction which took place under the Bengal Tenancy Act was repealed with effect from 1.8.63 and, as such, respondent No.2 was not entitled to any relief as prayed for in the aforesaid ML Case. Their further case is that section 95A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Ac which came into operation in 1972 covers an out and out sale with an agreement for reconveyance to be treated as complete usufructuary mortgage for a period not exceeding 7 years and that the instant transaction is an out and out sale and even assuming that there is an agreement, seven years period having been elapsed long before the promulgation of President's Order No.88 of 1972 the transaction is past and closed and beyond the jurisdiction of any Revenue Officer authorised for that purpose. The matter was heard by the Upazila Revenue Officer, Patiya, Chittagong who by his judgment and order dated 10.4.85 allowed the restoration of the mortgaged land The petitioners then moved this Court and obtained the present Rule. 3. Mr. S R Pal, the learned Counsel appearing on behalf of the petitioners, at the very outset submits that the transaction dated 13.12.1949 is out and out a sale and the purchaser never entered into any agreement with the vendor for reconveyance of the purchased land and he has also not authorised Yunus Mia to execute any agreement on his behalf. He submits that the facts and circumstance indicated that the transaction is out and out a sale and can never be construed as an usufructuary mortgage. He also submits that the transaction dated 13.12.49 is past and closed on the date of promulgation of President's Order 88/72 and respondent No. 1, the Upazila Revenue Officer acted without jurisdiction in allowing the application of respondent No. 2 treating the transaction as usufructuary mortgage. He submits that the said transaction governed by the Transfer of Property Act and the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act having no retrospective effect in the facts and circumstances of the case the same was wrongly applied in the present case before us. He further submits that in view of the provisions of law any transfer of a holding or part thereof by a raiyat by way of an out and out sale with an agreement to reconvey shall notwithstanding anything contained in the document relating to the transfer be deemed to be a complete usufructuary mortgage for period of maximum seven years and in the facts and circumstances of the instant case as the alleged transaction of 13.12.49 is not subsisting on the day of promulgation of President's Order No. 88 of 1972, Respondent No. 1 acted illegally and without jurisdiction in allowing the application because the alleged transaction was not alive on the date of the promulgation of the aforesaid President's Order and the transaction is very much past and closed. 4. Mvi. Mohammad Wahidullah, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the respondent No. 2, submits that the transaction dated 13.12.49 is nothing but a complete usufructuary mortgage as Yunus Mia was the authorised agent of the purchaser and he paid the money to the vendor on his behalf and he himself executed and registered a deed of agreement on the same date. He argued that the conduct of the parties at the relevant time indicate that the transaction is a complete usufructuary mortgage and as it is a complete usufructuary mortgage the Upazila Revenue Officer rightly allowed the case under section 95A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. 5. Section 95A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act was incorporated in the said Act by President's Order 88 of 1972 and it runs as follows: "95A. Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, any transfer of a holding or of a portion or share thereof, either by way of an out and out sale with an agreement to reconvey, or where the transferor receives from the transferee any consideration and the transferee acquires the right to possess, and to enjoy the usufruct of, such holding or portion or share thereof for a specified period of time in lieu of such consideration, shall notwithstanding anything contained in the document relating to the transfer, be deemed to be a complete usufructuary mortgage for a period not exceeding seven years and the provisions of section 95 shall apply to such transfer whether made before or after the date of commencement of the State Acquisition and Tenancy (Second Amendment) Order, 1972 (president's Order No. 88 of 1972)." 6. In the back-drop of the provision of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, let us examine the deed dated 13.12.1949 and also the deed of agreement executed and registered on that date. The deed of transfer dated 13.12.1949 is annexed to the petition as Annexure-B. We have carefully gone through the deed and it appears to us that one Mohammad Abdus Salam sold the land described in the schedule attached to this deed at a consideration of Taka 2,500.00 to one Md. Ibrahim Mia and the vendor received the consideration money through Md. Yunus Mia who is a relation of said Mvi. Ibrahim Mia. From a recital of Annexure-B it appears that it is an out and out sale deed. Now to make it a complete usufructuary mortgage something more is required to be done and that is an agreement to reconvey this land as provided under section 95A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. It is the definite case of the respondents that on 13.12.1949 a deed of agreement was executed and registered on behalf of said Mvi. Ibrahim Mia by his attorney Md. Yunus Mia who is a close relation of said Ibrahim Mia. A copy of this agreement is annexed to the petition as Annexure-C. We have carefully gone through Annexure-C and it appears that on 13.12.1949 the said Yunus Mia executed and registered a deed of agreement for reconveyance wherein he promised to get the land reconveyed to said Abdus Salam on his receiving Taka 2,500.00 (which is the consideration money of the aforesaid sale deed) within 3 years from 13.12.1949. It is the definite case of the respondent that this agreement made the said transaction a complete usufructuary mortgage. We have already found that the transaction dated 13.12.1949 is out and out a sale and now to make it a mortgage it must be found that Annexure-C is a valid agreement as required under section 95A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. From this Annexure-C it appears that the said Yunus Mia while executing and registering this Annexure-C has not styled himself as a constituted attorney of Mvi. Ibrahim Mia who purchased the disputed land. Nowhere in Annexure-C he mentioned that he acted on behalf of Mvi. Ibrahim Mia or that he acted as constituted attorney of Md. Ibrahim Mia, the vendee of the land in question. From the recital of Annexure-C it appears that Md. Yunus Mia promised that on receipt of consideration of Taka 2,500.00 he will get the mortgage redeemed and he will also get the land transferred to the vendor. It appears that this is a promise by one Yunus Mia who had no power of attorney on behalf of said Ibrahim Mia who purchased the land from Md. Abdus Salam. In such a case of mortgage the agreement to reconvey must have been executed and registered by the purchaser himself or at best by his attorney constituted for that purpose and unless that is done, an agreement by a third party cannot be constituted as an agreement as provided under section 95A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. After consideration of Annexures B & C, we are of the view that this Annexure-C has not in any way made Annexure-D a complete usufructuary mortgage as required under section 95A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Furthermore, before executing Annexure-C, the vendee ought to have appointed said Yunus Mia as his constituted attorney and when a land is in question the power of attorney ought to have been registered which is very much lacking in the present case before us. Thus after considering these two Annexures we hold that Annexure-B is nothing but an out and out sale deed and by Annexure-C the same has not been made a usufructuary mortgage to attract section 95A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. 7. It appears that Annexure-B was executed and registered on 13.12.1949. Now assuming for argument's sake that this annexure-B is a complete usufructuary mortgage where the provision of section 95A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act is applicable. Section 95A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act is in Part V of the aforesaid Act and this Part V of the said Act came into operation in the District of Chittagong on 1st August, 1963. The principle of law on the effectiveness of Part V of the Act is well settled in the case of Abdul Mannan & others vs. Kuloda Ranjan Mowali & others, reported in 31 DLR (AD) 195. The Appellate Division observed in that case that the retrospectivity of the provision of sub-section (2) of section 87 cannot be pushed beyond the date of commencement of Part V of the Act in the area where the accretion in question has taken place. Following this principle of law we hold that Part V of the said Act came into effect from 1.8.1963 and the provisions of section 95A which is within the Part V of the said Act cannot be pushed beyond 1.8.1963. Admittedly this transaction is dated 13.12.1949 and even if we take this transaction as complete usufructuary mortgage this cannot be redeemed under section 95A of the State Acquisition & Tenancy Act when on the date of coming into effect of Part V in Chittagong, the period of 7 years had already elapsed and, as such, the transaction is past and closed. Furthermore, from 1.8.1963 the Bengal Tenancy Act has been repealed in Chittagong. The transaction in question took place under the aforesaid Bengal Tenancy Act and the said Act was repealed on 1.8.1963 which is beyond the period as provided in Annexure-C and after the promulgation of President's Order 88 of 1972 the petition for redemption of mortgage as made out by the petitioner in the aforesaid case cannot be entertained as the matter has already became past and closed. 8. Mvi. Wahidullah, the learned Advocate relying on a decision reported in 34 DLR (AD) 237 (Abu Bakkar vs. Nazir Ahmed) submits that the present transaction is out and out a complete usufructuary mortgage. We have thoroughly considered his viewpoints and the decision as reported in 34 DLR (AD) and we are of the view that this decision has no manner of application in the facts and circumstances of the present case. In that decision the Appellate Division considered a document where it has been clearly mentioned that it was an instrument of mortgage. In that document it has been stated that it was a “মেয়াদী নির্নয় কবলা”. The original document Annexure-B of this present case clearly indicates that it was out and out a sale and on that count the same is distinguishable from the facts of the case mentioned above and, as such, that decision has no manner of application in the present case before us. 9. We have thoroughly considered materials on record particularly Annexures-B and C and we hold that Annexure-B is out and out a sale without any condition for reconveyance and the same cannot be construed as a complete usufructuary mortgage. The Upazila Revenue Officer illegally applied section 95A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and it requires interference by this Court. We hold that the transaction is out and out a sale and section 95A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act has no manner of application in the present case before us. 10. The Rule is, accordingly, made absolute without any order as to costs. The impugned order passed by the Upazila Revenue Officer in the aforesaid ML Case was passed without any lawful authority and is of no legal effect. End.

case_source: (From the Judgment and Decree dated 16.1.1985 passed by the High Court Division, Chittagong Bench, in Second Appeal No. 703 of 1962)
full_judgment:
Shahabuddin Ahmed, CJ.: I have gone through the judgments written by my learned brothers Mustafa Kamal and Latifur Rahman, JJ: I concur with the judgment of Mustafa Kamal. J.

MH Rahman J: I have had advantage of going through the judgments proposed to be delivered by my learned brothers Mustafa Kamal and Latifur Rahman, JJ: I concur with the judgment of Mustafa Kamal, J:

ATM Afzal J: I have perused the judgments prepared by my learned brothers Mustafa Kamal and Latifur Rahman , JJ: I concur with the judgment of Mustafa Kamal. J:

Mustafa Kamal. J: Defendant No.3 is the appellant in this appeal by special leave. Upon dismissal of the plaintiff-respondent's Title Suit No. 129 of 1958 by the learned Munsif, Cox's Bazar by judgement and decree dated 24-11-60 the learned Subordinate Judge, Chittagong by those dated 20-12-61 allowed the appeal and decreed the suit and in Second Appeal No. 703 of 1962 a learned Single Judge of the High Court Division, Chittagong Bench, affirmed those of the first appellate Court by judgment and decree dated 16-1-85.

5. The plaintiff-respondent's suit was for declaration of title and confirmation of possession or alternatively khas possession in the land of Schedule 2 to the plaint and for permanent injunction. It is his case that 6 kanis of land of Schedule 1 to the plaint belonged to Abdul Hakim and others in raiyati interest under landlord Badruddoza Chowdhury who obtained a rent decree in RS No. 780 of 1934 against the tenants and in execution thereof in Execution Case No. 721 of 1935 auction purchased the holding for Rs. 25/-. Abdul Hakim and others amicably gave up possession of Schedule 1 land after obtaining remission of balance of decretal dues and being sentenced to jail in a murder case left for Arakan and other places after release. Badruddoza possessed the Schedule 1 land for 2 years then settled by pattas 5 kanis out of 6 kanis land of the holding to proforma-defendant Nos. 21-30, the rest 1 kani being now in possession of his heirs proforma-defendant Nos. 31-34. The plaintiff purchased the suit Schedule 2 land from out of Schedule 1 land from proforma-defendant Nos 21, 22, 28 and 29 by a kabala dated 20-5-58 and is possessing the same. Abdul Hakim's heirs. the defendants, have no title and possession in the suit land. They are threatening the plaintiff with dispossession. Hence the suit.

6. The contesting defendant Nos. 1, 3 and 4, heirs of original tenant Abdul Hakim and others, contended in their joint written statement that there was never any auction-sale of the suit land and Badruddoza never obtained possession of the suit land. Abdul Hakim and others never left for Arakan. The alleged pattadars from Badruddoza never possessed the suitland on the basis of any patta. As such by purchase from some of them, the plaintiff also did not acquire any right, title and interest in the suit land and the contesting defendants never threatened him with dispossession. These defendants have been possessing the suit land from the time of their ancestors. The suit land has been recorded in the S.A. Khatian in their names. They have sold 2 kanis of land to one Kabir Ahmed Master. Yusuf Ali, an alleged pattadar, filed a criminal case against the defendants in respect of the suit, but he lost.

7. The trial Court found that the suit register of Rent. Suit No. 780 of 1934, Ext. 8 did not relate to the suit land. There is no certificate or writ of delivery of possession to show that the landlord obtained delivery of possession through Court. The story that the tenants obtained remission of balance decretal dues and after voluntarily surrendering possession left for Arakan is a fictitious one, because there is "no witness" and" no evidence" for the plaintiff to prove it. PWI admits in cross-examination that the defendants have their house on suit lands all along. The pattas Ext. 5 series have never been acted upon. There is no evidence of possession by the pattadars. The records of criminal cases and the revenue proceedings Ext. C series show that the contesting defendants and their predecessors were all along in possession of the suit land for more than 12 years and hence the suit is barred by limitation. On these material findings, the suit was dismissed.

8. The lower appellate Court also found that there was no sale certificate and and writ of delivery of possession and that Ext.8 did not show any particulars so as to connect it with the suit land. The rate of rent of the suit khatian also did not tally with the total claim of 4 year's rent as in Ext. 8. Yet the lower appellate Court held that the suit land was attracted by Ext. 8, because "it was not the case of the defendants that Abdul Hakim and others held any other land in their tenancy under Badruddoza Chowdhury." It further held that there was no documentary evidence to show that the tenants gave up their possession of the suit holding in favour of the landlord on gelling exemption from payment of balance decretal dues. But the subsequent conduct of the landlord, namely, the settlement with proforma-defendant Nos. 21-30 stand proved by the pattas Ext.5 series, Touzi Ext.3 series and Bakijai Ext.4 series, which are in the handwriting of Badruddoza Chowdhury. The lower appellate Court held that from the evidence of the plaintiff as PWI "nothing satisfactory regarding the possession of his vendors could be found". It also found that the story of Abdul Hakim and others leaving for Arakan was inconsistent. As regards the pattadar's possession, the lower appellate Court relied upon the evidence of P.Ws. 3,4 and 5, and on a consideration of Exts. 3, 4, C(2) to C(4) and Ext. G, found that the pattas were acted upon and that the pattadars possessed the suit land till they were dispossessed by the contesting defendants in 1956. The suit having been filed in 1958, it was not barred by limitation. Hence the trial Court's judgment and decree were set aside and the suit was decreed.

9. In second appeal, the High Court Division did not find anything to interfere with the findings of fact of the first appellate Court.

10. Leave was granted to consider whether in the absence of sale certificate, writ of delivery of possession and particulars to connect the suit land with the suit Register Ext. 8, the auction-sale was established by evidence. Leave was also granted to consider whether in view of the facts that as heirs of the original tenant the defendants' names were recorded in the RS and SA khatians, that the revenue authorities found the contesting defendants to be in possession of the suit land upon objections being raised by the plaintiffs vendors, that the criminal Courts too found possession of the contesting defendants in the suit land, it was imperative upon the lower appellate Court to decide the question of limitation from the standpoint as to whether the plaintiff filed the suit within 12 years of dispossession. The two Courts below concurrently found that the contesting defendants got their homestead in the suit land, a fact which belies the plaintiffs claim that Abdul Hakim and others had voluntarily surrendered possession of the suit land to the landlord and left for Arakan and leave was granted also to consider whether the story of voluntary surrender of possession was established by evidence.

11. Mr. Miah Abdul Gafur, learned Advocate-on-Record of the defendant No. 3 appellant, has reiterated the foregoing submissions at the time of the hearing of the appeal.

12. It may be mentioned in this connection that the lower Court's records including plaint, written statement, deposition and exhibited documents were destroyed and the High Court Division had no opportunity to look into the lower Court's records. The records have not been reconstructed and upon the application of the appellant, filing of paper book has been dispensed with at his risk. The respondent has also filed no paper book.

13. We do not attach much importance to the submission that no auction-sale of the suit land teak place because of the lack of particulars in Ext. 8. The suit land may have been auction-sold for arrears of rent and may have been auction-purchased by wr landlord as the recital of the pattas Ext. 5 shows, but it is not the plaintiffs case that the landlord took possession thereof through Court. The manner of the landlord's taking over of possession is by way of an amicable settlement with the tenants. Their balance decretal dues were remitted and they voluntarily surrendered possession. In the absence of a writ of delivery of possession, this assertion of the plaintiff is of critical importance and upon its proof or otherwise the subsequent story of patta, possession and sale will rise or fall. Every case has its own evidentiary centre of gravity and this particular manner of obtaining possession is the foundation upon which the plaintiffs edifice of subsequent title and possession is built. It is not enough for the plaintiff to prove that the landlord somehow took possession of the suit land and the pattadars were also somehow in possession of the tenant's surrender cannot be proved, then the suit cannot be decided merely on the believability of the pastas, touzis and bakijais. It will be putting the cart before the horse. The superstructure will collapse if the foundation is not laid.

14. It is on this central issue of the plaintiffs case that the finding of the trial Court is positive, unequivocal and unambiguous. The trial Court found that there is 'no witness' and 'no evidence' on this point and therefore the plaintiffs story is fictitious. The appellate Court below did not reverse this finding at all. There is nothing in the treatment of the evidence of PWs 1, 4 and 5 that they spoke at all about the tenants surrendering possession to the landlord. Only PW 3, according to the lower appellate Court, said' that the recorded tenants surrendered their possession in favour of the Malik. There is no finding that PW 3 was a witness to surrender. In cross-examination PW 3 is equivocal about surrender and the lower appellate Court itself is tentative in its acceptance of the evidence of PW 3. It leaves the question of surrender for future consideration by saying ' if at all there was a surrender'. Then, after summing up the evidence of both sides, the lower appellate Court skipped the issue and gave a finding on the superstructure, namely, that the landlord 'really' entered into khan possession and the pattadars were also in possession leaving the issue of manner of entry completely unresolved. The lower appellate Court failed to realise that the landlord and the pattadars could not be in possession, unless the tenants voluntarily surrendered. Then, introducing a story of possession of the defendants from 1956 the lower appellate Court, by way of narrating a story and not by way of coming to a finding of fact, states, "Now it appears that the contesting defendants, after they gave up their possession in favour of the landlord  etc." This is what is called begging the question.

15. Thus the lower appellate Court completely missed the real issue and the High Court Division too failed to locate the central focus of the plaintiffs case. The lower appellate Court proceeded to decide the case on pasta, touzi, bakizai and dakhilas, little realising that the superstructure cannot stand without foundation.

<u>16. Both the Courts below concurrently found from copies of orders in criminal cases and revenue proceedings, Ext. C series that the contesting defendants were in possession of the suit land. But the two Courts differed with regard to the period of possession. The trial Court noticed the report of the Revenue Circle Officer on local inquiry stating that the heirs of Abdul Hakim and others were in possession of lands of suit holding all along since RS operation (in 1940 or 1941, i.e. a few years after the pattadars allegedly went into possession). The lower appellate Court did not consider the RS record at all, which stands in the name of the contesting defendants, but considered only the SA khatian Ext. D and held that the defendants came to possess the suit land since 1956. The lower appellate Court has not explained why this particular year was selected for the purpose of this finding. No. averment in the plaint has been referred to, no evidence either. This finding seems to be a gratuitous finding in favour of the plaintiff. The lowest common denominator in the judgments of the two Courts below is that the plaintiffs vendors were out of possession in 1956. When the plaintiff purchased the suit land in 1958 he never obtained possession. When he filed the suit in 1958 he and his vendors were already out of possession. The case is squarely covered by Article 142 of the First Schedule to the Limitation Act. The trial Court holds that the suit is barred by limitation, because the defendants are in possession since the time of their ancestors. The lower appellate Court holds that the suit in not barred by limitation because the plaintiffs vendors were dispossessed in 1956, which is neither the plaintiffs case nor the defendants, and which is clearly based on conjecture and surmise, not on evidence on record. The plaintiff, having been concurrently found to be out of possession at the time of the institution of the suit was required to allege in the plaint and prove at the trial that he and his vendors were dispossessed within 12 years before the institution of the suit. He has failed to do either. The suit is thus barred by limitation. The lower appellate Court and the High Court Division failed to decide the issue in its correct perspective.</u>

For all the above reasons the appeal is allowed without any order as to costs.

Latifur Rahman J. I have gone through the judgment of my learned brother Mustafa Kama, J. and I find it difficult to agree with him as in the Second Appeal the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division affirmed the Judgment of the lower appellate Court, which to my mind does not suffer from any error of law or defect in procedure calling for any interference by this Division.

19. Before going into the facts of this case, I may mention that the exhibits and other relevant papers could neither be seen by us nor by the High Court Division as the lower court records and the exhibits were destroyed. Hence, in all fairness, I think, that the factual aspect of the matter as arrived by the last court of fact and affirmed by the High Court Division should be accepted by me.

20. This appeal by defendant No. 3 is directed against the judgment and decree passed by the High Court Division, Chittagong Bench, in Second Appeal No. 703 of 1962 affirming the judgment and decree of the Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Chittagong in Title Appeal No. 538 of 1960 reversing the judgment and decree passed in Title Suit No. 129 of 1958 of the Court of Munsif, Cox's Bazar.

21. Plaintiff filed a suit for declaration of title, confirmation of possession or in the alternative for recovery of khas possession in the suit land and also for permanent injunction. Plaintiffs case, in short, is that, the suit land belonged to Abdul Hakim and others in raiyati interest under landlord Badruddoza Chowdhury predecessors-in-interest of proforma-defendants 31-34 as recorded in RS. khatian. The landlord obtained a decree in Rent Suit No. 780 of 1934 against the tenants and in Rent Execution Case No. 721 of 1935 auction purchased the holding for Rs. 25/- after exempting the balance of the decretal dues as the tenants were unable to pay the balance of Tk.129/- and odd. In such circumstances, the tenants gave up possession amicably in favour of landlord Badaraddoza Chowdhury who held the land for two years in khas possession after merging the raiyati with his Taluki interest. Abdul Hakim and others were entangled in a murder case and they were sentenced to jail and after release from jail they left for Arakan and other places. The landlord settled 5 kanis of lands out of entire 6 kanis of the holding toproforma defendants 21-30 on 26.1.1937 by pattas and the rest one kani is in possession of the heirs of Badaraddoza namely, proforma defendants 31-34. Plaintiff purchased the suitland of Schedule 11 of the plaint out of the land of Schedule I from proforma defendants 21, 22, 28 and 29 by kahala on 30.5. 1958 and is in possession of the same. According to the plaintiff, Abdul Hakim, others and their heirs defendants have no title and possession in the suit land. The positive case of the plaintiff, is that, defendant No. 17, a pleader's clerk who conducted the suit at his instance the defendants threatened the plaintiff with dispossession as defendant No. 17 failed to purchase the land.

22. Defendants 1, 3 and 4 contested the suit by filing a joint written statement. They contended that the suit land of Schedule 1 of the plaint belonged to their predecessors-in-interest Abdul Hakim and others and that there was never any alleged auction sale of the holding and landlord Badaraddoza never got khas possession in the same. Defendants also assert that the subsequent patta holders namely, defendants 21-30 did not get khas possession in the disputed land and consequently the plaintiff also did not acquire any right, title and interest in the disputed land. The defendants' positive case, is that, they are in possession of the suit land from the time of their predecessors. In the recent settlement operation the suit lands had been recorded in the name and possession of the defendants. It is further asserted in the written statement that Yusuf Ali, proforma defendant No. 30 flied a criminal case being Criminal case No. 374 of 1956 on 13.7.56 under section 447 of the Penal Code against the defendants with the allegation that the defendants dispossessed Yusuf Ali from the suit land and the said criminal case was dismissed for non-prosecution by said Yusuf Ali.

23. The Trial Judge dismissed the suit and the learned lower appellate Court reversed the findings of the trial Court and decreed the suit. In Second Appeal the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division affirmed the judgment and decree of the learned lower appellate Court.

24. Leave was granted primarily to consider whether the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division in Second Appeal in proper appreciation of oral and documentary evidence on record correctly affirmed the findings of fact of the lower appellate Court which reversed the findings of the trial Court

25. The learned Munsif disbelieved the plaintiffs case of auction sale of the holding at the instance of landlord Badaraddoza and his khas possession for 2 years and subsequent resettlement by him by pattas to the plaintiffs vendors. The trial Judge also found that the defendants are in continuous possession since the time of their predecessors. Thus, according to the learned Munsif, the suit was barred by limitation as the heirs and successors of the original tenants were in possession for more than 12 years.

26. On the contrary, learned lower appellate Court believed the auction sale of the holding by landlord and khas possession by the landlord for two years and subsequent settlement of the suit land to proforma defendant Nos. 21-30, vendors of the plaintiff. The lower appellate Court found title with the plaintiff by virtue of his kabla dated 30.5.1958. The lower appellate Court found that the plaintiffs vendors were in possession and the plaintiff though purchased the suit land in 1958 by kabala, was not in present possession of the disputed land and further found that the defendants were not in continuous possession from the time of their predecessors-in-interest, but they were in possession since 1956 and consequently the suit was not barred by limitation and decreed the suit.

27. At the outset, I like to mention that all the material findings of fact arrived at by the trial Court were duly reversed by the lower appellate Court by giving reasons thereof. The learned Single Judge of the High Court Division also affirmed those findings of the lower appellate Court and refused to interfere with the findings of fact of the lower appellate Court as there was no error of law or procedure in arriving at such findings. I have very carefully gone through the judgment of the trial Court and the lower appellate Court and find that whatever findings the trial Court had given, the lower appellate Court had taken note of those and after giving his own reasonings had discarded the same. In that view of the matter, the pertinent question that comes" up in deciding the appeal, is whether the learned lower appellate Court committed any error of law or procedure in reversing the judgment of the trial Court. Further, I also find that the most material question in this case is the question of possession of the respective parties in the suit land. This material question on point of possession had been arrived at by the trial Court without at all considering the oral evidence of the defendants' witnesses. As a matter of fact, the trial Court only considered the oral evidence of the plaintiffs witnesses but nowhere I find that any consideration was made in respect of the defendants' witnesses who spoke of defendants' possession. On the other hand, I find from the judgment of the lower appellate Court that not only documents were considered but independently both the plaintiffs witnesses and the defendants' witnesses were considered to arrive at a finding with regard to the period of possession of the parties which is of vital importance in the case. Thus, the lower appellate Court having decided the case, on consideration of the oral and documentary evidences, I think it will be wholly uncalled for this Division to interfere into the findings of fact.

28. Hereinbelow, I will consider the respective case of the parties to see whether, the High Court's judgment or for that matter the judgment of the lower appellate Court suffers from any error of law or illegality.

29. Admittedly, the disputed land originally belonged to Abdul Hakim and others in their raiyati right. The plaintiffs case, is that, the holding was auction purchased in Rent Suit No. 780 of 1934 and the same was taken possession in Rent Execution Case No. 721 of 1935. In the instant case neither the sale certificate nor the writ of delivery of possession was produced by the plaintiff, except the certified copy of the suit register Ext. 8 to prove the auction sale. From Ext. 8 it appears that the land was auction purchased by decree holder for Rs. 25/- only, leaving a balance of Rs. 129/9/-including the cost of the execution. It is the plaintiffs case, that the tenants Abdul Hakim and others could only pay Rs. 25 and Abdul Hakim and others after taking exemption of the balance dues from the landlord gave up possession in favour of the landlord as their financial condition was precarious and landlord went into amicable possession. Along with this the learned lower appellate Court considered a very material aspect, that it was not the case of the defendants that Abdul Hakim and others held any other land in their tenancy under Badaraddoza Chowdhury other than the suit land. Thus the lower appellate Court held as follows "

"So in all fairness, I can say that the suit referred to in exhibit 8 was instituted by the landlord against Abdul Hakim and others in the very holding which is in dispute here."

The learned lower appellate Court considered Ext. 8, the suit register as the basis for institution of the auction sale in respect of the holding itself as Abdul Hakim and others had no other lands under the landlord Badaraddoza Chowdhury.

30. The learned Munsif disbelieved the auction sale only because the sale certificate and the writ of delivery of possession were not produced by the plaintiff in this case. But the lower appellate Court considered the suit Register Ext. 8 and the oral evidence on record and found that the auction sale was for Rs. 25.00 only and after exempting the balance dues, the landlord took amicable possession of the suit land. There is unequivocal statement in the plaint that the tenants took exemption of the balance decretal amount and gave khas possession in favour of the landlord and the landlord took possession thereon. As a matter of fact there is clear averment in the plaint that Badaraddoza after auction purchase got possession in the entire land as far back as 23 years and was in khas possession of the holding of the land by merging the same with the taluki land of the landlord and there was no existence of raiyati land. This was the averment in the plaint and in order to prove khas possession of the landlord evidence was also led that the landlord was in possession for 2 years through one Sarafat Ali. The learned lower appellate Court rightly pointed out that there was no documentary evidence that the landlord took delivery of possession, as sale certificate and the writ of delivery of possession were not produced in the case. But the lower appellate Court considered the oral evidence and other attending facts and circumstances in arriving at a finding that the suit register exhibit 8 relates to the suit and the landlord in the circumstances of the present case went into possession amicably after giving exemption of the dues to the tenants. The lower appellate Court considered the evidence of PW 3 Abdul Jabbar admittedly who was a Tahsildar of the Estate of landlord Badaraddoza Chowdhury since 1932 upto War period. This witness testified that the suitland was auctioned purchase by Badaraddoza for Rs. 25.00 after giving exemption to the tenants who gave up possession and the landlord was in possession for 2 years through borgadars. This witness in cross-examination also admitted that when the tenants gave up the land in favour of Badaraddoza he was present and that was 24/25 years back and one Sarafat Ali was the borgadar for 2 years. The lower appellate Court found this witness PW 3 to be a competent witness as he was the Tahsildar of the Estate and defendants' witnesses also admitted that this witness PW 3 was a Tahsilder of the Estate at the relevant time.

31. The trial Court, on the other hand, held in its judgment to this effect.

"Seeing these defects, I think, in the plaint a story had been introduced that the tenant Abdul Hakim and others amicably gave up possession of suit lands of Khatian 252 and obtained remission of the balance of the decretal dues as the landlord auction purchased the land for Rs. 25.00 only."

32. This observation of the trial Court is nothing but a product of surmise and conjecture, as because there is clear statement in the plaint and the plaintiff had adduced oral evidence in support of the khas possession of the landlord, Badaraddoza Chowdhury as indicated above. It is surprising to note that a positive statement in the plaint has been commented by the learned Munsif in such a manner. Further, the trial Court found that.

"Though there is no mention in the plaint still at the time of hearing of the suit the plaintiff side tried to say that Badaraddoza possessed suit lands through one Sarafat Ali for two years, after auction purchase as alleged."

This observation of the trial Court is not correct, as because in the plaint there is clear averment that the suit land was taken in khas possession by the landlord and the same was merged with the Taluki land of the landlord and the landlord was in khas possession. Further the evidence of PW 3 also shows that the landlords were in khas possession for 2 years. The appellate Court further found that there was mentioned in the plaint regarding the khas possession by the landlord and re-settlement thereafter to proforma defendant Nos. 21-30 by pattas Exts. 5-5(c). The appellate Court also considered that in these pattas there are recitals of the rent suit and the execution case as in Exhibit 8 and also clear recitals that the landlord was in khas possession by letting out temporarily. The learned lower appellate Court believed these pattas to be genuine documents and held that those were acted upon. But the trial court disbelieved these pattas as because only proforma defendant No. 30 Yusuf Ali deposed in the case as PW 5. The appellate Court as a Court of fact took a contrary view as taken by the trial Court with respect to these documents. Further, the lower appellate Court also considered Touzi Ext. 3 series and Bakiza Ext. 4 series proved to have been written in the handwriting of landlord Badaroddaza. The appellate Court believed these documents and ultimately found that the plaintiff purchased in 1958 by kabala from the heirs of some of the Pattandars and also from some of pattandars. Further, the appellate Court found that Sarafat Ali was in temporary possession for 2 years under the landlord before he let out these lands to plaintiffs vendor as far back as 24/25 years. The appellate Court also considered Ext. 7 by which one of the pattandars transferred a portion of his patta land by way of Waqf. to a mosque in the locality in the year 1952. The learned lower appellate Court as a court of fact believed these documents and found that plaintiffs vendors had title and possession from whom plaintiff purchased by kabala in 1958. The plaintiff in reality came in picture in 1958 after his purchase. It appears from the evidence of PW 5 Yusuf Ali (proforma defendant No. 30) one of the Pattandars that he brought a criminal case on 13.7.56 being criminal Case No. 374. of 1956 under section 447 of 11e Penal Code against the defendants for dispossessing him. In his testimony PW 5 stated that he did not proceed with the case as defendant No.1 gave up possession in his favour. In the written statement the defendants admitted that the case was not proceeded by proforma defendant No. 30. The lower appellate Court believed this judgment of this criminal case, Exhibit C(2), and the copies of orders in criminal cases Exts. C,C(1). The lower appellate Court as a court of fact considered both the oral and documentary evidences and came to a positive finding that the plaintiffs vendors were in possession of the disputed land and the trouble arose in 1956 when the criminal cases as per Exhibit C(2), and the proceeding under section 107 of the Criminal Procedure Code (Ext. C) was started by defendant No. 31 in 1957. Thus, according to the lower appellate Court, the trouble arose in 1956 when the defendants entered into possession of the same. The trial Court as a court of fact found the defendants to be in continuous possession since the time of their predecessors-in-interest. Whereas the lower appellate Court on consideration of the oral and documentary evidences found that the trouble arose in 1956-57, when the defendants went into possession. This is a factual determination by the lower appellate Court and the appellate Court believed this material aspect regarding possession of the parties. The lower appellate Court also considered the present mutation proceedings, that is, Exhibit C(3) and C(4) dated 6.6.1959 which speaks of the possession of the defendants. Since the lower appellate Court found possession of the defendants from 1956, these mutation proceedings of 1959 were not found to be the basis of continuous possession of the defendants since the time of their predecessors-in-interest.

<u>33. A reference to the oral evidence on record will show that the trial Court did not at all speak: a word in the judgment about the defendants' witnesses. It is really surprising that the court of original jurisdiction which was to decide this most vital question of possession of the defendants did not at all consider any of the defendant's witnesses before arriving at the decision that the defendants were in continuous possession since the time of their predecessors-in-interest. In such circumstances, I must refer to the relevant oral evidence on record to see whether the determination of the period of possession by the appellate Court was correct, which was of prime importance in the case. PW 1 Nur Mohammad, the plaintiff came in picture after purchase in 1958 and as such the appellate Court did not give any importance to the testimony of this witness. The material evidence is of PW 3 Abdul Jabbar, a Tahsildar of the Estate whose evidence had already been mentioned earlier in my judgment in extenso. PW 4 Nazir Ahmed, the grand son of one of the proforma-defendants, Yusuf Ali testified that they possessed the land and paid rents. PW 5 Yusuf Ali, (proforma defendant No. 30) testified that they possessed the land for 24/25 years after patta and I defendants never possessed the land. DW 1 Musa Ali, defendant No.3 (present appellant) testified that his father died 20/22 years back and they are in possession of the suit land. DW 2 Badruzzaman was disbelieved by the appellate Court as the evidence of possession given by him was found to be vague by the appellate Court. DW 3 Golam Kader was disbelieved by the lower appellate Court as he had no knowledge as to which lands were possessed by Abdul Hakim and others. The appellate Court found him to be a tutored witness. DW 4 only proved dakhilas, exhibit A series of the defendants. The appellate Court disbelieved these dakhilas as the l origin and genuineness of these dakhilas were very suspicious. DW 5 Sabar Ali was aged about 13 years at the time of deposition and as such both the appellate Court and the High Court Division found that he was not a competent witness to depose about defendants' continuous possession. This being the nature of evidence, the lower appellate Court as a court of fact held that the defendants were not in continuous possession but only entered into possession in 1956-57. Thus, with regard to the evidence on record, the material issue as to the period of possession was correctly determined by the appellate Court Consequently, the suit is not barred 1 by limitation under Article 142 of the Limitation Act Article 142 speaks of recovery of possession of immovable property when the plaintiff while in possession of the property has been dispossessed within 12 years from the institution of the suit. This Article applies only where the plaintiff, while in possession has been dispossessed In the four comers of the plaint no where it has been stated that the plaintiff had been dispossessed. The averment in the plaint is that, the defendants are threatening the plaintiff with dispossession though the defendants have got no right, title and interest in the suit land. There being no assertion of dispossession this suit does not come under Article 142 of the Limitation Act The plaintiff though found to have acquired title was not in present possession and the suit having been filed within 12 years from acquisition of title and the defendants having failed to establish their adverse possession for more than 12 years, this suit cannot be governed by Article 142 of the Limitation Act. The plaintiff having proved his title he is entitled to a declaration of title and recovery of khas possession. The present suit really comes within the purview of Article 144 of the Limitation Act. As the suit is governed under Article 144 of the Limitation Act, the plaintiff is entitled to the decree on proof of his title only. I may also point out that the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division correctly , decided the question of limitation in this case by holding as follows :</u>

<u>"In that view of the matter also there is no error on the part of the appellate Court to find that the suit is not barred by limitation. The plaintiff is out of possession but his predecessor-in-interest was in possession within 12 years previous to the institution of the suit"</u>

34. Thus, there being no misreading and misappreciation of the evidence as found by the last court of fact and affirmed by the High Court Division, I cannot lawfully and legitimately set aside the findings of fact in this appeal.

35. Consequently, the appeal is dismissed and the suit is decreed without any order as to cost.

Before parting with the case, it may be mentioned that original records having been lost and there being no reconstruction of the records, I obtained the ordinary copy of the plaint, written statement and the typed copy of the deposition of the witnesses from the learned Advocate for the respondents and have gone through them in this case.

Order of the Court.

By majority decision the appeal is allowed without any order as to costs.

End.

lawyer:
AKM Faiz, Advocate -----For the Petitioner. 
Jyotirmoy Narayan Deb with Md. Anowarul Islam, Advocates ----- For the Opposite Party No.1
parties:
Shamser Ali alias Mobassar Ali being dead his heirs 1(A). Ashik Tara Begum ----- Petitioner
Vs.
Toimus Ali and others ----- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule is directed against the judgment and order dated 9-3-91 passed by the Assistant Judge, Chhatak allowing the application filed by the opposite party No. 1 for possession of pre-empted land after condoning the delay in Miscellaneous Case No. 6 of 1990 of the said court.

2. The opposite party No. 1 filed an application under section 96 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 for preemption of the case land against the purchaser-petitioner. The case of the opposite party No. 1, in short, is that the land mentioned in the application for pre-emption under section 96 was sold by the petitioner's husband Mobassar Ali by a registered kabala and after knowing the same the opposite party No.1 filed the application under section 96 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act for pre-emption including the petitioner-purchaser on the ground that the opposite party No.1 is a contiguous owner and accordingly, he prayed for pre-emption of the case land. The said Miscellaneous Case No. 197 of 1970 was allowed by his judgment and order dated 12-12-81 ex parte when the present petitioner was found to be absent on repeated calls at the time of hearing of the case.

3. Against the aforesaid ex-parte order dated 12-12-81 passed by the Court of Assistant Judge, Chhatak, Sunamganj in Miscellaneous Case No. 197 of 1970 the husband of the petitioner filed a Miscellaneous Case No. 5 of 1982 which was subsequently renumbered as 69 of 1984 under Order 9, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the ex parte order dated 12-12-81 but on a subsequent date the said Miscellaneous Case No.69 of 1984 was transferred to newly created upazila Chhatak. The said Misc. Case 69 of 1984 was also dismissed for default on 17-12-86. The opposite party No.1 subsequently filed an application under section 96(9)(c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 on 15-2-90 for getting delivery of possession of the pre-empted land on the ground, amongst others, that the pre-emption case was allowed on 12-12-81 by ex parte order and after ex parte order there was a Miscellaneous Case under Order 9, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure to set aside the ex parte order dated 12-12-81 but the same was also dismissed for default on 17-2-86 and as such, the opposite party No. 1 herein prayed for recovery of khas possession of the pre-empted land.

4. The learned Assistant Judge, Chhatak received the said application on 15-2-90 and registered the same as Miscellaneous Case No. 6 of 1990 on 25-2-90. Thereafter the Assistant Judge by his order dated 25-2-90 directed the present petitioner to show cause as to why the said application should not be allowed. On 25-9-90 the petitioner herein appeared and filed written objection and contended, inter alia, that the Miscellaneous Case No. 6 of 1990 is not maintainable and the same is also barred by limitation. The learned Assistant Judge, Chhatak after hearing the parties and perusing the evidence on record was pleased to allow the said Miscellaneous Case No. 6 of 1990 by the impugned order dated 9-3-91 after condoning the delay under section 5 of the Limitation Act. In fact, the prayer for recovery of khas possession of the preempted land was allowed by order dated 9- 3-91.

5. As against the impugned judgment and order dated 9-3-91 passed by the Assistant Judge, Chhatak in Miscellaneous Case No. 6 of 1990, the petitioner herein moved this court and obtained the present Rule.

6. Mr AKM Faiz, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the purchaser-petitioner, submits that the said Miscellaneous Case No. 6 of 1990 ought to have been filed within three years from the date of cause of action in as much within three years from the date when the Miscellaneous Case filed by the present petitioner was dismissed ex parte on 17-2-86. The learned Advocate submits that no period of limitation is provided in section 96(9)(c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act for filing application for possession. Therefore, residuary Article 181 of the Limitation Act would apply. Accordingly, the opposite party No.1 should have filed the Miscellaneous Case for possession of the pre-empted land within three years from 17-2-86 as per Article 181 of the Limitation Act. The opposite party No. 1 herein having not filed the application for possession of the pre-empted land within three from 17-2-86 the application, numbered as Miscellaneous Case No. 6/90, is ex facie barred by limitation. The learned Advocate further submits that where residuary Article 181 applies section 5 of the Limitation Act would not apply. Therefore, the learned Assistant Judge has committed an error of law in condoning the delay under section 5 of the Limitation Act and allowing the application under section 96(9)(c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950.

7. The opposite party No. 1 by filing counter-affidavit has denied the material allegations made in the petition and, contended, mainly that section 5 of the Limitation Act is applicable in an application filed under section 96(9)(c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act.

8. Mr JN Deb, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite party No. 1, submits that section 151 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 is very clear and has provided that sections 6, 7, 8, and 9 and sub-section (2) of section 29 of the Limitation Act, 1908 (Act IX of 1908) shall not and, subject to the provisions of part V of this Act, the remaining provisions of the Limitation Act shall, so far as applicable, apply to all suits, appeals and applications arising under the said part. Application of sections 6, 7, 8 and 9 and sub-section (2) of section 29 of the Limitation Act has been excluded, other provisions including section 5 of the Limitation Act have been made applicable under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. The learned Advocate further submits that opposite party No.1 filed as many as 9 medical certificates showing that he was a TB patient and the delay for filing the application under section 96(9)(c) of the said Act has been explained sufficiently. The Court having been satisfied with the explanation has condoned the delay under section 5 of the Limitation Act and allowed the application under section 96(9)(c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. Therefore, no error of law has been committed in condoning the delay in preferring the application under section 96(9) (c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950.

<u>9. I have heard the learned Advocates of the respective parties, perused the judgment passed by the courts below as well as relevant provisions of law. It appears. that section 151 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 is very clear in as much as section 5 of the Limitation Act has been made applicable in a proceedings under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 including the proceeding under section 96(9)(c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. For convenience the relevant portion of section 151 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act is quoted as under:</u>

<u>"151.(1) Sections 6, 7, 8 & 9 and sub-section (2) of section 29 of the Limitation Act, 1908, (Act IX of 1908) shall not and, subject to the provisions of part V of this Act, the remaining provisions of the former Act, shall so far as applicable, apply to all suits, appeals and applications arising under the said part."</u>

<u>Therefore, it appears that the application of section 5 of the Limitation Act in a proceeding under section 96(9)(c) State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 has been made applicable. Whereas applications of sections 6, 7, 8 & 9 and sub-section (2) of section 29 of the Limitation Act, 1908 have been clearly made not applicable in a proceeding under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Mr. JN Deb, the learned Advocate on this point has submitted that in a proceedings under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act section 5 of the Limitation Act has been made applicable in the case of Abdul Hamid Kazi vs. Abdul Jabbar Jamadar and others reported in 26 DLR (SC) 68.</u>

10. Mr AKM Faiz, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner, on the other hand, has submitted that when residuary Article 181 of the Limitation Act has been applied in this particular case, there is hardly any scope for application of section 5 of the Limitation Act and therefore he submits that the learned court has committed an error of law in condoning the delay under section 5 of the Limitation Act and allowing the application. The proceeding under section 96(9) (c) of the State Acquisition & Tenancy Act is identical to that of the proceedings for execution of decree and the period of limitation is three years and the learned Court having not followed the aforesaid principles of law he has committed an error of law in condoning the delay in a proceeding under section 96(9)(c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act.

<u>11. It appears that section 96(9)(c) of the State Acquisition & Tenancy Act clearly provides that "(c) the Court on further application of such applicant or applicants may place him or them, as the case may be, in possession of the property vested in him or them "but no period for making such application has been provided in the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Therefore, the residuary Article 181 of the Limitation Act shall apply. To this the learned Advocate for the opposite party No. 1 also concedes that Article 181 is applicable in the case of application under section 96(9)(c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act but relying on section 151 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act the learned Advocate on behalf of the opposite party No. 1 has submitted that section 5 of the Limitation Act has not been ousted from application or filing application under section 96(9) (c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The opposite party No.1 having successfully shown that he was suffering from TB for a long time and he has adduced as many as 9 medical certificates that he was prevented by sufficient cause for not being able to file the application under section 96(9)(c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act within prescribed period of 3 years, the trial Court in his discretion has condoned the delay in filing the application under section 96(9)(c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The learned Advocate on behalf of the petitioner though has vehemently argued that once residuary Article 181 of the Limitation Act has been applied, there is no scope for application of section 5 of the Limitation Act but he has failed to cite any decision in support of his arguments. Mr JN Deb, the learned Advocate, on the other hand, has cited a decision reported in 26 DLR (SC) 68 wherein section 5 of the Limitation Act has been made applicable in a proceeding under section 96(9)(c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Therefore, I am of the view that application of section 5 of the Limitation Act in a proceedings under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act has not been barred where residuary Article 181 of Limitation Act has been made applicable. The Court may in his discretion condone the delay in preferring an application under section 96(9)(c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act provided the condition of section 5 of the Limitation Act is fulfilled.</u>

12. In this particular case the trial Court has considered the facts and circumstances of the case in as much as the applicant was suffering from TB for a long time and the opposite party produced as many as 9 medical certificates, and the court has believed the same and for that cause he has condoned the delay in preferring the application under section 96(9)(c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. Under the aforesaid facts and circumstances of the case and position of law as enumerated in section 151 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, I find hardly any reasons to interfere with the same.

13. In the result the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs. The judgment and order dated 9-3-91 passed by the Assistant Judge, Chhatak in Miscellaneous Case No.6 of 1990, allowing the application under section 96(9)(c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act after condoning the delay under section 5 of the Limitation Act in filing the application under section 96(9)(c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, is hereby affirmed.

The order of stay granted on 19-5-91 by this court is hereby vacated.

End.

lawyer:
MA Matin with MA Jabbar, Advocates-----For the petitioner.
BK Das Advocate-s-----For the Opposite Parties.
parties:
Abdul Khaleque ----- Petitioner
Vs
Abdur Noor and others ----- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
This revisional application arises out of the judgment and order dated 30-5-79 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Sylhet in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 81 of 1977 passed by the learned Munsif 1st Court, Sylhet in Miscellaneous Case No-76 of 1970 arising out of a an application for pre-emption under section 24 of the Non- Agricultural Tenancy Act. 1949.

2. The facts leading to the issuance of this Rule are that the petitioner instituted the said Miscellaneous Case under section 24 of the East Bengal Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act stating that the land appertains to khatian No. 554 and it constituted a residential homestead with adjuncts not connected with agriculture. The petitioner is a co-sharer in the case land and the opposite party No. 1 is a stranger and no notice was served about the sale dated 5-11-69, as such, the petitioner is entitled to pre-empt the case land. The said pre-emption case was opposed by the opposite party No. 1 contending that petitione's case is not maintainable under section 24 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act inasmuch as the purchase made by two separate Kabalas and two separate cases ought to have been filed by the petitioner. On a review of the evidence led, the trial Court allowed the pre-emption case in favour of the petitioner against which the opposite party No. 1 preferred appeal and the lower appellate Court upon hearing the parties reversed the decision of the trial Court and allowed the appeal. The petitioner being aggrieved by the aforesiid decision of the lower appellate Court moved this Court and obtained the present Rule.

3. Mr. MA Matin the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner submits that the trial Court, upon consideration of the materials on record, found that the case holding being homestead is not connected with agriculture and the court of appeal below having not averted to said finding without is signing cogent reason wrongly arrived at a decision that the homestead adjunct with chara land being situated in rural area is connected with agriculture and thereby committed error of law resulting in an error in the decision causing failure of justice.

4. It has been further submitted that the lower appellate Court misconstrued the provision of section 96 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950 as well as the provision of section 24 of the East Bengal Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act 1949 and thereby misdirected himself in disallowing the petitioner's application for pre-emption causing failure of justice.

5. Mr. BK Das, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite party No. 1, on the other hand, contends that the suit holding comprised of two plots namely the plot No. 1975 as chara land and plot No. 1936 as a homestead land and because of two plots being included in the same Khatian No. 544 and situated in the rural area are agricultural homestead land and, as such, the right of pre-emption will accrue under section 96 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and not under Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act and therefore the court of appeal below rightly held that the petitioner's application under section 24 of the East Bengal Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act was not maintainable.

6. Mr. Das has further argued that if it is accepted that the homestead plot is unconnected with agriculture then the right of pre-emption accrues under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act and the other plot attached to the homested being as agricultural land then the pre-emption under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act will arise and in that situation a question of partial pre-emption in respect of the lands of the same Khatian will arise and it is not permissible as a settled principle of law.

7. While repelling the above contention of Mr. BK Das, Mr. Matin, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner, having clborated his submission, argued that the word holding as defined in sub-section (13) of section 2 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act means "a parcel or parcels of land or an undivided share thereof held by a raiyat or an under-raiyat and forming the subject of separate tenancy" and as such the word "Homestead" as defind in sub-section (14) of section 2 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and the word "non-agricultural land" as defined in sub-section (4) of section 2 of the Non agricultural Tenancy Act are both holding with regard to the nature and character of the holding. Mr. Matin thus contends that the suit holding being homestead with adjuncts is unconnected with agriculture held by a non-agricultural tenant is pre-emptible under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act.

8. Mr. Matin has made further argument to impress upon me that there being no reference of the word "municipality" either in definition of homestead or in the definition of non agricultural land, the right of pre-emption as provided in the afore-said two enactments depend upon the nature and character of the land or holding and not of their situation either in the rural area or within municipality.

9. The only point that has arisen in this revision is whether an application for pre-emption under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act in respect of the homestead with adjunct lands not within municipal area is maintainable.

10. I have heard the learned Advocates of both sides, perused the records as well as the judgments of the courts below. In order to appreciate the above submissions of the learned Advocates, the various definition clauses occurring in both the enactments are necessary to be quoted below.

11. The word holding has been defined in sub-section (13) of section 2 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act which means a parcel or parcels of land or an undivided share thereof held by a raiyat or an under raiyat and forming the subject of separate tenancy.

12. The sub-section (14) of section 2 defines "Homestead" in the following terms:

"Homestead means a dwelling house with the land under it, together with any courtyard, garden, tank, place of worship and private burial or cremation ground attached and appertaining to such dwelling house, and includes any out buildings used for the purposes of enjoying the dwelling house or for purpose connected with agriculture and such lands within well defined limits, whether vacant or not, as are treated to be appertaining thereto."

13. The expression non-agricultural land has been defined in section 2(4) of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act:

"It means land which is used for purposes not connected with agriculture or horticulture and includes any land which is held on lease for purposes not connected with agriculture or horticulture irrespective of whether it is used for any such purposes or not.

14. It appears that suit holding comprised of two plots being homestead plot and the plot adjuncts (Chara land) thereto. The court of appeal below in consideration of the materials on record as a final court of fact found that "the suit land is situated in the rural area. Chara land indicates that vegetables, paddy seedlings, etc are grown therein and the chara land is an adjunct to the homestead, From the above local feature we can safely conclude that homestead is connected with the agriculture".

<u>15. It appears that the suit holding being homestead with adjuncts is admittedly situated in the rural area. It is true that a homestead land cannot be a raiyati land (agricultural land) even if some part of the land is used for gardening or growing vegetables or for the purposes connected with agriculture but the fact remains the holding does not lose the character of homestead. In the instant case the determining factor is of the situation of homestead. Considering the nature and character of the suit holding and its situation. I am of the view that the homestead with adjunct is very much connected with agriculture. There is nothing on record to show the suit holding was used for the purposes not connected with agriculture and it is non agricultural land for all practical purposes. It is profitable to cite a case of Lutfun Nahar vs. Syeeda Hashmat Ara Begum reported in 21 DLR 633 to find a complete answer to the arguments advanced by Mr. Matin. Their Lordships held in the aforesaid decision that homestead within a municipality or non-agricultural land cannot be pre-empted under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Having considered the facts and circumstances of the case and in view of principle laid down in the said decision. I hold that the suit holding being homestead situated in the rural area is an agricultural land and section 96 of the Act is only available.</u>

16. In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs.

End.
